n: Renal Tubular Acidosis & Drugs and the Kidney

qs.q: Define renal tubular acidosis (RTA).
qs.a:
• A number of pathophysiologically distinct entities of tubular function
  • Common feature: non-anion-gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis

qs.q: Mention the types of RTA with the site of the defect.
qs.a:
• Type I (distal, hypokalaemic): defect of H⁺ secretion at the DCT
  • Type II (proximal): impaired HCO₃⁻ reabsorption at the PCT
  • Type IV: aldosterone defect → hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism or aldosterone resistance of the distal nephron

qs.q: How does the anion gap help in metabolic acidosis? How do you differentiate renal from GIT causes of normal-AG acidosis?
qs.a:
• AG = cations − anions; normal ≈ 12 ± 2
  • Most metabolic acidosis → high AG; RTA → normal AG (Cl⁻ rises to compensate)
  • Normal-AG acidosis = renal or GIT cause → differentiate by urinary anion gap: positive = renal cause

qs.q: Mention the causes of distal (type I) RTA.
qs.a:
• Inherited: autosomal dominant & autosomal recessive
  • Autoimmune / inflammatory: Sjögren's syndrome, sarcoidosis
  • Urinary tract: obstruction, UTI, interstitial cystitis
  • Drugs: amphotericin B, lithium

qs.q: Mention the features of distal (type I) RTA.
qs.a:
• Unable to acidify urine despite systemic acidosis → urine pH > 5.5
  • Positive urinary anion gap (↓ ammonium excretion)
  • Hypokalaemia
  • Hypercalciuria → nephrocalcinosis & stone formation
  • Chronic: osteomalacia (long-term buffering of acidosis by bone)

qs.q: Explain why chronic type I RTA is associated with hypercalciuria and osteomalacia.
qs.a:
• Persistent H⁺ excess → body buffers it with alkaline salts of bone
  • Calcium & phosphate leave bone → ↑ in blood → excreted → hypercalciuria
  • Bone becomes soft → osteomalacia

qs.q: Mention the features of proximal (type II) RTA.
qs.a:
• Defect in HCO₃⁻ reabsorption at PCT
  • Usually with Fanconi features: glycosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, uricosuria
  • DCT intact → urine acidification preserved → urine pH < 5.5
  • No stones, no nephrocalcinosis

qs.q: Mention the causes of proximal (type II) RTA.
qs.a:
• Isolated: hereditary dysfunction of basolateral Na⁺–HCO₃⁻ cotransporter
  • Fanconi syndrome: inherited or acquired → myeloma, chronic interstitial nephritis (Chinese herbal nephropathy)
  • Drugs: ifosfamide, tenofovir

qs.q: Mention the treatment of proximal RTA and its main precaution.
qs.a:
• Large doses of bicarbonate: 5–15 mmol/kg/day
  • Bicarbonate aggravates hypokalaemia (intracellular K⁺ shift) → give potassium too

qs.q: Mention the causes and features of type IV RTA.
qs.a:
• Causes: hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism, or distal nephron resistance to aldosterone
  • Hyporeninaemic type: volume expansion, mostly elderly / diabetic patients with CKD
  • Hyperkalaemia (aldosterone normally excretes K⁺)
  • Mild non-AG acidosis, urine pH ≈ 5.5, positive urinary anion gap

qs.q: Compare type I, type II and type IV RTA.
qs.a:
Feature Type I (distal) Type II (proximal) Type IV
Site / defect H⁺ secretion – DCT HCO₃⁻ reabsorption – PCT Aldosterone ↓ / resistance
Serum K⁺ ↓ Hypokalaemia ↓ (worse with HCO₃⁻) ↑ Hyperkalaemia
Urine pH > 5.5 < 5.5 ≈ 5.5
Stones / nephrocalcinosis Yes (hypercalciuria) No No
Associations Sjögren, amphotericin B Fanconi, myeloma Elderly diabetic CKD

qs.q: Mention the types of Fanconi syndrome.
qs.a:
• De Toni–Debré–Fanconi syndrome (cystinosis) – childhood
  • Adult Fanconi syndrome

qs.q: Mention the features of cystinosis (De Toni–Debré–Fanconi syndrome).
qs.a:
• Inherited metabolic disorder of childhood
  • Widespread cystine deposits (kidney, eye) + tubular renal defects
  • Death usually from renal failure, may be with renal rickets

qs.q: Mention the causes of adult Fanconi syndrome.
qs.a:
• Idiopathic inherited
  • Heavy metal poisoning, some antibiotics (tetracycline)
  • Renal transplantation
  • Multiple myeloma & amyloidosis
  • Wilson disease

qs.q: Mention the substances lost in urine in Fanconi syndrome.
qs.a:
• Phosphate · amino acids · glucose · bicarbonate · uric acid
  • Mnemonic: "PAG-BU" (Phosphate, Amino acids, Glucose, Bicarbonate, Uric acid)

qs.q: Explain how Fanconi syndrome leads to renal osteodystrophy.
qs.a:
• Phosphaturia → hypophosphataemia → osteodystrophy
  • Proximal tubular dysfunction → ↓ 1α-hydroxylase → ↓ calcitriol → ↓ Ca²⁺ absorption → impaired mineralisation
  • Presents in adult life as renal osteodystrophy; relatively good prognosis

qs.q: When do you modify or stop a drug according to GFR?
qs.a:
• GFR > 60: continue the usual dose
  • GFR < 60: reduce the dose
  • GFR < 15: stop the drug

qs.q: Mention the factors that predispose the kidney to toxic (drug) injury.
qs.a:
• Kidneys receive ≈ 20% of resting cardiac output
  • High metabolic rate of tubules (active transport) → vulnerable
  • Large glomerular capillary surface area → trapping of immune complexes / in-situ Ag–Ab reactions
  • Selective concentration: aminoglycosides in cortex (PCT transport); phenacetin in medulla (countercurrent)
  • Conversion to less soluble forms with acidification (urate → uric acid) → tubular obstruction

qs.q: Mention the mechanisms of drug-induced nephropathy with an example of each.
qs.a:
• ↓ Renal perfusion: NSAIDs
  • Renal vasculitis: penicillins, antithyroid drugs
  • Immune glomerular injury: D-penicillamine
  • Immune interstitial injury: allopurinol, cephalosporins, anti-TB, sulphonamides, ciprofloxacin
  • Toxic cell injury: aminoglycosides (ATN), amphotericin B (type I RTA / ATN), analgesic abuse (chronic IN), tetracycline (Fanconi + chronic IN)
  • Tubular obstruction: acute hyperuricaemic nephropathy (tumour lysis after chemotherapy)
  • Ureteric obstruction: methysergide → retroperitoneal fibrosis

qs.q: Mention drugs causing toxic tubular cell injury.
qs.a:
• Aminoglycosides → ATN
  • Amphotericin B → type I RTA or ATN
  • Analgesic abuse → chronic interstitial nephritis
  • Tetracycline → Fanconi syndrome + chronic interstitial nephritis

qs.q: Mention the questions asked to decide whether a drug dose needs adjustment in kidney disease.
qs.a:
• (1) Is the drug primarily excreted through the kidneys?
  • (2) Are increased drug levels likely to cause toxicity?
  • (3) If both → with renal failure adjust the dosing regimen
  • Critical with long half-life + small therapeutic index (e.g. digoxin)

qs.q: Mention antibiotics needing major / moderate dose reduction and those that should not be used in renal failure.
qs.a:
• Major reduction: amikacin, gentamicin, quinolones, tetracycline, vancomycin
  • Moderate reduction: carbenicillin, kanamycin, cefazolin, cephaloridine, streptomycin, cephalothin, cloxacillin, co-trimoxazole, methicillin, oxacillin, penicillin G, ticarcillin
  • Not used: bacitracin, chlortetracycline, nitrofurantoin (renal tubular defect)
  • Major = ¼ of dose (100 → 25); moderate = ½ (100 → 50)

qs.q: Define interstitial nephritis.
qs.a:
• A form of AKI from immunologically mediated lymphocytic infiltration of the renal interstitium, often with eosinophils
  • Swelling / oedema and inflammatory cells between the kidney tubules
  • May be acute (sudden) or chronic (gradual)

qs.q: Mention the causes of acute interstitial nephritis (AIN).
qs.a:
• Drugs = 70–75% (allergic reaction); > 100 drugs
  • Antibiotics: penicillins, sulpha · diuretics: thiazides, frusemide · allopurinol
  • NSAIDs · proton pump inhibitors
  • Infections (4–10%): Legionella, Leptospira, CMV, Streptococcus, M. tuberculosis
  • Immunological: SLE

qs.q: Mention the causes of chronic interstitial nephritis.
qs.a:
• NSAIDs · lead · irradiation
  • Sickle cell anaemia
  • Chronic pyelonephritis · gouty nephropathy
  • Mnemonic: "SLING-P" (Sickle, Lead, Irradiation, NSAID, Gout, Pyelonephritis)

qs.q: Mention the groups at risk for interstitial nephritis.
qs.a:
• Older adults (multiple drugs, confusion about combinations); drug reactions more severe & more permanent damage
  • Chronic use of OTC pain relievers
  • Autoimmune disease: SLE, Sjögren
  • Sarcoidosis

qs.q: Mention the clinical presentation of drug-induced AIN.
qs.a:
• Non-specific acute renal dysfunction: nausea, vomiting, malaise
  • Oliguric or non-oliguric
  • Classic allergic triad: rash, fever, eosinophilia
  • Many patients are asymptomatic (found by low-grade proteinuria)

qs.q: Mention the investigations of interstitial nephritis.
qs.a:
• CBC: eosinophilia
  • Blood urea & creatinine · ABG (acid–base)
  • Urinalysis: eosinophiluria, WBCs, RBCs, WBC casts (sterile pyuria)
  • 24-h urine protein: usually < 1 g
  • Abdominal US: exclude obstructive uropathy
  • Renal biopsy = definitive diagnosis

qs.q: When is renal biopsy needed in AIN?
qs.a:
• Biopsy = definitive diagnosis
  • Often unnecessary if renal failure clearly follows a drug and improves immediately on stopping it
  • Done if unexplained or rapidly progressive renal affection

qs.q: Mention the treatment of interstitial nephritis.
qs.a:
• Stop the offending drug (most important) + treat the cause
  • Corticosteroids → speed recovery (SLE, Sjögren, allergic)
  • Chronic: supportive – control BP
  • Dialysis / transplantation if irreversible (anuria, severe acidosis)

qs.q: Mention the prognosis of interstitial nephritis.
qs.a:
• Function usually improves on stopping the drug; some scarring is common
  • Worse when the drug is an NSAID
  • Gradual inflammation → progresses to involve both kidneys → irreversible

qs.q: What is TINU syndrome? Mention its diagnosis.
qs.a:
• Tubulointerstitial nephritis + uveitis (bilateral non-granulomatous anterior uveitis)
  • Pathogenesis unknown: autoantigen to modified CRP, delayed hypersensitivity, T-cell predominance
  • Uveitis usually mild, nephritis self-limited
  • Diagnosis: uveitis + renal involvement + biopsy consistent with AIN

qs.q: Define a renal cyst and mention the types of cystic kidney disease.
qs.a:
• Closed sac lined by epithelium, filled with fluid / semi-solid material; mostly benign
  • Types: ADPKD · ARPKD · medullary cystic kidney disease · medullary sponge kidney · simple cysts · acquired cystic disease (ESRD on dialysis)

qs.q: Mention the features of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD).
qs.a:
• Commonest inherited nephropathy; manifests at 30–40 y
  • Both kidneys affected (one may be earlier)
  • Extrarenal: hepatic & pancreatic cysts, cardiovascular (MVP), berry aneurysm
  • Gene: chromosome 16 (short arm) in 85%
  • Pathology: enlarged kidneys, multiple non-communicating cysts compressing parenchyma

qs.q: Mention the clinical manifestations of ADPKD.
qs.a:
• Dull aching loin pain (↑ renal size)
  • Acute loin pain / haematuria (haemorrhage or infection in a cyst)
  • Renal stones (uric acid)
  • Hypertension (RAS activation)
  • Chronic renal failure
  • Hepatic cysts, mitral valve prolapse
  • Subarachnoid haemorrhage (rupture of berry aneurysm) → brain MRI
  • Exam: large irregular kidneys ± hepatomegaly

qs.q: Mention the features of autosomal recessive PKD (ARPKD).
qs.a:
• Previously infantile PKD
  • Cystic dilation of renal collecting ducts
  • Defective hepatobiliary ductal plate → congenital hepatic fibrosis → portal hypertension (check spleen, varices)

qs.q: Mention the features of medullary cystic kidney disease (MCKD).
qs.a:
• Autosomal dominant; cysts in the medulla; kidneys shrink
  • Impaired function in teens; ESRD at 20–70 y
  • Defect in distal & collecting tubules → polyuria, polydipsia, stunted growth
  • Suspect: unexplained CKD + strong family history → genetic testing (MUC1, chr 1q21)
  • Childhood equivalent: juvenile nephronophthisis

qs.q: Mention the features of medullary sponge kidney.
qs.a:
• Cysts in collecting ducts (Bellini ducts) of one or both kidneys; may be congenital / familial
  • Nephrocalcinosis in 50%; stones & recurrent UTI
  • Kidney failure rare; no cure → reduce stones & infections

qs.q: Differentiate acquired cystic kidney disease from ADPKD.
qs.a:
Feature Acquired cystic disease ADPKD
Setting ESRD on dialysis Inherited
Family history Absent Present
Kidney size Small to normal, smooth Large, cystic contour
Complication Carcinoma Berry aneurysm, CKD

qs.q: Mention the features of simple renal cysts.
qs.a:
• Mostly asymptomatic, discovered accidentally on imaging
  • Most often > 50 years; solitary or multiple, bilateral
  • Clear content, thin wall → follow-up only

qs.q: Mention the investigations of cystic kidney disease.
qs.a:
• Examination: high BP, enlarged kidneys
  • Urine: blood or protein · blood tests: kidney function
  • Renal ultrasound (detects even small cysts)
  • CT / MRI if US inconclusive
  • Genetic testing: ADPKD gene chr 16 (family studies, not routine); MKD → MUC1
  • Negative screen for acquired cystic disease → rescreen when symptomatic or after 3–5 y

qs.q: Mention the treatment of cystic kidney disease.
qs.a:
• No cure → manage symptoms & reduce complications
  • ADPKD: control BP (ACEi/ARB with caution), treat stones, clots, UTI; laparoscopic surgery for pain
  • MCKD: fludrocortisone + high-sodium diet (hypothetical → suppress abnormal renin); ESRD → dialysis / transplant
  • Medullary sponge kidney: reduce stones & UTIs
  • Choice depends on type, severity, complications, renal failure, age & general health

qs.q: Mention the disorders of the large renal vessels.
qs.a:
• Renal artery stenosis · renal vein thrombosis · athero-embolic disease
  • Present with HTN, pain, haematuria, proteinuria

qs.q: Mention the causes of renal artery stenosis.
qs.a:
• Atherosclerosis (75%): old > 50, smoker, DM, HTN; affects ostia / proximal renal artery
  • Fibromuscular dysplasia (25%): females < 40 y; affects middle & distal parts
  • Others: dissecting aortic aneurysm, vasculitis (Takayasu), trauma

qs.q: Explain how renal artery stenosis causes hypertension.
qs.a:
• Stenosis → renal hypoperfusion → activation of JGA → renin
  • Angiotensin II → vasoconstriction; aldosterone → salt & water retention → ↑ BP
  • Ischaemia, inflammation, fibrosis → kidney injury

qs.q: Mention the clinical clues suggesting renal artery stenosis.
qs.a:
• Sudden onset HTN before 30 or after 50 y
  • Refractory HTN (uncontrolled on 3 drugs)
  • Recent worsening of HTN (short duration)
  • Deterioration of renal function with ACEi / ARB
  • Recurrent (flash) pulmonary oedema / HF
  • Asymmetrical kidney size on US (> 1.5 cm)
  • Unexplained hypokalaemia ± metabolic alkalosis
  • Abdominal (flank) bruit

qs.q: Mention the investigations of renal artery stenosis.
qs.a:
• Renal US / duplex (asymmetry, resistance; operator-dependent)
  • Plasma renin activity
  • Renal angiography = gold standard (needs contrast; allows intervention)
  • MR angiography: in renal impairment → avoid contrast nephropathy
  • Renal scan

qs.q: Mention the treatment of renal artery stenosis.
qs.a:
• Medical (unilateral): ACEi, ARB, β-blocker; monitor creatinine & K⁺ (stop if creatinine ↑ > 30%) → alternatives e.g. CCB
  • ACEi & ARB NOT allowed if bilateral RAS suspected
  • Surgical: arterial reconstruction · balloon dilatation with stent · nephrectomy

qs.q: Compare atherosclerotic RAS and fibromuscular dysplasia.
qs.a:
Feature Atherosclerosis Fibromuscular dysplasia
Frequency 75% 25%
Patient Old, smoker, metabolic syndrome Female, < 40 y
Site Ostia & proximal renal artery Middle / distal parts

qs.q: Mention the causes of renal vein thrombosis (Virchow's triad).
qs.a:
• Endothelial damage: endovascular intervention or surgery
  • Venous stasis: dehydration (more in males), compression / kinking by retroperitoneal fibrosis or neoplasm
  • Hypercoagulability: nephrotic syndrome (esp. membranous), antiphospholipid syndrome, protein C & S or antithrombin deficiency

qs.q: Mention the clinical picture of renal vein thrombosis.
qs.a:
• Flank pain & tenderness
  • Haematuria
  • Rapid decline in renal function
  • Massive proteinuria

qs.q: Mention the diagnostic methods of renal vein thrombosis.
qs.a:
• Doppler US: more sensitive than US alone, less accurate than CT
  • CT angiography: 100% sensitive
  • MR angiography: more expensive
  • Venography

qs.q: Mention the treatment of renal vein thrombosis.
qs.a:
• Anticoagulant (heparin / LMWH → warfarin, INR control) + treat the cause
  • Endovascular thrombolysis: severe cases
  • Nephrectomy: life-threatening complications
  • IVC filters: prevent thrombus migration

qs.q: Describe athero-embolic renal disease.
qs.a:
• Showers of cholesterol-rich material from an ulcerated atheromatous plaque
  • From aorta / renal artery after catheterisation or angioplasty
  • Anticoagulants or thrombolytics may precipitate it
  • Presents as rapidly progressive renal failure + systemic embolisation (stroke, livedo reticularis)

qs.q: Compare renal artery stenosis, renal vein thrombosis and athero-embolic disease.
qs.a:
Feature RAS RVT Athero-embolic
Cause Atherosclerosis / FMD Virchow's triad Cholesterol emboli
Presentation Refractory HTN, hypoK, bruit Flank pain, haematuria, proteinuria RPRF + systemic emboli
Key test Angiography (gold standard) CT angiography (100%) —
Treatment ACEi/ARB/BB, stent Anticoagulant, lysis, filter —

qs.q: Define thrombotic microangiopathy and mention the associated diseases.
qs.a:
• Injured endothelial cells thickened, swollen or detached from arterioles & capillaries → haemolysis + thrombocytopenia + renal affection
  • TTP · HUS · scleroderma renal crisis · antiphospholipid syndrome · preeclampsia/HELLP · malignant HTN · HIV · radiation nephropathy

qs.q: Mention the laboratory evidence of haemolysis in TMA.
qs.a:
• ↑ indirect bilirubin, LDH, reticulocytes
  • Blood film: schistocytes
  • Platelet activation → microthrombi → thrombocytopenia

qs.q: Mention the types of haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS).
qs.a:
• Diarrhoeal (typical): children, after diarrhoea; Shiga-toxin E. coli O157:H7
  • Non-diarrhoeal (atypical): any age; complement dysregulation

qs.q: Mention the presentation of HUS.
qs.a:
• MAHA + renal impairment
  • Cramping abdominal pain & vomiting
  • Most cases children < 5 y (adults susceptible)
  • Neurological (less than TTP): dysphasia, hyperreflexia, blurred vision, seizures, encephalopathy
  • Fever typically absent

qs.q: Mention the treatment of HUS. Why are antibiotics and antimotility drugs avoided?
qs.a:
• Avoid antibiotics (→ more toxin release) and antimotility drugs (→ more toxin absorption)
  • Supportive: fluids, correct acid–base
  • Atypical severe: eculizumab (complement inhibitor)
  • Severe: haemodialysis & exchange transfusion

qs.q: Mention the pentad of TTP.
qs.a:
• MAHA · thrombocytopenia · neurological symptoms · fever · renal failure
  • Mnemonic: "FAT RN" (Fever, Anaemia (MAHA), Thrombocytopenia, Renal, Neuro)
  • Not all five need to be present

qs.q: Mention the cause, associations and treatment of TTP.
qs.a:
• Classic idiopathic TTP: ADAMTS13 deficiency → large VWF multimers not cleaved → platelet aggregation → microthrombi
  • Associations: infection, malignancy, intense inflammation (pancreatitis)
  • Treatment: plasma transfusion / plasma exchange; immunomodulators (rituximab, anti-CD20)

qs.q: Define HELLP syndrome and mention its course and treatment.
qs.a:
• Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets – dangerous pregnancy complication
  • Renal failure in half of patients
  • Usually resolves after delivery (small % post-partum)
  • Glucocorticoids ↓ inflammatory markers; plasma exchange if refractory to steroids / delivery

qs.q: Mention the features of antiphospholipid syndrome.
qs.a:
• Predisposition to systemic thrombosis (arterial & venous) + fetal morbidity (recurrent abortion)
  • Antibodies: antiphospholipid, anticardiolipin, lupus anticoagulant, anti-β2 glycoprotein
  • Suspect in young patients with stroke / DVT, especially females

qs.q: Mention the renal involvement in APS.
qs.a:
• Vascular compartment = main site
  • Suspect RVT in lupus anticoagulant + nephrotic-range proteinuria
  • Hypertension common; progression to ESRD can occur

qs.q: How do you investigate primary vs secondary APS?
qs.a:
• Primary: lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2 GP; if negative → repeat after 12 weeks
  • Secondary (SLE): ANA, anti-dsDNA; activity → C3 & C4

qs.q: Mention the treatment of APS.
qs.a:
• Lifelong anticoagulant (heparin/LMWH → warfarin, INR 2–3 + low-dose aspirin; pregnancy: LMWH + low-dose aspirin)
  • Glucocorticoids in accelerated HTN
  • Immunosuppression & plasma exchange in catastrophic APS (sudden failure of > 3 organs)

qs.q: Compare HUS, TTP, HELLP and APS.
qs.a:
Feature HUS TTP HELLP APS
Defining MAHA + renal Pentad H + EL + LP Thrombosis + fetal loss
Cause Shiga E. coli; < 5 y ADAMTS13 ↓ Pregnancy Antiphospholipid Abs
Fever Absent Present — —
Treatment Supportive Plasma exchange Delivery, steroids Lifelong anticoagulant

qs.q: Define chronic kidney disease (CKD).
qs.a:
• Renal structure or function abnormalities present for ≥ 3 months
  • GFR < 60, or > 60 with evidence of kidney damage (albuminuria, casts)
  • Gradual, progressive, irreversible loss of renal function
  • Symptoms when 75% of function is lost; dialysis needed due to accumulation of uraemic toxins

qs.q: Mention the risk factors for CKD.
qs.a:
• Family history of heritable renal disease
  • Diabetes · hypertension
  • Autoimmune disease
  • Old age
  • Prior episode of ARF

qs.q: Mention the causes of CKD.
qs.a:
• Long-standing DM – diabetic nephropathy (most common)
  • Long-standing systemic HTN
  • Chronic GN · chronic interstitial nephritis
  • Obstructive uropathy · analgesic nephropathy
  • Lupus nephritis · congenital polycystic kidney · gout · unknown

qs.q: Describe the pathophysiology of CKD (final common pathway).
qs.a:
• Causes (DM, HTN, GN, cystic, tubulointerstitial) → loss of nephron mass
  • Remaining nephrons → structural / functional hypertrophy (hyperfiltration)
  • Mediated by vasoactive molecules, cytokines, growth factors, RAS
  • → sclerosis of remnant nephrons → further nephron loss (vicious circle)

qs.q: Mention the GFR stages of CKD.
qs.a:
Stage Description GFR (ml/min/1.73 m²)
G1 Kidney damage, normal or ↑ GFR ≥ 90
G2 Mildly decreased 60–89
G3 Moderately decreased 30–59
G4 Severely decreased 15–29
G5 End-stage renal disease < 15 (or dialysis)

qs.q: Mention the albuminuria categories of CKD.
qs.a:
• A1: ACR < 30 mg/g – normal to mildly increased
  • A2: 30–300 mg/g – moderately increased (microalbuminuria)
  • A3: > 300 mg/g – severely increased
  • CKD classified by cause + GFR + albuminuria (KDIGO heat map: green → yellow → orange → red)

qs.q: Mention the symptoms of CKD according to stage.
qs.a:
• Stage 1–2: asymptomatic
  • Stage 3–4: anaemia, HTN, ↓ appetite, Ca/PO₄ abnormalities, Na/water/K/acid–base abnormalities
  • Stage 5: all accentuated → overt uraemia

qs.q: Mention the GIT manifestations of CKD.
qs.a:
• Nausea & vomiting · hiccough
  • Hepatitis · gastritis · reflux oesophagitis
  • GIT bleeding
  • Due to accumulation of uraemic toxins

qs.q: Mention the causes of anaemia in CKD.
qs.a:
• Erythropoietin deficiency
  • ↓ intake / haematinic deficiency: iron, B12, folate
  • ↓ RBC life span + toxic bone marrow depression
  • Blood loss: haemodialysis, GIT
  • Bone marrow fibrosis (hyperparathyroidism)
  • Mostly normochromic normocytic

qs.q: Mention the causes of bleeding tendency in CKD.
qs.a:
• Capillary fragility
  • Platelet dysfunction (thrombasthenia) due to uraemic toxins

qs.q: Mention the cardiovascular and chest manifestations of CKD.
qs.a:
• CVD is the most common cause of death in CKD
  • Pericarditis (haemorrhagic effusion) · systolic & diastolic dysfunction · arrhythmia
  • HTN (Na retention)
  • Chest: pneumonia, non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, acidotic (Kussmaul) breathing

qs.q: Mention the endocrine and metabolic manifestations of CKD.
qs.a:
• Hyperglycaemia (insulin resistance) but ↓ insulin requirement in diabetics (↓ insulin clearance)
  • Thyroid: ↓ T4 → T3 conversion
  • 2ry & 3ry hyperparathyroidism (hyperphosphataemia)
  • Sex hormones: ↓ testosterone; disturbed oestrogen, progesterone, FSH
  • Fat: ↑ TG, ↓ HDL · Protein: ↑ catabolism (wasting, gout)

qs.q: Mention the types / mechanism of renal osteodystrophy.
qs.a:
• ↓ Active vitamin D → hypocalcaemia → osteomalacia
  • Phosphorus retention → 2ry hyperparathyroidism
  • 2ry hyperparathyroidism → osteoclastic activity, cysts, marrow fibrosis → osteitis fibrosa cystica
  • Long-standing hyperparathyroidism → ↑ bone density → osteosclerosis
  • ↑ Ca × PO₄ → metastatic calcification

qs.q: Mention the neurological manifestations of CKD.
qs.a:
• Neuropathy: motor, sensory (glove & stocking), autonomic (impotence, gastroparesis, orthostatic hypotension)
  • Uraemic myopathy, uraemic myoclonic jerks
  • Convulsions: disequilibrium syndrome (rapid dialysis → brain oedema)
  • Uraemic encephalopathy; stroke (HTN + bleeding tendency)
  • Carpal tunnel · restless legs · dialysis dementia

qs.q: Mention the skin manifestations of CKD.
qs.a:
• Itching: hyperphosphataemia & hyperparathyroidism
  • Urea frost: whitish powder on skin
  • Recurrent pyogenic infection
  • Earthy look = yellow (urochrome) + pallor (anaemia) + brown (melanin)
  • Bronze colour: haemosiderosis

qs.q: Mention the acid–base, electrolyte and urinary manifestations of CKD.
qs.a:
• Hypocalcaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hyperkalaemia
  • High anion-gap metabolic acidosis (H⁺ retention)
  • Na & water retention
  • Urinary: early polyuria & nocturia; features of chronic pyelonephritis / obstruction

qs.q: Mention the points differentiating CKD from acute renal failure.
qs.a:
• Creatinine rise: gradual (months–years) vs sudden (days–weeks)
  • Hypocalcaemia & anaemia: mostly in CKD
  • US: small kidneys (< 9 cm) in CKD
  • BUN/creatinine ratio > 20:1 → acute
  • Importance: ARF can be reversible

qs.q: Mention CKD with normal or enlarged kidneys on ultrasound.
qs.a:
• Diabetic nephropathy · polycystic kidney · amyloidosis · kidney tumour (± hydronephrosis)
  • Mnemonic: "DAPT" (Diabetes, Amyloid, Polycystic, Tumour)

qs.q: Mention the laboratory findings of CKD.
qs.a:
• ↑ Blood urea (normal 10–20 mg/dl) · ↑ creatinine (0.5–1.2) – better indicator
  • ↓ Creatinine clearance (24-h urine; normal > 100 ml/min)
  • ABG: metabolic acidosis · CBC: normocytic anaemia
  • ↑ K⁺, ↑ PO₄, ↓ Ca, ↑ PTH; Na ↑ in 80% (RAAS), ↓ in 20% (Na losers)
  • Urine: broad casts, fixed low specific gravity 1010 (isosthenuria)

qs.q: Mention the imaging findings in CKD.
qs.a:
• US: shrunken kidneys, poor cortico-medullary differentiation, hydronephrosis, polycystic kidney
  • Isotope scan: confirms blood flow + differential function of each kidney
  • ECG: electrolyte effects (peaked T in hyperkalaemia)

qs.q: Mention the lifestyle measures in CKD.
qs.a:
• Stop smoking · healthy balanced diet
  • Salt < 6 g/day · protein 40 g/day (0.8 g/kg) · restrict fat
  • Exercise ≥ 150 min/week · lose weight
  • Avoid NSAIDs

qs.q: Mention drugs that slow progression of early CKD.
qs.a:
• ACEi / ARBs: ↓ proteinuria
  • SGLT2 inhibitors (flozins): renal & cardiac protection, down to GFR 20
  • GLP-1 RA · vitamin D

qs.q: Mention the treatment of hyperkalaemia in CKD.
qs.a:
• Cation exchange resins (remove K⁺ via GIT)
  • Glucose–insulin infusion
  • β2 agonist
  • Refractory (> 6.5 with ECG changes or > 7) → dialysis

qs.q: Mention the treatment of CKD complications (acidosis, Ca, PO₄, fluid, anaemia).
qs.a:
• Acidosis: Na bicarbonate
  • Hypocalcaemia: Ca + vitamin D (1α-vitamin D when PO₄ controlled)
  • Hyperphosphataemia: phosphate binders – sevelamer, aluminium hydroxide gel
  • Fluid overload: fluid restriction, diuretics → dialysis
  • Anaemia: iron, blood, erythropoietin (+ folic acid & iron)
  • Hyperparathyroidism: 1α-vit D → cinacalcet → parathyroidectomy

qs.q: Mention the four treatment options of CKD.
qs.a:
• Lifestyle changes (all stages)
  • Medicine (control complications – no specific drug for CKD)
  • Dialysis (stage 5)
  • Kidney transplant (stage 5) – treatment of choice for ESRD

qs.q: Mention the clinical indications for initiating dialysis.
qs.a:
• Acute pulmonary oedema
  • Pericarditis / tamponade
  • Persistent vomiting & diarrhoea
  • Preoperative
  • Coma · convulsion
  • Deterioration of general health
  • Drug intoxication (dialysable drugs only)

qs.q: Mention the laboratory indications for initiating dialysis.
qs.a:
Parameter Dialysis threshold Normal
Urea > 200 mg/dl 20–40
Creatinine > 8 mg/dl (> 7 in DM) 0.7–1.2
K⁺ > 7 mEq/L (ECG changes) 3.5–5.5
HCO₃⁻ < 14 mEq/L —
pH < 7.2 —

qs.q: Mention the types of vascular access for haemodialysis.
qs.a:
• Temporary: jugular (preferred), subclavian, femoral (≤ 1 week – DVT)
  • Permanent: AV fistula (artery + vein, matures in 30–50 days) · AV graft (synthetic tube, 2–6 weeks)
  • Tunnelled cuffed catheter: wide use, easy, immediate use – but poor flow, loss of function, infection

qs.q: Mention the instructions for AV fistula care.
qs.a:
• No BP and no IV on the fistula arm
  • Protect the arm from injury
  • Control obvious haemorrhage
  • A thrill is normal

qs.q: Mention access problems in haemodialysis.
qs.a:
• AV graft thrombosis
  • Fistula / graft bleeding
  • Graft infection
  • Steal phenomenon (subclavian steal – retrograde vertebral flow)

qs.q: Mention the complications of haemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis.
qs.a:
• HD: disequilibrium, filter rupture / clotting, hypotension, cardiac arrest, air embolism, haemolysis, water contamination, allergy, access haemorrhage, bloodstream infection
  • PD: peritonitis (cloudy fluid, > 100 cells/mm³, > 50% PMNs), exit-site cellulitis, outflow failure, catheter leak, perforation, hydrothorax, encapsulating peritoneal sclerosis, UF failure, weight gain, hyperglycaemia, hypoalbuminaemia

qs.q: Compare CAPD and APD.
qs.a:
• CAPD: continuous, no machine, 3–5 exchanges/day, patient can move
  • APD (CCPD): a machine (cycler) performs exchanges, mostly during sleep

qs.q: Mention the drawbacks and criteria of kidney donors in transplantation.
qs.a:
• Drawbacks: find a donor, long waiting, lifelong immunosuppression, rejection (hyperacute, acute)
  • Donor: no transmissible disease, no kidney disease, similar blood group + HLA match, excellent health, motivated; brain-dead eligible
  • Transplant = ultimate treatment of choice for ESRD; 1-year graft survival > 95%

qs.q: Define Acute Kidney Injury (AKI).
qs.a:
• Sudden interruption/loss of kidney function over hours to days (within 48 h)
  • Due to obstruction, reduced circulation, or disease of the renal tissue
  • Leads to retention of toxins, fluids and end products of metabolism
  • Usually reversible with medical treatment
  • Without treatment it may progress to ESRD, uremic syndrome and death

qs.q: What creatinine rise defines AKI (doctor's definition)?
qs.a:
• Rise in serum creatinine ≥ 0.3 mg/dL above baseline within 48 h
  • OR ≥ 1.5 × baseline (within 7 days)

qs.q: How does AKI differ from CKD?
qs.a:
• AKI: sudden loss of function and usually reversible; may need dialysis temporarily, then recovers (within about a month)
  • CKD: loss of function for more than 3 months

qs.q: Classify AKI according to urine output.
qs.a:
• Non-oliguric: UOP > 400 mL/24 h
  • Oliguric: UOP < 400 mL/24 h
  • Anuric: UOP < 50 mL/24 h (some sources say < 100 mL)

qs.q: Define azotemia and uremia.
qs.a:
• Azotemia: accumulation of nitrogenous waste products (no symptoms)
  • Uremia: symptomatic AKI, e.g. vomiting, loss of appetite, tremors

qs.q: What is the mortality of AKI?
qs.a:
• 10–80%
  • Linked to high mortality and poor long-term outcomes; it is becoming more common in inpatients

qs.q: Mention the patient risk factors for AKI.
qs.a:
• Age over 75
  • Pre-existing CKD (the most important risk factor)
  • Diabetes
  • Heart failure
  • Liver disease
  • Peripheral vascular disease

qs.q: Mention the AKI risk events.
qs.a:
• Sepsis
  • High-risk medications
  • Hypotension
  • Hypovolaemia
  • Major surgery
  • Contrast scans

qs.q: What is the most important risk factor for AKI?
qs.a: • Pre-existing CKD (acute-on-chronic, e.g. after hypovolaemia, surgery or infection)

qs.q: Classify the causes of AKI.
qs.a:
• Prerenal: hypoperfusion or vasoconstriction
  • Renal (intrinsic): glomerular, tubular, interstitial, vascular
  • Postrenal: obstruction

qs.q: Define prerenal AKI and mention its causes.
qs.a:
• Reduced renal perfusion, usually from a fall in systemic BP; this type is correctable
  • Sepsis
  • Blood loss
  • Dehydration
  • Cardiac failure (cardiorenal syndrome)
  • Liver failure (hepatorenal syndrome)
  • Ineffective distribution of blood volume
  • Drugs that impair renal autoregulation (NSAIDs)

qs.q: Mention the renal (intrinsic) causes of AKI.
qs.a:
• Acute tubular necrosis (ATN)
  • Acute interstitial nephritis
  • Acute severe pyelonephritis (in DM)
  • Rapidly progressive GN
  • Malignant hypertension
  • Atheroembolic renal disease

qs.q: Mention the postrenal causes of AKI.
qs.a:
• Bilateral ureteric obstruction
  • Stones
  • Blood clots
  • BPH
  • Urethral oedema after invasive procedures
  • Urological malignancy
  • Stricture

qs.q: Define ATN.
qs.a: • Death of the tubular epithelial cells that form the renal tubules

qs.q: Classify ATN with examples.
qs.a:
• Ischaemic: tubules not perfused enough for a long time, e.g. hypotension, shock, sepsis
  • Nephrotoxic, exogenous: radiocontrast, aminoglycosides, vancomycin, amphotericin B, cisplatin, acetaminophen, chemotherapy
  • Nephrotoxic, endogenous: haemoglobin (haemolysis), myoglobin (rhabdomyolysis), bilirubin, urate crystals

qs.q: Mention the phases of ATN.
qs.a:
• Initiation
  • Maintenance
  • Recovery

qs.q: Mention the characteristics of ATN.
qs.a:
• Mortality ranges from very low to very high
  • Potentially preventable
  • Very good long-term outcome in survivors

qs.q: Mention the endogenous pigments that cause tubular injury, with their causes.
qs.a:
• Haemoglobin, from haemolysis
  • Myoglobin, from rhabdomyolysis (e.g. severe cold or heat, some drugs)
  • Bilirubin, which causes nephropathy

qs.q: What share of hospital-acquired ATN is contrast-induced?
qs.a: • 10%; it is mild and transient in most cases

qs.q: Mention the risk factors for radiocontrast nephropathy.
qs.a:
• Amount of dye (> 100 cc)
  • Volume depletion
  • Renal insufficiency
  • DM
  • Old age
  • Heart failure
  • ACEI or NSAIDs

qs.q: Mention the clinical characteristics of contrast-induced AKI.
qs.a:
• Onset 24–48 h after exposure
  • Lasts 5–7 days
  • Non-oliguric in most cases
  • Dialysis rarely needed

qs.q: Describe the risk of radiocontrast nephropathy by baseline creatinine.
qs.a:
• Normal kidney function: negligible
  • Creatinine < 2: 5–10%
  • Creatinine < 2 with DM: 10–40%
  • Advanced renal disease: > 50%

qs.q: Mention the pathogenesis of radiocontrast nephropathy.
qs.a:
• Not fully understood
  • Severe renal vasoconstriction within seconds of contrast
  • Direct renal tubular injury

qs.q: Mention the prophylactic strategies for contrast-induced AKI.
qs.a:
• Use IV contrast only when necessary
  • Hydration, with adequate fluid before the scan
  • Minimise the contrast volume
  • Use low-osmolar (nonionic) or iso-osmolar contrast
  • N-acetylcysteine (reduces ROS) or bicarbonate
  • Stop drugs that affect autoregulation: NSAIDs, ACEI, ARBs, metformin

qs.q: Mention the drugs to stop before giving contrast.
qs.a:
• NSAIDs
  • ACEI
  • ARBs
  • Metformin

qs.q: Mention the predisposing factors for rhabdomyolysis.
qs.a:
• Alcoholism
  • Hypokalaemia
  • Drugs, e.g. statins
  • Severe cold or heat

qs.q: How does myoglobinuria cause AKI?
qs.a:
• Renal vasoconstriction
  • Proximal tubular damage
  • Intratubular casts causing obstruction
  • Metabolic acidosis and electrolyte imbalance may also be present

qs.q: Mention the features of aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity.
qs.a:
• Usually appears after 7–10 days
  • Depends on dose and frequency
  • Direct proximal tubular injury
  • Once-daily dosing may be less nephrotoxic

qs.q: Mention the risk factors for aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity.
qs.a:
• Age
  • Renal insufficiency
  • Dose
  • Volume depletion

qs.q: Mention the features of atheroembolic AKI.
qs.a:
• Needs a high degree of suspicion
  • Caused by cholesterol emboli
  • Renal failure from haemodynamic and inflammatory effects
  • Multisystem disorder
  • Follows a vascular procedure
  • Acute form may need dialysis within a few days
  • Subacute form worsens in staggered steps separated by stable renal function
  • Patients on anticoagulants are at high risk
  • High mortality

qs.q: Mention the clinical clues to atheroembolic AKI.
qs.a:
• Livedo reticularis
  • Embolic phenomena with preserved peripheral pulses
  • Eosinophilia

qs.q: Mention the clinical stages of AKI.
qs.a:
• Onset: 1–3 days, with rising BUN and creatinine and possibly falling UOP
  • Oliguric: UOP < 400 mL/d with rising BUN, creatinine and K; may last up to 14 days
  • Diuretic: UOP rises up to 4000 mL/d but waste products are not cleared; improvement may start at the end of this stage
  • Recovery: return to normal, or persisting insufficiency that becomes chronic

qs.q: Why does polyuria happen in the diuretic phase, and how is it managed?
qs.a:
• Glomeruli recover before the tubules, which are responsible for concentrating urine
  • So urine is dilute and plentiful, and fluids must be replaced in this phase

qs.q: Mention the subjective symptoms of AKI.
qs.a:
• Nausea and vomiting
  • Loss of appetite
  • Headache
  • Lethargy
  • Tingling in the extremities
  • Itching

qs.q: Mention the objective signs of AKI.
qs.a:
• Disorientation, convulsions, coma
  • Generalised weakness
  • Lower limb oedema
  • Pulmonary oedema
  • Uremic breath
  • Hypotension and tachycardia, mostly in prerenal AKI

qs.q: Mention the systemic manifestations of uremia in AKI.
qs.a:
• Cerebral: headache, confusion
  • GIT: nausea, vomiting, hiccup
  • Haematological: pallor from normocytic normochromic anaemia
  • Skin: pruritus from raised phosphorus
  • Oliguric phase: fluid overload (HTN, pulmonary oedema)
  • Metabolic acidosis causing Kussmaul breathing

qs.q: What causes pruritus in AKI?
qs.a: • Raised serum phosphorus

qs.q: Mention the investigations for AKI.
qs.a:
• History and examination
  • BUN and creatinine
  • ABG (metabolic acidosis may need dialysis)
  • Na, K
  • CBC (anaemia)
  • Ca, phosphorus, PTH (more affected in chronic than acute disease)
  • Urine analysis and urine studies
  • Kidney US
  • Renal CT/MRI
  • Renal isotope scan
  • FENa and FEUrea
  • Renal biopsy

qs.q: What is the normal serum creatinine?
qs.a:
• Women: 0.5–1.0 mg/dL (45–90 µmol/L)
  • Men: 0.7–1.2 mg/dL (60–110 µmol/L)

qs.q: What is the role of kidney ultrasound in AKI?
qs.a:
• It is the first investigation
  • Excludes obstruction (postrenal causes)
  • Echogenicity and cortical thickness separate CKD (acute-on-chronic) from AKI

qs.q: What can urine analysis show in AKI?
qs.a:
• WBC casts point to infection or interstitial disease
  • RBC casts point to glomerular disease
  • Proteinuria

qs.q: Mention the indications for renal biopsy in AKI.
qs.a:
• Prerenal and postrenal causes excluded and the intrinsic cause is unclear
  • Clinical and lab findings suggest a diagnosis that needs confirmation before specific therapy (e.g. immunosuppressives)
  • Urgently in oliguria with rapidly worsening AKI, haematuria and RBC casts
  • To support special therapies, e.g. plasmapheresis in Goodpasture syndrome

qs.q: When is renal biopsy done urgently?
qs.a: • Oliguria with rapidly worsening AKI, haematuria and RBC casts

qs.q: Define FENa and give its formula.
qs.a:
• The share of filtered sodium that leaves the body in urine
  • It is a calculation, not a test
  • FENa = (Urine Na × Plasma Cr) / (Plasma Na × Urine Cr) × 100

qs.q: Interpret FENa.
qs.a:
• < 1%: prerenal
  • 1–2%: sometimes prerenal, sometimes ATN
  • > 2%: ATN, because damaged tubules cannot reabsorb Na

qs.q: In which conditions is FENa inaccurate?
qs.a:
• Mild AKI
  • AKI on top of CKD
  • Recent diuretic use
  • Exceptions with low FENa despite ATN, e.g. radiocontrast
  • It also depends on fluid and Na intake

qs.q: What is the alternative to FENa, and how is it interpreted?
qs.a:
• FEUrea (fractional excretion of urea), useful after diuretics
  • < 35%: prerenal
  • > 35%: ATN

qs.q: Mention the novel biomarkers of intrinsic AKI.
qs.a:
• Cystatin C
  • NGAL
  • KIM-1
  • L-FABP
  • IL-18
  • IGFBP-7
  • TIMP-2
  • Their best use is still uncertain

qs.q: Mention the AKIN diagnostic criteria for AKI.
qs.a:
• An abrupt fall in kidney function within 48 h, defined by any of:
  • Absolute rise in SCr of ≥ 0.3 mg/dL, OR a rise of ≥ 50%
  • OR documented oliguria < 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h

qs.q: Mention the components of the RIFLE criteria.
qs.a:
• Risk
  • Injury
  • Failure
  • Loss: needs renal replacement therapy for more than 4 weeks
  • ESRD: needs it for more than 3 months

qs.q: Mention the KDIGO staging of AKI.
qs.a:
• Stage 1: Cr 1.5–1.9 × baseline OR a rise ≥ 0.3 mg/dL; UOP < 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6–12 h
  • Stage 2: Cr 2–2.9 × baseline; UOP < 0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥ 12 h
  • Stage 3: Cr ≥ 3 × baseline OR Cr ≥ 4 mg/dL OR dialysis started; UOP < 0.3 mL/kg/h for ≥ 24 h OR anuria ≥ 12 h
  • Patients are staged by the single most concerning feature

qs.q: How is the KDIGO stage chosen when the creatinine and urine criteria disagree?
qs.a: • By the single most concerning (highest-stage) feature

qs.q: Mention the complications of AKI.
qs.a:
• Metabolic acidosis
  • Uremia
  • Hyperkalaemia
  • Pulmonary oedema (fluid overload)
  • Electrolyte disturbance
  • ESRD needing lifelong dialysis or a transplant

qs.q: Mention the lines of management of AKI.
qs.a:
• Treat the underlying cause (prerenal: correct sepsis and fluid loss)
  • Correct predisposing factors
  • Avoid nephrotoxins: aminoglycosides, chemotherapy, contrast, NSAIDs
  • Correct acid-base and electrolyte problems, especially K to protect the heart
  • Monitor renal function with serial creatinine and electrolytes
  • Monitor urine output
  • Urinary catheter
  • Specific therapies

qs.q: What are the uses of a urinary catheter in AKI?
qs.a:
• Monitoring urine output
  • Relieving bladder outlet obstruction, e.g. an enlarged prostate
  • Related procedures: ureteric stent or nephrostomy tube

qs.q: Mention the specific therapies in AKI.
qs.a:
• IV fluids
  • Central venous catheter to monitor volume and avoid over- or under-replacement
  • Inotropes (norepinephrine, dobutamine) to improve cardiac output and renal perfusion
  • Diuretics (furosemide)
  • Renal replacement therapy (haemodialysis)

qs.q: How are hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis treated in AKI?
qs.a:
• Hyperkalaemia: antihyperkalaemic measures to protect the heart
  • Metabolic acidosis: bicarbonate
  • Severe or refractory cases: dialysis

qs.q: Mention the nephrotoxins to avoid in AKI.
qs.a:
• Aminoglycosides
  • Chemotherapy
  • Contrast dye
  • NSAIDs

qs.q: Mention the indications for acute dialysis (AEIOU).
qs.a:
• A – Refractory metabolic acidosis
  • E – Electrolytes: refractory hyperkalaemia, K > 6.5 with ECG changes, or K > 7 with severe metabolic acidosis
  • I – Intoxication (nephrotoxins)
  • O – Refractory fluid overload / pulmonary oedema
  • U – Uremia: creatinine > 8, BUN > 100 mg/dL

qs.q: At what K level is dialysis indicated?
qs.a:
• K > 6.5 with ECG abnormalities
  • OR K > 7 with severe metabolic acidosis

qs.q: Mention the creatinine and BUN values that indicate dialysis.
qs.a:
• Serum creatinine > 8 mg/dL
  • BUN > 100 mg/dL

qs.q: Describe recovery from AKI.
qs.a:
• Most cases recover once the insult resolves
  • Recovery may be impaired with pre-existing CKD or a prolonged, severe or irreversible insult
  • Signs of recovery: urine output gradually returns and serum creatinine falls steadily

qs.q: What can impair recovery from AKI?
qs.a:
• Pre-existing CKD
  • A prolonged, severe or irreversible insult

qs.q: Compare prerenal AKI and ATN.
qs.a:
FeaturePrerenal AKIATN
CauseHypoperfusionTubular cell death
FENa< 1%> 2%
FEUrea< 35%> 35%
ReversibilityCorrectable with fluidsInitiation → maintenance → recovery phases

qs.q: Compare contrast nephropathy and aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity.
qs.a:
FeatureContrast nephropathyAminoglycoside nephrotoxicity
Onset24–48 h7–10 days
MechanismVasoconstriction + direct tubular injuryDirect proximal tubular injury
CourseLasts 5–7 days, mostly non-oliguric, dialysis rarely neededDepends on dose and frequency

qs.q: Define renal replacement therapy and mention its classification.
qs.a:
• Therapy that replaces the normal blood-filtering function of the kidney (AKI or CKD)
  • Dialysis: haemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis
  • Transplantation: cadaver donor, living (related & unrelated) donor

qs.q: Mention the indications for initiating dialysis.
qs.a:
• Volume overload refractory to diuretics (acute pulmonary oedema)
  • Encephalopathy not otherwise explained / uraemic symptoms (vomiting)
  • Hyperkalaemia not responding to measures (K⁺ > 7 mEq/L, ECG changes)
  • Pericarditis, pleurisy, other serositis (friction rub)
  • Severe metabolic acidosis (HCO₃⁻ < 14, pH < 7.2)
  • ESRD with GFR < 15 (stage 5)
  • Mnemonic: "AEIOU" (Acidosis, Electrolytes (K⁺), Intoxication, Overload, Uraemia – encephalopathy/pericarditis)

qs.q: Describe the principle of haemodialysis.
qs.a:
• Substitutes solute removal + fluid removal
  • Solute removal by diffusion (blood → dialysate along concentration gradient)
  • Blood pumped through a dialyser with semi-permeable membrane (cellulose / polysulphone) + heparin
  • Dialysate flows in the opposite direction (countercurrent)
  • Fluid removed by hydrostatic gradient = ultrafiltration
  • Dialysate K⁺ 0–1.5 mEq/L (negative K balance); Na & Ca at normal levels

qs.q: Compare acetate and bicarbonate dialysate.
qs.a:
• Acetate: easier to prepare, metabolised to HCO₃⁻ in liver; hypotension, headache, intolerance → no longer used in developed countries
  • Bicarbonate: preferred for elderly & cardiovascularly unstable patients

qs.q: Describe the vascular access, sessions and care of a haemodialysis patient.
qs.a:
• AV fistula: radial artery–cephalic vein or ulnar artery–basilic vein at wrist; flow 300–450 ml/min
  • Sessions: 3 times/week, 4–6 h each
  • HTN: controlled by gradual removal of salt & water
  • Protein ↑ to 1.2 g/kg/day (protein–calorie malnutrition)
  • Anaemia: IV iron + recombinant EPO; target Hb 11–12 g/dl

qs.q: Mention the complications of haemodialysis.
qs.a:
• Access: infection (local / systemic), thrombosis, thrombophlebitis, poor peripheral circulation (elderly, diabetic)
  • Machine / dialyser: bio-incompatibility, contamination → complement activation & hypoxia, hypersensitivity
  • Acute: hypotension (esp. diabetics), cramps, bleeding / line clotting, air embolism, chest & back pain, disequilibrium syndrome
  • Chronic: hepatitis B/C, psychogenic disorders, accelerated atherosclerosis, carpal tunnel (β2-microglobulin amyloidosis)
  • Inadequate dialysis: uraemic symptoms, neuropathy, pericarditis
  • Dialysate-related: haemolysis, acidosis, aluminium toxicity

qs.q: Why is hypotension common during haemodialysis in diabetic patients?
qs.a:
• IV volume depletion normally → compensatory VC & tachycardia
  • Diabetic autonomic neuropathy prevents these responses → hypotension

qs.q: Define dialysis disequilibrium syndrome and mention its prevention.
qs.a:
• Rapid marked ↓ of blood urea in severe uraemia → brain oedema
  • Headache, confusion, rarely seizures – early in dialysis history before adaptation
  • Prevention: start with shorter duration, lower blood flow, lower dialysate flow (e.g. 2 h instead of 4)

qs.q: Describe continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD).
qs.a:
• No direct access to circulation; soft silicone catheter surgically placed in abdomen
  • Peritoneum = semi-permeable membrane (artificial kidney); solution must be sterile
  • 2 L dialysate, 3–5 exchanges/day; potassium-free dialysate
  • Less efficient than HD → longer duration
  • Protein ↑ to 1.3 g/kg/day; anaemia easier (no blood loss) → EPO, Hb 11–12

qs.q: Mention the advantages of CAPD.
qs.a:
• Widely available, technically easy
  • Easy, gradual correction of acid–base & electrolytes
  • No arterial / venous puncture and no anticoagulation

qs.q: Mention the disadvantages / complications of CAPD.
qs.a:
• Peritonitis: abdominal pain, cloudy dialysate, leucocytes > 100/µL, > 50% neutrophils
  • Organisms: Staph. aureus (gram +ve), pseudomonas, fungi
  • Treatment: IV / intraperitoneal antibiotics, remove catheter & switch to HD if needed
  • Hernia (weak abdominal muscles)

qs.q: Compare haemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis.
qs.a:
Feature Haemodialysis Peritoneal dialysis
Filter Dialyser Peritoneum
Access AV fistula / catheter Abdominal catheter
Anticoagulation Heparin needed Not needed
Schedule 3×/week, 4–6 h 3–5 exchanges daily
Protein intake 1.2 g/kg/day 1.3 g/kg/day
Dialysate K⁺ 0–1.5 mEq/L Potassium-free
Main complication Hypotension, disequilibrium Peritonitis, hernia

qs.q: Mention the prerequisites of renal transplantation.
qs.a:
• Graft: cadaver, sibling, parent or unrelated donor
  • ABO compatibility is essential
  • Donor selected on HLA compatibility; cross-match before transplant

qs.q: Mention the immunosuppressive regimen after renal transplantation.
qs.a:
• Triple therapy: cyclosporine + steroids + mycophenolate mofetil or azathioprine
  • Cyclosporine: 6–8 mg/kg in 2 doses, reduced over 3–4 months by blood levels; high levels → nephrotoxicity
  • Steroids: big doses → maintenance 15–20 mg/day
  • Azathioprine: 2 mg/kg/day; reduce if marrow depression / ↑ liver enzymes
  • Mycophenolate: 1 g/12 h; more potent & expensive

qs.q: Mention the complications of immunosuppressive drugs.
qs.a:
• ↑ Liver enzymes → follow up
  • Bone marrow suppression → CBC monitoring → reduce / taper

qs.q: Mention the types of graft rejection.
qs.a:
• Hyperacute: preformed antibodies / ABO incompatibility → avoided by cross-match; may need graft removal
  • Acute cellular: T-lymphocyte mediated, most common in 1st month → IV big-dose steroids
  • Chronic: ischaemic changes; non-immune causes – long-standing HTN, dyslipidaemia, infection, calcineurin inhibitor (cyclosporine) toxicity

qs.q: Mention the complications of renal transplantation.
qs.a:
• Rejection (hyperacute, acute, chronic)
  • Infection: bacterial (1st month – wound, UTI, IV line); viral CMV (after 1st month); fungal (Candida); Pneumocystis; Cryptococcus
  • Malignancy: skin (Kaposi), PTLD
  • Prolonged steroids: avascular necrosis of femoral head, DM, infection

qs.q: Mention the factors that decrease graft survival in renal transplantation.
qs.a:
• HLA mismatch
  • Very young / older donor age · female donor
  • Large recipient body size
  • Recipient diabetes as the cause of ESRD
  • African-American donor / recipient
  • Hepatitis C infection

qs.q: Mention the classification of systemic diseases affecting the kidney.
qs.a:
• Metabolic: diabetes mellitus, amyloidosis
  • Autoimmune: SLE, vasculitis (also RA, scleroderma)
  • Infectious:
    • Viral: HBV, HCV, HIV
    • Bacterial: post-streptococcal GN, infective endocarditis, shunt nephritis
    • Parasitic: schistosomiasis, malaria
  • Haematologic: multiple myeloma, sickle cell anaemia
  • Others: hypertension, malignancy (and liver disease, heart failure)
  • Mnemonic: "My Aunt Is Hiding Outside"

qs.q: Mention the ways in which a systemic disease can present in the kidney.
qs.a:
• Nephritic syndrome (e.g. lupus class III/IV, vasculitis, post-infectious GN)
  • Nephrotic syndrome (e.g. diabetic nephropathy, amyloidosis, lupus class V)
  • Tubular dysfunction (e.g. myeloma → Fanconi, sickle cell → distal tubulopathy, Wilson → RTA)
  • AKI / RPGN (vasculitis, Goodpasture, hepatorenal, cardio-renal) or CKD → ESRD
  • Always ask: compensated? functional loss? complications?
  • Early recognition is key to preventing progression to CKD

qs.q: Mention the incidence of diabetic nephropathy and why most patients have type 2 DM.
qs.a:
• Most common cause of ESRD / CKD in adults
  • 40% of type 1 or type 2 diabetics develop nephropathy
  • Most patients are type 2 because type 2 is far more prevalent (90% vs 10% type 1)
  • Type 2 is often undiagnosed for 3–5 years before diagnosis

qs.q: When should you screen for diabetic nephropathy in type 1 and type 2 diabetes?
qs.a:
• Type 2: from the first day of diagnosis (disease may have been present 3–5 years)
  • Type 1: after 5 years of diabetes (2026 guidelines; old: after 18–20 years)
  • Screen by urine albumin/creatinine ratio (or 24-h urine albumin) + eGFR

qs.q: Mention the risk factors of diabetic nephropathy.
qs.a:
• Hyperglycaemia (poor control)
  • Hypertension
  • Dyslipidaemia, obesity (DM is part of the metabolic syndrome)
  • Smoking
  • Family history of diabetic nephropathy
  • Gene polymorphisms affecting the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone axis

qs.q: Explain the pathogenesis of proteinuria in diabetic nephropathy.
qs.a:
• Haemodynamic: afferent dilatation + efferent constriction → ↑ intraglomerular pressure → hyperfiltration
  • Charge barrier: GBM is negative (heparan sulphate) and normally repels negative albumin
    • In DM heparan sulphate is lost → negatively charged albumin is filtered
  • Structural: GBM thickening, mesangial matrix expansion, ↓ podocytes → with time glomerulosclerosis
  • Vascular: hyalinosis of afferent AND efferent arterioles → ↑ intraglomerular pressure → ↑ proteinuria

qs.q: Describe the pathology of diabetic nephropathy.
qs.a:
• GBM thickening: sensitive indicator of diabetes but correlates poorly with clinical nephropathy
  • Loss of heparan sulphate (negative charge) → albuminuria
  • Mesangial matrix expansion → mesangial sclerosis
  • Diffuse glomerulosclerosis = commonest lesion
  • Nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules): eosinophilic, PAS-positive nodules – specific
  • IF: non-specific IgG / complement staining; no deposits on EM
  • Vessels: hyaline & hypertensive arteriosclerosis (afferent + efferent) → chronic glomerulosclerosis + tubulo-interstitial changes

qs.q: What is the specific biopsy finding of diabetic nephropathy?
qs.a:
• Nodular glomerulosclerosis = Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules
  • Eosinophilic, PAS-positive nodules of glomerular scar between normal capillaries
  • Compare: specific IgA deposits on biopsy → Henoch–Schönlein purpura / IgA nephropathy; DN shows only non-specific IF

qs.q: Mention the stages of diabetic nephropathy.
qs.a:
StageNameFindings
1HyperfiltrationGFR ↑ (90–120 → up to 150)
2SilentGBM thickening; GFR & albumin still normal
3IncipientMicroalbuminuria 30–300 mg/g – the alarm → intervene here
4OvertMacroalbuminuria > 300; dipstick protein becomes positive
5ESRDCreatinine rises; prepare RRT when GFR < 15
  • Note: US kidney size is unreliable in DM (normal / enlarged despite ↑ creatinine)

qs.q: What is the earliest test to detect diabetic nephropathy? Define microalbuminuria.
qs.a:
• Urine albumin (microalbuminuria) is the earliest clinically detectable sign – stage 3 (incipient)
  • Microalbuminuria = 30–300 mg/g creatinine (albumin/creatinine ratio) or 30–300 mg/24 h
    • Normal < 30 · macroalbuminuria > 300
  • Measured by urine albumin/creatinine ratio or 24-h urine (ordinary dipstick is positive only > 300)

qs.q: Mention the lines of management of diabetic nephropathy.
qs.a:
• Control: diabetes (glycaemia), BP target 130/80 (some books 125/75), lipids, stop smoking
  • ACE inhibitors / ARBs – anti-proteinuric (best while micro/macroalbuminuria and GFR > 60)
  • SGLT2 inhibitors – improve proteinuria and slow progression
  • Finerenone – non-steroidal mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonist (not if K > 5.3)
  • (Non-dihydropyridine CCB – "some books write it")
  • Lifestyle: weight loss; dietary protein 0.6–0.8 g/kg/day
  • ESRD: prepare RRT (dialysis / transplantation) when GFR < 15

qs.q: Mention the precautions when prescribing ACE inhibitors / ARBs, SGLT2 inhibitors and finerenone in diabetic nephropathy.
qs.a:
• ACEi / ARB: check creatinine & potassium after 2–3 weeks
    • If creatinine rises > 25–30% → kidney affection → stop
    • Not started when creatinine is already badly affected
  • SGLT2i: GFR dips a little at start – accepted up to 15–20%
  • Finerenone: expensive; check K first → not if K > 5.3

qs.q: Mention the renal involvement in systemic lupus erythematosus.
qs.a:
• Occurs in 35–90% of SLE patients (very important); female : male = 9 : 1
  • Typical case: malar rash + photosensitivity → renal affection = lupus nephritis
  • Can present as nephritic (class III/IV) or nephrotic (class V) syndrome
  • Diagnosis of SLE: 4 of 11 criteria / EULAR 2023 domain score; biopsy-proven class III or IV alone diagnoses lupus

qs.q: Mention the ISN/RPS classification of lupus nephritis.
qs.a:
ClassLesion
IMinimal mesangial nephritis
IIMesangial proliferative nephritis
IIIFocal proliferative (< 50% of glomeruli, capillary involvement)
IVDiffuse proliferative (> 50% of glomeruli) – most common
VMembranous – presents as nephrotic syndrome
VIAdvanced sclerosis without residual activity
  • III & IV (most severe) are further described as active / chronic and global / segmental (prognostic value)
  • Mnemonic: "Mini-Mes, Focal, Diffuse, Membranous, Sclerosis"

qs.q: Mention the investigations of lupus nephritis.
qs.a:
• Antibodies: ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith, antiphospholipid antibodies
  • Activity: low C3 and C4 (complement consumption)
  • Urine: proteinuria (24-h urine), microscopic haematuria, casts
  • Renal function: creatinine / eGFR
  • CBC: haemolytic anaemia (an SLE criterion), leucopenia, thrombocytopenia
  • Renal biopsy is a must: shows class, activity & chronicity → decides treatment
  • Anti-Ro & anti-La – important in pregnancy (neonatal lupus)

qs.q: Mention the indications of renal biopsy in lupus and why it is important.
qs.a:
• Indications:
    • Proteinuria > 500 mg/24 h
    • Rising creatinine or active sediment (microhaematuria) – e.g. stable SLE + ↑ creatinine + microhaematuria
    • No response to treatment → repeat biopsy
  • Why: defines the class, activity and chronicity index (proliferation vs sclerosis)
    • Sclerosis / interstitial fibrosis → supportive only → dialysis
    • Proliferative → aggressive immunosuppression

qs.q: Mention the treatment of lupus nephritis according to class.
qs.a:
• Hydroxychloroquine for all classes (fundus exam first, follow up the retina)
  • Class I: no specific treatment
  • Class II: supportive (ACEi/ARB for proteinuria, control BP); corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus) if nephrotic-range proteinuria
  • Class III & IV: aggressive immunosuppression – induction then maintenance
  • Class V: steroid + immunosuppressive if superimposed proliferative lesions; otherwise anti-proteinuric
  • Class VI: not treated – end stage → dialysis / transplant
  • Mnemonic: "3 & 4 = war, 6 = stop"

qs.q: Describe the treatment protocol of class III / IV lupus nephritis.
qs.a:
• Induction:
    • Pulse methylprednisolone 0.5–1 g × 3–5 days → oral prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg, taper → 5–7.5 mg
    • + cyclophosphamide (1 g monthly × 6 months) or MMF 3 g/day or rituximab by severity
  • Maintenance: MMF or azathioprine (choice by fertility plans) + lowest steroid dose (5–7.5 mg)
  • Response: proteinuria ↓ > 25% at 3 months, > 50% at 6 months, remission by 1 year
  • Others for resistant cases: plasmapheresis
  • MMF is teratogenic – stop before pregnancy
  • Goal: never let III/IV progress

qs.q: Mention the role of hydroxychloroquine in lupus nephritis and its precautions.
qs.a:
• Should be considered for all patients with lupus nephritis, regardless of class
  • Precaution: retinal toxicity → fundus examination before starting and regular retinal follow-up
  • If the retina is already affected → do not give

qs.q: Enumerate the antiphospholipid antibodies.
qs.a:
• Lupus anticoagulant
  • Anticardiolipin antibody
  • Anti-β2 glycoprotein I antibody
  • Hypercoagulable state → APS; treatment by severity: low-dose aspirin or anticoagulation

qs.q: Mention the renal involvement in rheumatoid arthritis and scleroderma.
qs.a:
• Rheumatoid arthritis:
    • Chronic inflammation → AA amyloidosis → nephrotic syndrome
    • Analgesic nephropathy → papillary necrosis ("ring shadows")
    • Drug nephrotoxicity (NSAIDs, methotrexate, gold, penicillamine)
  • Scleroderma: scleroderma renal crisis → malignant HTN + thrombotic microangiopathy
    • Treated with ACE inhibitors; if no response → add CCB

qs.q: Classify systemic vasculitis according to vessel size and mention the renal affection of each.
qs.a:
VesselExamplesKidney
LargeGiant cell (temporal) arteritis, Takayasu arteritisRenal artery stenosis → renovascular HTN
MediumPolyarteritis nodosa (HBV)HTN, renal infarction, renal / perirenal haemorrhage
SmallGPA, MPA, EGPA (ANCA); HSP, cryoglobulinaemia, anti-GBMCrescentic GN / RPGN
  • Small-vessel vasculitis is the most famous (pulmonary–renal)

qs.q: Mention the renal manifestations of large-vessel vasculitis.
qs.a:
• Giant cell (temporal) arteritis: > 50 years, with polymyalgia rheumatica; old age + headache → sudden ↓ vision (urgent)
  • Takayasu arteritis: < 50 years; aorta & major branches
    • Renal artery stenosis → renovascular hypertension, ↓ GFR
    • Aortic aneurysm, unequal pulses & BP

qs.q: Mention the renal manifestations of polyarteritis nodosa.
qs.a:
• Hypertension
  • Renal infarction
  • Renal and perirenal haemorrhage (aneurysm rupture)
  • Progressive renal failure
  • Associated with hepatitis B (post-infectious)

qs.q: Mention the ANCA-associated vasculitides and their antibodies.
qs.a:
• Group strongly associated with ANCA and pauci-immune necrotizing crescentic GN
  • c-ANCA → granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's)
  • p-ANCA → microscopic polyangiitis and eosinophilic GPA (Churg–Strauss)
  • Present as pulmonary–renal syndrome / RPGN (nephritic + rapid creatinine rise)
  • Mnemonic: c-ANCA = C for "Cough + Crescents"; p-ANCA = P for Polyangiitis & "P-uffer" (asthma)

qs.q: Mention the clinical features of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's).
qs.a:
• Granulomatous inflammation of the upper and lower respiratory tract
  • Upper: epistaxis, nasal ulcer, sinusitis
  • Lower: haemoptysis, alveolar haemorrhage
  • Kidney: necrotizing crescentic GN → oliguria, RPGN
  • c-ANCA positive; high mortality if not treated aggressively

qs.q: What is Churg–Strauss syndrome? How is it recognised?
qs.a:
• Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA)
  • Like PAN but with more frequent bronchial asthma
  • Clue: asthma + eosinophilia + renal impairment
  • p-ANCA; causes pulmonary–renal syndrome

qs.q: Describe Henoch–Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis).
qs.a:
• Small-vessel vasculitis with IgA-dominant immune deposits
  • Affects skin (palpable purpura – raised, not petechiae), gut (abdominal pain, up to intestinal obstruction), glomeruli, with arthritis
  • Typical patient: child with palpable purpura + abdominal pain
  • Biopsy: IgA deposition
  • Platelets are normal – HSP does NOT cause thrombocytopenia
  • vs IgA nephropathy (Berger): haematuria immediately with infection; PSGN comes 2–3 weeks after

qs.q: Describe essential mixed cryoglobulinaemia and its renal involvement.
qs.a:
• Small-vessel vasculitis associated with hepatitis C (also HBV)
  • Involves skin and glomeruli (MPGN pattern)
  • Case: HCV + renal impairment + purpura / skin rash + peripheral neuropathy + cold limbs ± digital ischaemia
  • Labs: low C3 and C4
  • Best test to confirm: serum cryoglobulins (strict collection & temperature)
  • Treatment: treat the cause (HCV / HBV) first, then by severity: steroid, immunomodulator, rituximab, plasmapheresis

qs.q: Describe Goodpasture's syndrome (anti-GBM disease).
qs.a:
• Anti-basement-membrane autoantibodies directly attack the α3 chain of type IV collagen (alveolar + glomerular BM)
  • Picture: severe crescentic GN (RPGN) + pulmonary haemorrhage
  • Biopsy: linear IgG deposition; complement normal
  • Diagnosis: anti-GBM antibody (ABMA), renal biopsy
  • Treatment: plasmapheresis + steroids + cyclophosphamide (massive, aggressive – high mortality)

qs.q: Mention the causes of pulmonary–renal syndrome.
qs.a:
• Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's)
  • Microscopic polyangiitis / Churg–Strauss (EGPA)
  • Goodpasture's (anti-GBM) syndrome
  • (Also SLE)
  • NOT IgA nephropathy – the usual EXCEPT answer

qs.q: Define RPGN and mention its management.
qs.a:
• Rapidly progressive GN: nephritic syndrome with rapid rise of creatinine (crescents on biopsy)
  • Why urgent: reaches ESRD quickly, high mortality
  • Management:
    • Biopsy, but if suspected → start aggressive treatment at once (result takes 7–10 days)
    • Pulse steroid + cyclophosphamide or rituximab (induction)
    • Plasma exchange / plasmapheresis
    • Dialysis if needed

qs.q: Mention the investigations and treatment of renal vasculitis.
qs.a:
• Investigations: ANCA, anti-GBM antibody (ABMA), cryoglobulins, complement, urine (haematuria, casts), creatinine
  • Renal biopsy – definitive and very important
  • Treatment:
    • Induction: steroid + cyclophosphamide or rituximab
    • Plasmapheresis / plasma exchange
    • Treat the cause: HCV / HBV
    • High suspicion → start treatment before the biopsy result

qs.q: Mention the types of cardio-renal syndrome with examples.
qs.a:
TypeNameMechanism / example
IAcute cardio-renalAcute heart failure → AKI (e.g. ACS → cardiogenic shock)
IIChronic cardio-renalChronic HF → CKD
IIIAcute reno-cardiacAKI → acute HF (volume overload, uraemic inflammation, metabolic)
IVChronic reno-cardiacCKD → chronic HF (LVH, CKD cardiomyopathy, β2M amyloid)
VSecondarySystemic disease → both (sepsis, amyloidosis, cirrhosis, lupus)
  • Mnemonic: "1–2 heart first, 3–4 kidney first, 5 both"

qs.q: Mention the principle of management of cardio-renal syndrome.
qs.a:
• Treat by the primary cause
  • Types 1–2: fix the heart → kidney improves
  • Types 3–4: RRT + fluid restriction → heart improves
  • Type 5: treat the systemic disease
  • Renal patient with desaturation / HF → echo (many have EF 15–20%)

qs.q: Mention the renal involvement in multiple myeloma.
qs.a:
• Think myeloma: bone pain + anaemia + renal affection ± hypercalcaemia (old age, ↑ globulin)
  • Cast nephropathy (myeloma kidney): light chains + Tamm–Horsfall protein form casts in tubules
  • AL amyloidosis (light-chain amyloid)
  • Fanconi syndrome (proximal tubulopathy)
  • Hypercalcaemia → AKI
  • Aggravated by NSAIDs, hypercalcaemia, contrast, dehydration

qs.q: Mention the investigations of suspected multiple myeloma.
qs.a:
• Serum protein electrophoresis → monoclonal (M) band; immunofixation; serum free light chains
  • Urine: Bence Jones protein (light chains)
  • Bone marrow: plasma cells > 46% → myeloma (isolated ↑ IgG with normal others → MGUS)
  • Calcium, creatinine, CBC (anaemia), ESR ↑
  • Skeletal survey / imaging (lytic lesions)
  • Treatment: bortezomib-based regimen

qs.q: Mention the types of amyloidosis.
qs.a:
• AL (primary systemic): immunoglobulin light chains; clonal B-cell disorder, usually myeloma
  • AA (secondary): acute-phase reactant serum amyloid A; chronic inflammation / infection (RA, TB, FMF…)
  • AF (familial): most commonly transthyretin (ATTR)
  • Aβ2M: β2-microglobulin in long-standing ESRD / dialysis (→ cardiomyopathy, type 4 cardio-renal)
  • Aβ: most common localized amyloidosis
  • Mnemonic: "AL-Light, AA-Acute phase, AF-Familial (TTR), β2M-dialysis"

qs.q: Mention the causes of AA (secondary) amyloidosis.
qs.a:
• Collagen / inflammatory: rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, other collagen disorders, IBD
  • Chronic infection: tuberculosis, suppurative lung disease (bronchiectasis), osteomyelitis
  • Familial Mediterranean fever
  • Presents with bilateral LL oedema + proteinuria (nephrotic)

qs.q: Mention the clinical features and diagnosis of renal amyloidosis.
qs.a:
• Kidney: nephrotic syndrome (often > 5 g/day) with large kidneys despite CRF
  • Multisystem: large tongue (macroglossia), cardiac involvement (cardiomyopathy), peripheral neuropathy
  • Diagnosis: biopsy + Congo red stain → apple-green birefringence under polarized light
  • Typing: confirm by mass spectrometry
  • Search for the cause: protein electrophoresis (AL), inflammatory disease (AA), genetic test (FMF)

qs.q: Mention the treatment of amyloidosis.
qs.a:
• AL: high-dose IV melphalan + autologous stem cell transplantation (better than oral melphalan + dexamethasone) ± bortezomib
  • AA: treat the underlying inflammatory / infectious disease + supportive for proteinuria
  • FMF: colchicine 1.2–1.8 mg/day (up to 2 mg)

qs.q: Mention the renal involvement in familial Mediterranean fever and its treatment.
qs.a:
• Recurrent fever + serositis / abdominal pain since childhood → AA amyloidosis → nephrotic syndrome
  • Diagnosis: genetic testing (MEFV)
  • Treatment: colchicine, start low → 1.2–1.8 mg/day (up to 2 mg)
  • Main side effect: diarrhoea

qs.q: Define hepatorenal syndrome and mention its diagnostic criteria.
qs.a:
• Functional AKI in advanced liver disease (cirrhosis with ascites) due to renal vasoconstriction
  • AKI definition (revised consensus): creatinine ↑ ≥ 0.3 mg/dL within 48 h or > 50% from baseline within 7 days
  • Criteria:
    • Cirrhosis with ascites
    • No response to volume expansion (albumin) – exclude hypovolaemia
    • No shock, no nephrotoxic drugs
    • No parenchymal renal disease: proteinuria < 0.5 g/day, no haematuria (< 50 RBC/HPF), normal US
  • Urine is bland

qs.q: Mention the types of hepatorenal syndrome.
qs.a:
• Type 1 (HRS-AKI): acute, rapidly progressive renal failure in < 2 weeks, unresponsive to volume expansion; usually severe liver failure → urgent
  • Type 2 (HRS-CKD): more gradual course; main clinical consequence is refractory ascites

qs.q: Mention the precipitating factors of hepatorenal syndrome.
qs.a:
• Excess diuretics
  • Lactulose-induced diarrhoea
  • GI bleeding (portal hypertension – varices)
  • Nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides)
  • Infection / SBP, large-volume paracentesis without albumin
  • Prevention: antibiotic for 7 days after GI bleed; albumin when indicated

qs.q: Mention the treatment of hepatorenal syndrome type 1 (HRS-AKI).
qs.a:
• Stop diuretics and nephrotoxic drugs; treat precipitant (infection, bleeding)
  • Albumin + vasoconstrictor (terlipressin or norepinephrine)
  • Liver transplantation = definitive
  • Type 2 (HRS-CKD) is treated as refractory ascites

qs.q: Mention the causes of renal failure in liver cirrhosis.
qs.a:
• Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS-AKI / HRS-CKD)
  • Hypovolaemia-induced (pre-renal): GI bleeding (commonest), excess diuretics, laxative / lactulose diarrhoea → prolonged → ATN
  • Parenchymal renal disease: HBV, HCV, IgA (alcohol), schistosomiasis – suspect if proteinuria > 500 mg/day or haematuria > 50 RBC/HPF
  • Drug-induced: NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, paracetamol, neomycin (now rifaximin)
  • Post-renal azotaemia: bilharziasis, stone, tumour

qs.q: Mention the renal diseases associated with the major liver diseases.
qs.a:
Liver diseaseRenal disease
Hepatitis BMembranous GN, PAN, essential mixed cryoglobulinaemia
Hepatitis CMembranoproliferative GN, cryoglobulinaemia
Alcoholic liver diseaseIgA nephropathy
Wilson diseaseRenal tubular acidosis
  • MPGN biopsy: mesangial proliferation + thickened BM
  • Mnemonic: "B-Members, C-MPGN, Alcohol-IgA, Wilson-RTA"

qs.q: Define thrombotic microangiopathy and mention its renal causes.
qs.a:
• TMA: renal affection + microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia + thrombocytopenia
  • Causes: malignant hypertension, scleroderma renal crisis, antiphospholipid syndrome, HSP, TTP / HUS
  • Treatment: control BP (ACEi/ARB); scleroderma crisis not responding → add CCB; treat the cause
  • Benign hypertension → hyalinosis → ischaemic glomerulosclerosis

qs.q: Mention the renal involvement in sickle cell anaemia and its management.
qs.a:
• Medullary hypoxia → papillary necrosis
  • Distal tubulopathy: concentrating defect, hyperkalaemia
  • Hyperfiltration → FSGS → may reach ESRD
  • Management: hydroxyurea (↓ hyperfiltration & albuminuria), avoid dehydration, avoid NSAIDs

qs.q: Mention the causes of glomerulonephritis with low complement (C3 / C4).
qs.a:
• Post-streptococcal (post-infectious) GN
  • Infective endocarditis and shunt nephritis
  • Membranoproliferative GN
  • Cryoglobulinaemia
  • Lupus nephritis
  • Normal complement: Goodpasture, IgA nephropathy, ANCA vasculitis, FSGS

qs.q: Mention the renal lesions associated with HIV and malignancy.
qs.a:
• HIV: collapsing FSGS (HIV-associated nephropathy)
  • Solid tumours: membranous nephropathy
  • Lymphoma (Hodgkin): minimal change disease
  • Myeloma: cast nephropathy, AL amyloid, Fanconi

qs.q: Define erythropoiesis.
qs.a:
• Production of RBCs from haematopoietic stem cells in red bone marrow
  • Stimulated by erythropoietin (EPO) from the kidneys in response to hypoxia (blood loss, anaemia, high altitude)

qs.q: Differentiate polycythaemia rubra vera from erythrocytosis.
qs.a:
• Polycythaemia rubra vera: disease of ↑ RBC production (primary)
  • Erythrocytosis: ↑ RBCs secondary to pathological causes (hypoxia)

qs.q: Define myelopoiesis and mention the cells it produces.
qs.a:
• Production of myeloid cells in bone marrow from HSCs → innate immune cells
  • Granulocytes: neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils (granulopoiesis)
  • Monocytes → macrophages & dendritic cells (monocytopoiesis)
  • Others: precursors of mast cells & megakaryocytes (platelets)
  • Origin: pluripotent HSC → common myeloid progenitor (CMP)

qs.q: Mention the sites of haematopoiesis during life.
qs.a:
• Yolk sac → AGM region → liver (± spleen) → bone marrow
  • Yolk sac: primitive haematopoiesis (nucleated RBCs), 0–2 months
  • AGM (aorta-gonad-mesonephros): 1st definitive HSCs
  • Fetal liver: main organ in fetal life (from ≈ 5–6 weeks), 2–7 months
  • Bone marrow: from 4th–5th month; main organ after birth
  • Adult: axial skeleton – sternum, vertebrae, ribs, skull, pelvis, proximal femur & humerus

qs.q: Differentiate red and yellow marrow.
qs.a:
• Red marrow: able to produce cells; all marrow in newborns
  • Yellow marrow: fat (adipocytes), cannot produce cells; replaces red marrow from distal bones with age
  • Yellow marrow can be reactivated with increased demand (blood loss)

qs.q: Mention the clinical importance of extramedullary haematopoiesis.
qs.a:
• Haematopoiesis in other sites (liver, spleen) due to haemolysis, e.g. thalassaemia
  • Main cause of hepatosplenomegaly in thalassaemic patients (if not transfused)
  • Elderly: fewer active bones → anaemia after nail & screw fixation may last 6 months

qs.q: Mention the characteristics of haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs).
qs.a:
• Pluripotent: give rise to all lineages
  • Rare: 1 in 10⁵ nucleated marrow cells
  • Mostly quiescent, divide by asymmetric division → self-renewal + progenitor
  • Express CD34, lack differentiation markers (CD38); express VEGF receptor, Sca-1
  • Mitotically quiescent → survive 5-fluorouracil
  • Loss of self-renewal → aplastic anaemia

qs.q: Mention the characteristics of progenitor cells.
qs.a:
• Multipotent
  • Do not self-renew (or very limited)
  • Respond best to multiple cytokines (G-CSF acts directly on progenitors)
  • Expand the number of cells dramatically; named by colonies (CFU-GEMM, CFU-GM)

qs.q: Mention the characteristics of bone marrow stromal cells.
qs.a:
• Large spread-out cells forming a bed for haematopoiesis
  • Derived from mesenchymal stem cells, not haematopoietic origin
  • Express class I HLA, but lack CD45
  • Produce extracellular matrix + locally produced cytokines

qs.q: Explain the role of the bone marrow microenvironment in multiple myeloma.
qs.a:
• Stromal cells & ECM help myeloma cells home to marrow
  • Myeloma cells produce cytokines → neogenesis & angiogenesis

qs.q: Mention the stages of erythropoiesis.
qs.a:
• PHSC → CFU-E → proerythroblast → basophilic erythroblast → polychromatophilic erythroblast → orthochromatic erythroblast → reticulocyte → erythrocyte
  • Mnemonic: "Pro Bas Poly Ortho Retic Ery"
  • Maturation ≈ 5–7 days (to reticulocyte)

qs.q: Mention the changes that characterise RBC development.
qs.a:
• ↓ Cell size
  • Disappearance of nucleus
  • Appearance of haemoglobin

qs.q: Mention the characteristics of reticulocytes.
qs.a:
• Reticulum = remnant of ER (RNA)
  • Still synthesise Hb & other proteins; few mitochondria
  • Young RBCs (80% Hb); < 1% of RBCs
  • Found with erythrocytes in peripheral blood

qs.q: Mention the clinical importance of the reticulocyte count.
qs.a:
• Normal: up to 2.5%
  • ↑ (> 3): haemolysis or blood loss (marrow activation)
  • ↓ (< 1): marrow suppression – aplastic anaemia, infection
  • Erythroblasts in peripheral blood = malignancy (erythroblastic AML)

qs.q: Describe the normal RBC.
qs.a:
• Round, biconcave disc, smooth contour, no variation in size & shape
  • Diameter 7–8 µm; deform easily
  • Hb 34 g/dl of cells; 14–16 g/dl blood
  • Enter circulation by diapedesis (in myelofibrosis → tear-drop cells)

qs.q: Mention the causes of hypoxia that stimulate EPO secretion.
qs.a:
• Anaemia (low RBC count)
  • Haemorrhage
  • High altitude
  • Prolonged heart failure
  • Lung disease

qs.q: Mention the sources and roles of erythropoietin.
qs.a:
• Glycoprotein: 90% from peritubular fibroblasts of renal cortex, 10% from liver
  • Low in renal failure & chemotherapy
  • ↑ cell division of erythroblasts & stem cells
  • Speeds maturation (↑ rate of Hb synthesis)
  • Maximum stimulation → RBC production ↑ tenfold

qs.q: Mention the stages of neutrophil maturation.
qs.a:
• Myeloblast → promyelocyte → myelocyte (mitotic pool, 7.5 days)
  • → metamyelocyte → band → segmented (post-mitotic pool – cannot divide)
  • Myeloblast–myelocyte in blood = malignancy (leukaemia)

qs.q: Mention the functions of neutrophils.
qs.a:
• Innate immunity – 1st line of defence
  • Surround microbes with pseudopodia → phagosome → granule release
  • Chemotaxis to FMLP → diapedesis
  • Killing: enzymes in granules + oxidative killing (NADPH oxidase; absent in chronic granulomatous disease)
  • Marrow = large reserve pool; half circulating, half marginated

qs.q: Define emergency myelopoiesis and mention its clinical importance.
qs.a:
• ↑ myeloid production in response to infection, inflammation, stress (cancer)
  • E.g. septic ICU patient: TLC 6,000 → 50,000 on recovery
  • Important to differentiate infection from CML

qs.q: How do you differentiate CML from infection (leukaemoid reaction)?
qs.a:
• TLC: very high in CML (100,000–150,000) with ↑ eosinophils & basophils
  • LAP / NAP score: ↑ in infection (↓ in CML)
  • High TLC + anaemia + no severe infection → think CML
  • Child with high TLC → search for infection first

qs.q: Mention the effect of chemotherapy on blood cells.
qs.a:
• Suppresses stem cell activity; order of affection = life span:
  • TLC first (≈ 4 days) → platelets (≈ 7 days) → RBCs (120 days)

qs.q: Mention the clinical uses of haematopoietic growth factors.
qs.a:
• EPO (epoetin alfa): anaemia of CKD, chemotherapy, some MDS
  • G-CSF: prevent / treat chemotherapy neutropenia; mobilise stem cells for transplantation
  • GM-CSF: granulocytes + macrophages
  • TPO receptor agonists (eltrombopag, romiplostim): chronic ITP, platelet recovery
  • Cytokine blockade in GVHD / CRS: IL-6 blocker tocilizumab, JAK inhibitor ruxolitinib

qs.q: What does the response to G-CSF tell you during chemotherapy?
qs.a:
• TLC low then rises after G-CSF → chemotherapy dose was high
  • No response or > 10 days to respond → toxic dose → mandatory dose reduction
