  • Seen with myeloablative protocols before stem cell transplantation

qs.q: Mention the characteristics of platelets.
qs.a:
• Cell fragments shed from megakaryocytes (budding)
  • Lack nuclei; have organelles & enzymes for energy and secretory products
  • High actin & myosin (change shape)
  • Life span ≈ 10 days; removed by tissue macrophages
  • Do not leave blood (unlike WBCs)
  • ⅓ stored in spleen, released by sympathetic splenic contraction

qs.q: Mention the source and role of thrombopoietin.
qs.a:
• Hormone produced by the liver
  • ↑ megakaryocytes → ↑ platelet production
  • Liver disease → ↓ TPO → thrombocytopenia → treat with TPO agonists

qs.q: Mention the structure of platelets.
qs.a:
• Membrane: specific receptors; repels normal endothelium
  • Contractile proteins: actin, myosin, thrombosthenin
  • Mitochondria: ATP & ADP · lipids: prostaglandins, thromboxane
  • ER & Golgi: enzymes · protein: fibrin-stabilising protein
  • α granules: fibrinogen, VWF, factors V, VII
  • Dense granules: ADP, ATP, 5-HT, Ca²⁺

qs.q: Mention the precautions of platelet transfusion.
qs.a:
• Stored at specific temperature; maximum viability 5 days
  • One bag pooled from ≈ 4 donors → ↑ allergies
  • Restricted to bleeding patients; not given if > 15,000 without bleeding / fever

qs.q: Define haemostasis.
qs.a:
• Spontaneous arrest of bleeding by physiological processes in an injured vessel
  • Prevents blood loss, keeps blood fluid; more effective in small vessels

qs.q: Mention the mechanisms of haemostasis.
qs.a:
• (1) Vascular constriction → primary haemostasis
  • (2) Platelet plug formation → primary haemostasis
  • (3) Blood clot formation → secondary haemostasis
  • (4) Clot retraction & fibrinolysis → tertiary haemostasis

qs.q: Mention the causes of vascular spasm after injury.
qs.a:
• Nervous reflexes
  • Local myogenic spasm
  • Local humoral factors: 5-HT, thromboxane A₂ (+ endothelin)
  • Effect: ↓ blood loss, platelets stay longer at injury site

qs.q: Mention the steps of platelet plug formation.
qs.a:
• (a) Adhesion: to exposed collagen via VWF (+ fibronectin) – first event after injury
  • (b) Activation & release: swell, pseudopodia; release ADP, TXA₂, serotonin, Ca²⁺
  • (c) Aggregation: ADP + TXA₂ → ↑ stickiness of more platelets → loose platelet plug

qs.q: Mention the source and role of von Willebrand factor.
qs.a:
• Synthesised by endothelial cells & megakaryocytes; adhesive protein (RGD sequence)
  • Binds integrins GP IIb/IIIa on platelets
  • Links platelets to subendothelial collagen (adhesion)
  • VWD: type 1 = quantity ↓; type 2 = quality defect (tested by ristocetin)

qs.q: Mention the clotting factors.
qs.a:
• I fibrinogen · II prothrombin · III tissue thromboplastin · IV Ca²⁺
  • V proaccelerin · (VI absent) · VII proconvertin
  • VIII antihaemophilic factor (haemophilia A) · IX Christmas factor (haemophilia B)
  • X Stuart–Prower · XI PTA · XII Hageman · XIII fibrin-stabilising factor
  • Others: HMW kininogen, kallikrein, prekallikrein, platelet phospholipids

qs.q: Mention the final three steps of clotting.
qs.a:
• (1) Prothrombin activator is formed
  • (2) Prothrombin → thrombin
  • (3) Thrombin converts fibrinogen → fibrin mesh (stabilised by XIII + Ca²⁺)

qs.q: Compare the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways.
qs.a:
Feature Intrinsic Extrinsic
Activation XII by contact with collagen / glass Tissue factor (thromboplastin) from damaged tissue
Factors XII, XI, IX, VIII VII
Test PTT PT
Defect example Haemophilia A & B (↑ PTT) Factor VII deficiency (↑ PT)

qs.q: Mention the blood products used in coagulation defects.
qs.a:
• Whole fresh blood: bleeding patients
  • Cryoprecipitate: rich in factor VIII → haemophilia A
  • Fresh frozen plasma: rich in factor VII → factor VII deficiency (or recombinant VII)

qs.q: Describe clot retraction.
qs.a:
• 50% of clot retracts in 1 hour
  • Pulls broken vessel edges together → wound healing
  • Impaired if platelets decreased or absent

qs.q: Describe fibrinolysis and the protein C system.
qs.a:
• Endothelium releases thrombomodulin + thrombin → activates protein C
  • Activated protein C + protein S → inactivates Va & VIIIa + activates plasminogen activator
  • Plasminogen → plasmin → breaks fibrin → FDPs, D-dimer
  • Protein C/S deficiency → thrombosis (young unprovoked DVT, stroke, MI)

qs.q: Why does blood not clot inside the vessels?
qs.a:
• Endothelial factors: smoothness, negative charge, thrombomodulin
  • Velocity of circulation
  • Natural anticoagulants: heparin, protein C, protein S
  • Negative feedback by thrombin

qs.q: Explain DIC.
qs.a:
• Dysregulation between coagulation & anticoagulation / fibrinolysis (sepsis, labour)
  • Widespread coagulation → microthrombi → consumption of platelets & factors → bleeding
  • Fibrinolysis → ↑ FDPs & D-dimer

qs.q: Mention vitamin K-dependent factors and causes of vitamin K deficiency.
qs.a:
• Factors II, VII, IX, X + protein C (mnemonic "1972" = X, IX, VII, II)
  • Causes: liver disease, GIT disease, ↓ dietary vitamin K
  • Treatment: vitamin K injection

qs.q: Mention the types of haemophilia.
qs.a:
• A: factor VIII deficiency (85%)
  • B: factor IX deficiency (15%)
  • C: factor XI deficiency (rare)
  • X-linked recessive: females carriers, males affected ("royal disease")

qs.q: Mention the clinical picture of haemophilia.
qs.a:
• Severity depends on factor VIII activity
  • Easy bruising, prolonged bleeding after trauma / procedures
  • Haemarthrosis (knee, elbow), muscle bleeding, internal bleeding
  • No purpura (purpura = capillary / platelet disorder)

qs.q: Mention the diagnosis and treatment of haemophilia.
qs.a:
• ↑ Clotting time (↑ PTT) with normal bleeding time
  • Fresh blood transfusion (VIII lost on storage)
  • Factor VIII / IX from FFP or recombinant factors

qs.q: Define bleeding time and clotting time with normal values.
qs.a:
• Bleeding time: onset of bleeding → temporary platelet plug; 2–5 min
  • Clotting time: onset of bleeding → first fibrin thread; 3–8 min

qs.q: Mention the types of platelet disorders.
qs.a:
• Thrombocytopenia: ↓ count secondary to another cause
  • Idiopathic thrombocytopenia (ITP): unknown cause – most important
  • Thrombasthenia: defective function (normal count)

qs.q: Mention the causes and risk factors of hypercoagulable state.
qs.a:
• Genetic: antithrombin III deficiency, protein C deficiency, plasminogen abnormalities
  • Acquired: atherosclerosis, hyperlipidaemia, slow blood flow, smoking, uncontrolled DM, HTN
  • Deep-seated tumours (pancreatic, ovarian)

qs.q: Define purpura and mention its types and causes.
qs.a:
• Capillary abnormality → spontaneous haemorrhage beneath skin, mucosa & organs
  • Primary (idiopathic): congenital, children · secondary: allergy, infection
  • Causes: ↑ capillary fragility (Marfan), thrombocytopenia, ITP, thrombasthenia, allergy, drug toxicity

qs.q: Mention the grades of thrombocytopenic purpura.
qs.a:
• Mild: < 50,000/cumm
  • Moderate: < 10,000/cumm
  • Fulminating: < 1,000/cumm

qs.q: Mention natural and synthetic anticoagulants.
qs.a:
• Natural: heparin, protein C, protein S
  • Synthetic in vivo: heparin (post-operative), aspirin (anti-platelet aggregation), vitamin K antagonists (dicoumarol, warfarin), NOACs
  • In vitro: heparin (arterial samples), oxalates, citrates, EDTA (↓ Ca²⁺)

qs.q: Compare warfarin and NOACs.
qs.a:
• Warfarin: vitamin K antagonist – slow onset
  • NOACs: act on thrombin or factor X – work within 12–24 h

qs.q: What is EDTA-induced pseudothrombocytopenia?
qs.a:
• EDTA → platelet aggregation in the tube → falsely low count
  • Repeat on citrate + manual count

qs.q: Mention the components of blood and the organs of the haemopoietic system.
qs.a:
• Blood = red cells, white cells, platelets suspended in plasma
  • Plasma = liquid part of un-clotted blood (contains soluble fibrinogen); serum = what remains after the fibrin clot forms
  • Haemopoietic system: bone marrow, liver, spleen, lymph nodes, thymus
  • Life span of RBCs ≈ 120 days

qs.q: Describe the sites of haematopoiesis from the embryo to adult life. What is extramedullary haemopoiesis?
qs.a:
• Embryo: yolk sac → then liver & spleen
  • From 7 months' gestation: bone marrow becomes the main source
  • Childhood & adult life: the bone marrow is the only source of blood cells
  • Extramedullary haemopoiesis = resumption of haemopoiesis in the liver & spleen when a disease interferes with normal marrow haemopoiesis (e.g. thalassaemia)

qs.q: Mention the stages of development of red blood cells.
qs.a: • Stem cell → proerythroblast → erythroblast → normoblast → reticulocyte → mature RBC

qs.q: Define MCV and RDW and give their clinical value.
qs.a:
• MCV (mean corpuscular volume) → classifies anaemia by RBC size: microcytic < 80 fL, normocytic 80–96, macrocytic > 96 fL
  • RDW (red cell distribution width) = variability in RBC size
  • ↑ RDW = anisocytosis → typical of iron deficiency
  • Haematocrit (PCV) = volume percentage of RBCs in blood

qs.q: What are reticulocytes? Mention the causes of a high and a low reticulocyte count.
qs.a:
• Young red cells, normally less than 2.5% of red cells
  • Reticulocyte count = guide to erythroid (marrow) activity
  • High: ↑ marrow activity → haemorrhage, haemolysis, response to a specific haematinic
  • Low with anaemia: inappropriate marrow response → bone marrow failure or haematinic deficiency

qs.q: Describe the structure of haemoglobin and mention the types of adult haemoglobin.
qs.a:
• Hb = 4 globin chains, each with an iron-containing haem (Fe²⁺ + protoporphyrin)
  • Function: carries O₂ to tissues and returns CO₂ to the lungs
  • HbA (α2β2): ≈ 97%
  • HbA2 (α2δ2): 1.5–3.2%
  • HbF (α2γ2): < 1%

qs.q: Define anaemia in adults.
qs.a:
• Males: haematocrit < 41% (Hb < 13.6 g/dL)
  • Females: haematocrit < 36% (Hb < 12 g/dL)

qs.q: Mention the classification of anaemia according to the MCV with examples.
qs.a:
TypeMCVExamples
Microcytic hypochromic< 80 fLIron deficiency, thalassaemia, anaemia of chronic disease, sideroblastic anaemia
Normocytic normochromicNormalAcute blood loss, anaemia of chronic disease, CKD, autoimmune rheumatic disease, marrow infiltration / fibrosis, endocrine disease, haemolytic anaemias
Macrocytic – megaloblastic> 96 fLVitamin B12 or folate deficiency
Macrocytic – normoblastic> 96 fLAlcohol, ↑ reticulocytes (haemolysis, haemorrhage), liver disease, hypothyroidism, drugs (azathioprine)

qs.q: Mention other ways of classifying anaemia.
qs.a:
• By mechanism: decreased production or increased destruction (haemolysis) ± blood loss
  • By origin: inherited or acquired
  • By red cell size: MCV (microcytic / normocytic / macrocytic)

qs.q: Mention the compensatory mechanisms in anaemia.
qs.a:
• ↓ Hb–O₂ affinity via ↑ 2,3-DPG → O₂ released easily to tissues
  • ↓ perfusion of non-vital organs (blood redirected to vital organs)
  • ↑ cardiac output, mainly by ↑ heart rate
  • ↑ erythropoietin secretion
  • Explains why slowly developing anaemia may be asymptomatic (e.g. Hb 9 found by chance)

qs.q: Mention the symptoms and general signs of anaemia.
qs.a:
• May be asymptomatic: slow fall in Hb allows haemodynamic compensation; rapid loss → severe symptoms, especially in the elderly
  • Symptoms (non-specific): breathlessness, fatigue, headache, palpitations, faintness
  • Exacerbates cardiorespiratory disease in the elderly → angina, intermittent claudication
  • Signs: pallor, tachycardia, systolic flow (haemic) murmur, heart failure in severe anaemia

qs.q: Mention the specific signs that point to the type of anaemia.
qs.a:
• Koilonychia (spoon nails) → longstanding iron deficiency
  • Jaundice → haemolytic anaemia
  • Bone deformities → thalassaemia major
  • Leg ulcers → sickle cell disease
  • Anaemia is not a final diagnosis – a cause must always be sought

qs.q: Mention the investigations of a patient with anaemia (low haemoglobin).
qs.a:
• Red cell indices (MCV, MCH, RDW)
  • Total leucocytic count & platelet count
  • Reticulocyte count (marrow activity)
  • Blood film – abnormal morphology may give the diagnosis
  • Bone marrow examination – to investigate abnormalities found in peripheral blood

qs.q: Mention the causes of iron deficiency anaemia.
qs.a:
• Deficient diet
  • ↓ Absorption: autoimmune gastritis, H. pylori gastritis, coeliac disease (even if asymptomatic)
  • ↑ Requirements: pregnancy, lactation
  • Chronic blood loss: GIT, menstrual, frequent blood donation; prolonged aspirin / NSAIDs
  • Most important cause in adults = chronic blood loss (menstrual & gastrointestinal)

qs.q: Why is iron deficiency the commonest cause of anaemia worldwide? When must the GIT be investigated?
qs.a:
• Most common cause of anaemia globally – affects 30% of the world's population
  • Body has limited ability to absorb iron + frequent loss by bleeding
  • Most dietary iron is ferric (Fe³⁺) – insoluble, poor bioavailability; ferrous (Fe²⁺) is better absorbed
  • If menorrhagia, uterine bleeding and blood donation are excluded → search for GIT bleeding (upper & lower endoscopy)

qs.q: Mention the clinical features specific to longstanding iron deficiency.
qs.a:
• Brittle nails & koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails)
  • Atrophy of tongue papillae, angular stomatitis (not pathognomonic)
  • Brittle hair
  • Plummer–Vinson syndrome: dysphagia + glossitis + oesophageal webs
  • Pica: craving for non-food items (ice, clay, soil, paper)

qs.q: Mention the investigations of iron deficiency anaemia.
qs.a:
• CBC: microcytic (MCV < 80 fL), hypochromic (MCH < 27 pg); poikilocytosis & anisocytosis (↑ RDW)
  • Iron profile: ↓ serum iron, ↓ ferritin, ↑ TIBC; ↓ transferrin saturation (more accurate than serum iron)
  • Low serum ferritin confirms the diagnosis (stored iron) – but it is an acute-phase reactant and may be normal with inflammation / malignancy
  • ↑ Serum soluble transferrin receptors
  • Investigations for the cause: upper & lower GIT endoscopy

qs.q: Mention the principles of management of iron deficiency anaemia.
qs.a:
• Find and treat the underlying cause (e.g. bleeding source)
  • Give iron to correct the anaemia and replace iron stores
  • Oral iron first; parenteral iron when oral fails or is not tolerated

qs.q: Mention the details of oral iron therapy and the expected response.
qs.a:
• Ferrous sulfate 325 mg once daily or every other day, on an empty stomach
  • Side effects: nausea, constipation → poor compliance; with food ↓ side effects but ↓ absorption
  • Response: haematocrit halfway to normal in 3 weeks, full recovery in 2 months
  • Continue for 3–6 months after normal values to replenish stores

qs.q: Mention the causes of failure of response to oral iron therapy.
qs.a:
• Non-compliance (commonest)
  • Wrong diagnosis: anaemia of chronic disease, thalassaemia
  • Coeliac disease (malabsorption)
  • Ongoing blood loss exceeding new erythropoiesis

qs.q: Mention the indications and preparations of parenteral iron.
qs.a:
• Indications: intolerance of or refractoriness to oral iron, GIT disease precluding oral iron (e.g. IBD), continued blood loss that cannot be corrected
  • Dose: most need 1–1.5 g (corrects deficit + refills stores)
  • Preparations: low-molecular-weight iron dextran, iron sucrose, ferric carboxymaltose, iron isomaltoside (slow IV infusion)
  • Iron dextran: test dose required because of the risk of anaphylactoid reactions

qs.q: Mention the causes of anaemia of chronic disease.
qs.a:
• Chronic inflammatory disease: Crohn's disease, rheumatoid arthritis, SLE
  • Malignant disease
  • Chronic infections: e.g. tuberculosis

qs.q: Explain the pathogenesis of anaemia of chronic disease.
qs.a:
• ↓ Release of iron from marrow stores to developing erythroblasts
  • Inadequate erythropoietin response to the anaemia
  • ↓ Red cell survival
  • Mediated by hepcidin, mainly through elevated IL-6 → ↓ iron absorption from gut + ↓ iron transfer from macrophages
  • = iron-restricted erythropoiesis: the patient has iron but cannot use it

qs.q: What is hepcidin? Mention its role in iron metabolism.
qs.a:
• Iron-regulating peptide hormone made in the liver
  • Controls delivery of iron to plasma from intestinal cells, macrophages (RBC recycling) and hepatocytes (stores)
  • ↑ Hepcidin (IL-6) → iron trapped → anaemia of chronic disease
  • Measuring hepcidin helps distinguish ACD (high) from IDA

qs.q: Mention the investigations of anaemia of chronic disease.
qs.a:
• CBC: normocytic or microcytic
  • ↓ Serum iron and ↓ TIBC; transferrin saturation may be very low (→ wrongly called IDA)
  • Serum ferritin normal or increased (inflammation); ferritin < 30 ng/mL = coexistent iron deficiency
  • Serum soluble transferrin receptors: normal
  • Elevated hepcidin

qs.q: Compare iron deficiency anaemia and anaemia of chronic disease.
qs.a:
FeatureIron deficiencyAnaemia of chronic disease
MCVMicrocyticNormocytic or microcytic
Serum iron↓↓
TIBC (transferrin)↑↓
Serum ferritin↓ (diagnostic)Normal / ↑
Soluble transferrin receptors↑Normal
Hepcidin↓↑ (IL-6)
TreatmentTreat cause + ironTreat cause; transfusion / EPO if severe

qs.q: Define transferrin and TIBC.
qs.a:
• Transferrin: plasma glycoprotein responsible for ferric-ion delivery – central role in iron metabolism
  • TIBC: capacity of blood to bind iron with transferrin → indirect measure of transferrin; cheaper than measuring transferrin directly
  • TIBC high in IDA, low in anaemia of chronic disease

qs.q: Mention the treatment of anaemia of chronic disease.
qs.a:
• Usually no treatment of the anaemia is needed – manage the cause
  • If severe or affecting quality of life: red cell transfusions or parenteral recombinant erythropoietin (e.g. Eprex)

qs.q: Define sideroblastic anaemia and explain its pathogenesis.
qs.a:
• Inherited or acquired disorder with refractory anaemia (not responding to simple haematinics)
  • Hypochromic cells in blood + excess iron and ring sideroblasts in the marrow
  • Disordered haem synthesis → iron accumulates in erythroblast mitochondria → ring of iron granules around the nucleus
  • Ineffective haem synthesis → microcytic hypochromic cells

qs.q: Mention the causes and management of sideroblastic anaemia.
qs.a:
• Acquired: myeloproliferative disorders, myeloid leukaemia, drugs (isoniazid), alcohol, lead toxicity
  • Also with RA, carcinomas, megaloblastic & haemolytic anaemias
  • Management: does not respond to iron; withdraw drugs / alcohol
  • Some respond to pyridoxine; folic acid for accompanying folate deficiency

qs.q: Mention the differential diagnosis of microcytic hypochromic anaemia and how to differentiate them.
qs.a:
• Iron deficiency: ↓ ferritin, ↑ TIBC, ↑ RDW
  • Anaemia of chronic disease: normal/↑ ferritin, ↓ TIBC
  • Thalassaemia trait: normal ferritin & iron stores, normal RDW, ↑ HbA2 on electrophoresis
  • Sideroblastic anaemia: ↑ iron, ring sideroblasts in marrow, refractory to iron

qs.q: Define megaloblastic anaemia and mention its causes.
qs.a:
• Marrow erythroblasts with delayed nuclear maturation because of defective DNA synthesis (megaloblasts)
  • Megaloblasts are large with large immature nuclei
  • Causes: vitamin B12 deficiency / abnormal metabolism and folic acid deficiency / abnormal metabolism

qs.q: Differentiate macrocytic from megaloblastic anaemia. Mention causes of macrocytosis without megaloblastic changes.
qs.a:
• Macrocytic = large RBCs in peripheral blood (↑ MCV)
  • Megaloblastic = large cells with delayed nuclear maturation in the bone marrow
  • Macrocytosis with a normoblastic marrow: pregnancy (physiological), newborn, alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, reticulocytosis, drugs (azathioprine)

qs.q: Mention the haematological findings of megaloblastic anaemia.
qs.a:
• MCV > 96 fL
  • Film: oval macrocytes + hypersegmented polymorphs (≥ 6 nuclear lobes)
  • If severe: pancytopenia (leucopenia + thrombocytopenia)
  • ↑ LDH (ineffective erythropoiesis)

qs.q: Mention the essentials of diagnosis of vitamin B12 deficiency. Mention the sources of vitamin B12.
qs.a:
• Macrocytic anaemia
  • Megaloblastic smear: macro-ovalocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils
  • Low serum vitamin B12
  • Sources: made by microorganisms; found in meat, fish, eggs, milk – not in plants

qs.q: Mention the causes of vitamin B12 deficiency.
qs.a:
• The most common cause in adults is pernicious anaemia
  • Diet (extremely rare): strict vegetarians (vegans) avoiding meat, fish and dairy
  • Malabsorption (mild): pancreatitis, coeliac disease, metformin

qs.q: Define pernicious anaemia and mention its associations and antibodies.
qs.a:
• Autoimmune atrophic gastritis → loss of parietal cells → failure of intrinsic factor production → ↓ B12 absorption
  • Associated autoimmune diseases: thyroid disease, Addison's disease, vitiligo
  • Parietal cell antibodies: in 90% (sensitive)
  • Intrinsic factor antibodies: only 50% but specific for the diagnosis

qs.q: Mention the clinical manifestations of vitamin B12 deficiency.
qs.a:
• Anaemia: moderate to severe, slow onset; ± leucopenia & thrombocytopenia (infection, bleeding)
  • GIT: glossitis, anorexia, diarrhoea
  • Neurological: subacute combined degeneration of the cord
  • Peripheral nerves affected first → paraesthesia
  • Posterior columns → impaired balance / proprioception
  • Advanced: altered cerebral function

qs.q: Mention the investigations of vitamin B12 deficiency.
qs.a:
• Hb: moderate–severe anaemia; MCV 110–140 fL
  • ↓ Reticulocytes; ↓ WBCs & platelets in severe cases (all cell lines affected)
  • Bone marrow: ↑ megaloblasts
  • ↑ Bilirubin & LDH (intramedullary destruction – ineffective erythropoiesis)
  • Serum B12 < 160 ng/L; parietal cell & intrinsic factor antibodies

qs.q: Mention the treatment of vitamin B12 deficiency.
qs.a:
• Initially parenteral B12: daily for 1 week → weekly for 1 month → monthly for life
  • Deficiency recurs if therapy stops
  • After correction: oral / sublingual methylcobalamin 1 mg/day may replace injections – continued indefinitely with B12 monitoring
  • Folic acid 1 mg daily for the first months (concurrent deficiency from mucosal atrophy)

qs.q: Mention the causes of folic acid deficiency.
qs.a:
• Folic acid is in most fruits and vegetables; requirement 50–100 mcg/day; stores ≈ 5 mg (2–3 months)
  • Most common cause: inadequate dietary intake
  • ↑ Requirements (5–10×): pregnancy, haemolytic anaemia, exfoliative skin disease
  • ↓ Absorption (rare): medications – phenytoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, sulfasalazine; GI mucosal atrophy with B12 deficiency

qs.q: Mention the essentials of diagnosis of folic acid deficiency.
qs.a:
• Macrocytic anaemia with megaloblastic smear (identical to B12 deficiency)
  • Red cell folate < 150 ng/mL = diagnostic
  • Normal serum vitamin B12 – must always be measured
  • No neurological abnormalities

qs.q: Why must vitamin B12 be measured before treating folic acid deficiency?
qs.a:
• Isolated folic acid deficiency does not cause neurological abnormalities
  • Large doses of folic acid correct the blood picture of B12 deficiency but permit neurologic damage to progress
  • Folate deficiency may itself be a consequence of GI mucosal atrophy from B12 deficiency
  • So B12 deficiency → give B12 (± folate); folate deficiency → check B12 first
  • Treatment of folate deficiency: oral folic acid 1 mg daily

qs.q: Compare vitamin B12 and folic acid deficiency.
qs.a:
FeatureVitamin B12 deficiencyFolic acid deficiency
SourceAnimal food onlyMost fruits & vegetables
Body storesLarge (years)≈ 5 mg (2–3 months)
Commonest causePernicious anaemiaInadequate diet
Blood pictureMegaloblastic, MCV 110–140Identical
Neurological featuresYes – subacute combined degenerationNo
DiagnosisSerum B12 < 160 ng/LRBC folate < 150 ng/mL, normal B12
TreatmentParenteral B12 for lifeOral folic acid 1 mg/day

qs.q: Define aplastic anaemia and mention its essentials of diagnosis.
qs.a:
• Bone marrow failure from suppression of / injury to the haematopoietic stem cell → hypoplastic marrow → pancytopenia
  • Essentials: pancytopenia · no abnormal haematopoietic cells in blood or marrow · hypocellular bone marrow

qs.q: Mention the causes of aplastic anaemia.
qs.a:
• Idiopathic (commonest): autoimmune T-cell-mediated suppression of haematopoiesis
  • Direct stem cell injury: radiation, chemotherapy, toxins, drugs
  • SLE (rarely)
  • Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH)
  • Viruses (complex immune responses)

qs.q: Mention the clinical picture of aplastic anaemia and the criteria of severe aplastic anaemia.
qs.a:
• RBCs ↓: weakness, fatigue
  • Neutropenia: bacterial & fungal infections
  • Thrombocytopenia: mucosal & skin bleeding
  • Severe: neutrophils < 500/mcL, platelets < 20,000/mcL, reticulocytes < 1%, marrow cellularity < 20% (normal 30–70%)

qs.q: Mention the laboratory findings of aplastic anaemia.
qs.a:
• Hallmark = pancytopenia (early: only 1–2 lines may be low)
  • Anaemia always with reticulocytopenia; RBC morphology unremarkable
  • ↓ Neutrophils & platelets with no immature or abnormal forms
  • Bone marrow aspirate & biopsy hypocellular with scant normal progenitors

qs.q: Mention the treatment of aplastic anaemia.
qs.a:
• Mild: supportive – erythropoietic (epoetin, darbepoetin) ± myeloid (filgrastim) growth factors
  • RBC & platelet transfusions as needed; antibiotics for infections
  • < 40 years with HLA-matched sibling: allogeneic bone marrow transplantation (treatment of choice)
  • > 40 years or no matched donor (severe idiopathic): immunosuppression & corticosteroids

qs.q: What is adult pure red cell aplasia? Mention its associations and treatment.
qs.a:
• Failure of one cell line only (red cells)
  • Associated with thymoma in 5–15% – thymectomy may induce remission
  • Also autoimmune disease or idiopathic
  • Treatment: steroids, cyclophosphamide, azathioprine, cyclosporin

qs.q: Define haemolytic anaemia. What is compensated haemolytic disease?
qs.a:
• Anaemia due to increased destruction of red cells → RBC survival much shorter than 120 days
  • Normal breakdown occurs in macrophages of marrow, liver and spleen
  • Compensatory increase in red cell production by the bone marrow – marrow can raise output 6–8 times
  • If loss is within marrow capacity → haemolysis without anaemia = compensated haemolytic disease
  • Marrow expansion into unusual sites (skull, phalanges) → thalassaemic features

qs.q: Compare extravascular and intravascular haemolysis.
qs.a:
FeatureExtravascularIntravascular
FrequencyMost haemolytic conditionsLess common
SiteMacrophages of RES, especially the spleenWithin the circulation
ExampleSpherocytosis (→ splenectomy, vaccinate first)Rapid destruction → free Hb
Free HbNoBound to haptoglobin → saturated → haemoglobinuria

qs.q: Mention the consequences (pathophysiology) of haemolysis.
qs.a:
• ↑ Indirect bilirubin – liver ↑ conjugation 8–10× → jaundice mild/absent; severe → frank jaundice
  • Anaemia – marrow ↑ output up to 8×; severe → frank anaemia
  • Free Hb (intravascular) binds haptoglobin & haemopexin → taken by RES → ↓ levels in blood
  • Excessive haemolysis saturating haptoglobin & haemopexin → haemoglobinuria

qs.q: Mention the causes of haemolytic anaemia.
qs.a:
• Intrinsic (intracorpuscular) – inherited (except PNH):
  • Membrane: hereditary spherocytosis, PNH (acquired)
  • Haemoglobinopathies: sickle cell anaemia, HbC
  • Globin synthesis defect: thalassaemia
  • Enzyme: G6PD & pyruvate kinase deficiency
  • Extrinsic (extracorpuscular) – acquired: autoimmune haemolysis, mechanical (prosthetic valve, microangiopathic), infection (malaria, clostridia), chemicals (drugs, snake venom), hypersplenism

qs.q: Mention the investigations of haemolytic anaemia.
qs.a:
• Blood picture: usually normocytic normochromic; brisk reticulocytosis; ↑ WBCs & platelets
  • Bone marrow: erythroid hyperplasia (normoblastic; megaloblastic if folate deficient); aplasia in aplastic crisis
  • ↑ Indirect bilirubin, ↑ LDH, ↓ haptoglobin & haemopexin
  • Urine & stool: ↑ urobilinogen, ↑ stercobilin
  • Special: blood film (spherocytes, target cells), Hb electrophoresis (HbF, HbS), osmotic fragility (spherocytosis), sickling test, Ham's test (PNH), Coombs' test (autoimmune)
  • Red cell survival: ⁵¹Cr-labelled RBCs

qs.q: Define thalassaemia and explain why it causes microcytic hypochromic anaemia.
qs.a:
• Hereditary disorders with reduced synthesis of globin chains (α or β)
  • ↓ Globin → ↓ Hb synthesis → defective haemoglobinisation → hypochromic microcytic anaemia
  • α-globin: 2 genes on each chromosome 16 (4 in total); no substitute for α in adult Hb
  • β-globin: 1 gene on each chromosome 11

qs.q: Explain the pathogenesis of β-thalassaemia.
qs.a:
• Homozygous or compound heterozygous: no β chains (β⁰) or very reduced (β⁺)
  • Excess of α chains precipitate in erythroblasts and red cells
  • → ineffective erythropoiesis and haemolysis
  • Carrier: excess α combines with δ → ↑ HbA2 (used for carrier screening)

qs.q: Mention the features of β-thalassaemia trait (carrier) and how to differentiate it from iron deficiency.
qs.a:
• Heterozygous carriers: asymptomatic microcytosis with or without mild anaemia
  • Hypochromic microcytic RBCs (↓ MCV, ↓ MCH) → may be confused with IDA
  • Serum ferritin and iron stores are normal; RDW usually normal
  • Hb electrophoresis: raised HbA2 + slightly ↑ HbF
  • Do not give iron unless coincidental iron deficiency is proven

qs.q: Mention the features of non-transfusion-dependent thalassaemia (thalassaemia intermedia).
qs.a:
• Symptomatic moderate anaemia (Hb 7–10 g/dL) without regular transfusions
  • Effects of excess α-chains are attenuated: co-inherited α-thalassaemia or ↑ γ chains (hereditary persistence of HbF)
  • → less α precipitation → ↓ ineffective erythropoiesis and haemolysis
  • Features: splenomegaly, bone deformities, recurrent leg ulcers, gallstones, infections

qs.q: Mention the clinical presentation of transfusion-dependent thalassaemia (thalassaemia major).
qs.a:
• Presents in the first year of life
  • Failure to thrive and recurrent bacterial infections
  • Severe anaemia from 3 to 6 months (switch from γ to β chains)
  • Extramedullary haemopoiesis → hepatosplenomegaly and bone expansion → thalassaemic facies
  • Skull X-ray: "hair-on-end" appearance; hand X-ray shows marrow expansion

qs.q: Mention the management of symptomatic (major) thalassaemia.
qs.a:
• Folic acid supplements
  • Regular transfusions every 4–6 weeks to keep Hb > 10 g/dL
  • Splenectomy if transfusion need > 200–220 mL RBCs/kg/year (↓ transfusions, iron overload & extramedullary haemopoiesis)
  • Splenectomy delayed until after age 6 because of infection risk; prophylaxis required (vaccines)
  • Iron chelation: oral deferasirox once daily (standard) or parenteral deferoxamine
  • Bone marrow transplantation: young patients with HLA-matched siblings

qs.q: Mention the complications of iron overload in thalassaemia.
qs.a:
• Caused by repeated transfusions = transfusion haemosiderosis
  • Damages endocrine glands, liver, pancreas, myocardium by adolescence
  • Cardiomyopathy & tachyarrhythmias = leading causes of morbidity and mortality
  • Prevented by iron chelation (deferasirox, deferoxamine)

qs.q: Mention the types of α-thalassaemia according to the number of deleted genes.
qs.a:
• 4 α-genes (2 loci on each chromosome 16); symptoms milder than β-thalassaemia
  • 1 gene deleted: no clinical effect
  • 2 genes: mild hypochromic anaemia
  • 3 genes: HbH disease – moderate anaemia (Hb 7–10) + splenomegaly; no specific therapy, avoid iron, folic acid if needed
  • 4 genes: Hb Bart's – cannot carry O₂ → hydrops fetalis, incompatible with life

qs.q: Compare thalassaemia trait, intermedia and major.
qs.a:
FeatureTrait (carrier)Intermedia (NTDT)Major (TDT)
GeneticsHeterozygous βAttenuated α excessHomozygous / compound heterozygous
AnaemiaAbsent / mildModerate (Hb 7–10)Severe from 3–6 months
TransfusionNoNot regularEvery 4–6 weeks
FeaturesAsymptomatic microcytosisSplenomegaly, leg ulcers, gallstonesHepatosplenomegaly, thalassaemic facies, failure to thrive
Key test↑ HbA2, normal ferritinElectrophoresisElectrophoresis, hair-on-end skull

qs.q: Mention the essentials of diagnosis of sickle cell anaemia.
qs.a:
• Recurrent pain episodes
  • Positive family history + lifelong haemolytic anaemia
  • Irreversibly sickled cells on peripheral smear
  • HbS = the major haemoglobin on electrophoresis

qs.q: Explain the pathogenesis of sickle cell anaemia.
qs.a:
• Autosomal recessive; single base change → valine substitutes glutamate at position 6 of the β chain (βˢ) → HbSS (α2βˢ2)
  • HbS is unstable and polymerises with stressors (hypoxaemia, acidosis) → sickled cells → haemolysis
  • Free Hb → endothelial dysfunction, vascular injury, pulmonary hypertension
  • Sickled cells obstruct the microcirculation → small vessel occlusion → tissue infarction

qs.q: Mention the factors that increase and decrease sickling.
qs.a:
• Increase: red cell dehydration, acidosis, hypoxaemia (↑ deoxy-HbS)
  • Rate depends on intracellular HbS concentration and other Hbs present
  • Decrease: HbF cannot join the polymer → markedly retards sickling (basis of hydroxyurea)

qs.q: Mention the clinical features (complications) of sickle cell disease.
qs.a:
• Vaso-occlusive crises: dactylitis (hands & feet) early; bone pain (femur, humerus, vertebrae, ribs, pelvis) later
  • Pulmonary hypertension (≈ 10%)
  • Acute chest syndrome (up to 30%)
  • Neurological: TIA, fits, cerebral infarction (≈ 25%)
  • Anaemia: chronic stable Hb 6–8 with acute falls (splenic sequestration, aplastic crisis, haemolysis)
  • Leg ulcers

qs.q: Describe the acute chest syndrome in sickle cell disease (causes, features and management).
qs.a:
• Up to 30%; the most common cause of death in adults with sickle cell disease
  • Causes: infection, fat embolism from necrotic marrow, pulmonary infarction from sequestration
  • Features: dyspnoea, chest pain, fever, hypoxia, new CXR consolidation; may kill within hours
  • Management: analgesia, high-flow O₂, antibiotics immediately
  • Exchange transfusion to HbS < 20% if no improvement; mechanical ventilation if needed

qs.q: Mention the causes of an acute fall in haemoglobin in sickle cell anaemia.
qs.a:
• Baseline Hb stable at 6–8 g/dL (chronic haemolysis)
  • Splenic sequestration: painful acute splenic enlargement, pooling of RBCs → hypovolaemia, circulatory collapse (in childhood, before the spleen infarcts and becomes fibrotic)
  • Bone marrow aplasia: usually parvovirus B19 → rapid fall with no reticulocytes; transfuse until recovery
  • Further haemolysis: drugs, acute infection, coexistent G6PD deficiency

qs.q: Mention the investigations of sickle cell anaemia.
qs.a:
• CBC: Hb 6–8 g/dL, high reticulocytes (10–20%)
  • Blood film: sickled cells + features of hyposplenism
  • Sickle solubility test: HbS gives a turbid solution (normal Hb clear)
  • Hb electrophoresis (always needed to confirm): no HbA, 80–95% HbS, 2–20% HbF
  • Parents: show sickle cell trait

qs.q: Mention the management of sickle cell anaemia.
qs.a:
• Avoid & treat precipitating factors quickly
  • Painful crisis: IV fluids + adequate analgesia – morphine is the drug of choice; O₂ & antibiotics only if indicated
  • Infection prophylaxis: penicillin 500 mg daily + pneumococcal, meningococcal & Hib vaccines (functional asplenia)
  • Folic acid for all
  • Transfusion for acute chest syndrome, splenic sequestration or aplastic crisis (target Hb 10, HbS < 30%) – not for steady-state anaemia
  • Hydroxyurea (↑ HbF) and stem cell transplantation

qs.q: What is the role of hydroxyurea in sickle cell anaemia? When is blood transfusion indicated?
qs.a:
• Hydroxyurea ↑ HbF → ↓ sickling
  • Reduces pain episodes, acute chest syndrome and transfusion needs
  • No transfusion: steady-state anaemia, minor surgery, uncomplicated painful episodes
  • Transfuse acutely: acute chest syndrome, splenic sequestration, aplastic crisis → aim Hb 10 g/dL, HbS < 30%

qs.q: Mention the features of sickle cell trait and compare it with thalassaemia trait.
qs.a:
• No symptoms unless extreme anoxia (e.g. flying in a non-pressurised aircraft)
  • 60% HbA + 40% HbS
  • Unlike thalassaemia trait, the blood count and film are normal
  • Diagnosis: positive sickle test or Hb electrophoresis
  • Thalassaemia trait instead shows microcytosis (↓ MCV, MCH) with ↑ HbA2

qs.q: Explain the role of G6PD in red cells.
qs.a:
• Key enzyme of the hexose monophosphate shunt: oxidises glucose-6-phosphate, reducing NADP → NADPH
  • In RBCs it is the only source of NADPH
  • NADPH (via glutathione) protects the red cell from oxidative damage

qs.q: Mention the clinical syndromes of G6PD deficiency.
qs.a:
• Acute drug-induced haemolysis (dose-related)
  • Favism – ingestion of fava beans
  • Chronic haemolytic anaemia (severe Mediterranean variants)
  • Neonatal jaundice
  • Infections & acute illnesses precipitate haemolysis

qs.q: Why is the haemolytic episode in G6PD deficiency self-limited?
qs.a:
• Patients are usually healthy between attacks – no chronic anaemia or splenomegaly
  • Haemolysis is episodic with oxidative stress (infection, drugs, fava beans)
  • Older RBCs (low enzyme activity) are destroyed
  • Replaced by young RBCs (reticulocytes) with adequate functional levels of G6PD

qs.q: Mention the laboratory findings of G6PD deficiency.
qs.a:
• Between episodes: blood is normal
  • During haemolysis: Hb rarely < 8 g/dL, reticulocytosis, ↑ indirect bilirubin
  • Film: "bite" cells / blister cells (splenic pitting of Heinz bodies)
  • G6PD enzyme assay: low – but may be falsely normal if done during or shortly after an episode (reticulocytosis) → repeat weeks later

qs.q: Mention the management of G6PD deficiency.
qs.a:
• Stop any offending drug (e.g. sulfa – do not complete the course)
  • Treat any underlying infection
  • Blood transfusion may be life-saving
  • Splenectomy is not usually helpful

qs.q: Mention the requirements of normal haemostasis (to prevent bleeding).
qs.a:
• Normal vascular wall integrity
  • Normal platelet count and function (normal count with abnormal function still bleeds)
  • Normal coagulation factors
  • Plus natural anticoagulants that keep blood fluid
  • Doctor's analogy: vessel wall = ground, platelets = bricks, coagulation factors = cement

qs.q: Describe the three responses to vessel injury.
qs.a:
• Vessel: vasoconstriction → ↓ blood flow so the plug is not washed away
  • Platelets: activation → adhesion → aggregation = primary plug
  • Coagulation factors: activated → fibrin formation
  • Together → stable haemostatic plug

qs.q: Describe the origin, life span and normal count of platelets.
qs.a:
• Origin: megakaryocytes in the bone marrow
  • Megakaryocyte formation and maturation stimulated by thrombopoietin made in the liver (TPO agonists are used in ITP)
  • Survival: 8–10 days (RBCs 120 days)
  • Destroyed mainly in the spleen
  • Normal count: 150–450 × 10³/µL

qs.q: Mention the platelet surface glycoprotein receptors and what each binds.
qs.a:
• GP Ia: collagen of damaged subendothelium (adhesion)
  • GP Ib: von Willebrand factor (adhesion)
  • GP IIb/IIIa: fibrinogen (aggregation)
  • Sequence: activation → adhesion (Ia, Ib) → aggregation (IIb/IIIa)
  • Doctor: memorise these receptors – everything else is built on them

qs.q: Mention the contents of platelet granules and the dense tubular system.
qs.a:
• Alpha granules: platelet-specific proteins – PF-4, vWF
  • Dense tubular system: Ca²⁺, prostaglandins and cyclo-oxygenase
  • Aspirin inhibits COX → ↓ platelet activation (antiplatelet)

qs.q: Mention the pathways of the coagulation cascade and the test for each.
qs.a:
• Extrinsic (tissue factor) pathway: factors 3 and 7 → measured by PT – initiates coagulation (mnemonic: "حرب 73")
  • Intrinsic (contact activation) pathway: factors 12, 11, 9, 8 → measured by PTT
  • Common pathway: factors 10, 5, 2, 1 (each number about half the one before) → fibrin
  • Factor 13 stabilises fibrin
  • Fibrin strands strengthen the platelet plug (secondary haemostasis)

qs.q: Mention the points of history in a bleeding case.
qs.a:
• Frequency and severity of bleeding
  • Sites and duration (epistaxis, menorrhagia, skin purpura…) – separate one disease from another
  • Age at presentation (inherited vs acquired)
  • Family history
  • Drug history (aspirin, anticoagulants)
  • Surgical / post-operative bleeding (CBC, PT/INR, PTT before any operation)
  • Spontaneous or after trauma (e.g. post-partum)
  • Other medical conditions – liver disease is one of the commonest causes

qs.q: Classify skin bleeding by size and differentiate thrombocytopenic from vascular purpura.
qs.a:
• Petechiae: pinpoint < 2 mm
  • Purpura: 2 mm – 1 cm
  • Ecchymoses: > 1 cm (can happen to anyone after a knock)
FeatureThrombocytopenic purpuraVascular purpura
PalpableNon-palpable, flatPalpable, raised
BlanchingNon-blanchableBlanchable
CauseLow platelet count, blood outside vesselVasculitis / vessel wall disease

qs.a:

SitesNose, gums, menstrual, skinJoints, muscles, internal (brain, retroperitoneal, renal)
PetechiaeCharacteristicRare

qs.q: Mention the laboratory investigations of a bleeding disorder and what each detects.
qs.a:

qs.q: Classify the haematological causes of bleeding disorders.
qs.a:
• Blood vessels: congenital (HHT); acquired (vasculitis, scurvy, senile purpura, HSP)
  • Platelets: thrombocytopenia (ITP); thrombasthenia (function defect)
  • Coagulation: extrinsic, intrinsic or combined

qs.q: Describe the Hess (capillary fragility) test and bleeding time.
qs.a:
• Hess test: BP cuff at 120/80 on the arm for 5 minutes; count petechiae in a 2.5 × 2.5 cm circle at the cubital fossa
  • > 10 petechiae = positive → vascular wall abnormality or platelet disorder (tests primary haemostasis)
  • To separate: CBC (low platelets = platelet disorder); if normal → platelet function test; if normal → vessel problem
  • Bleeding time: prolonged in platelet or vessel disorders; clinical test, rarely done now

qs.q: Describe hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler–Weber–Rendu).
qs.a:
• Inherited, autosomal dominant
  • Telangiectasia (dilated vessels) and small aneurysms on fingertips, face, tongue, nasal passages, lung and GI tract
  • Presents with recurrent epistaxis or iron deficiency from occult GI bleeding
  • GI lesions are the most dangerous – cannot be compressed
  • PAVMs (pulmonary AV malformations) → hypoxaemia from right-to-left shunt
  • Labs: platelets, PT and PTT normal (vascular fragility)

qs.q: Mention the treatment of hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia.
qs.a:
• Regular iron therapy lets the marrow compensate for blood loss
  • Local cautery or APC (argon plasma coagulation) / laser for single bleeding lesions
  • Every IDA patient needs upper and lower endoscopy
  • Screen all HHT patients for PAVMs; if found → percutaneous embolisation

qs.q: Describe vascular Ehlers–Danlos syndrome as a bleeding disorder.
qs.a:
• Type 4, rare, autosomal dominant
  • Defect in type 3 collagen → fragile vessels and organ membranes → bleeding and organ rupture
  • Bleeding usually after trauma; joint hypermobility often limited; typical skin and facial changes
  • Suspect when there is bleeding with normal laboratory tests

qs.q: Describe scurvy as a bleeding disorder.
qs.a:
• Vitamin C deficiency → defective collagen synthesis
  • Perifollicular and petechial haemorrhage, bruising, subperiosteal bleeding
  • Commonest: gingival bleeding and hypertrophy
  • Key to diagnosis: dietary history

qs.q: Mention the acquired vascular causes of bleeding.
qs.a:
• Vasculitis: small-vessel vasculitis and HSP (palpable purpura)
  • Senile purpura: ageing collagen → spontaneous purpura in the elderly (exclude low platelets first)
  • Drugs: steroids – thin skin and vessels (like striae in Cushing)

qs.a:

qs.q: Enumerate the inherited platelet function abnormalities.
qs.a:
• Glanzmann's thrombasthenia – aggregation defect; deficient GP IIb/IIIa; AR; worst type, may bleed spontaneously
  • Bernard–Soulier disease – adhesion defect; defective granules (dense/delta); thrombocytopenia
  • Congenital macrothrombocytopathies – adhesion defect; large platelets, Döhle bodies, sensorineural deafness, renal abnormalities
  • von Willebrand disease – adhesion defect
  • Asked last year as an enumeration

qs.q: Mention the investigations and treatment of inherited platelet function disorders.
qs.a:
• Bleeding time prolonged; platelet function test abnormal (adhesion vs aggregation tests separate them)
  • Usually mild – bleeding after trauma or surgery, rarely spontaneous (except Glanzmann)
  • Local mechanical measures
  • Antifibrinolytics (tranexamic acid)
  • Platelet transfusion in severe bleeding

qs.q: Mention the drugs affecting platelet function and their mode of action.
qs.a:
Mode of actionDrugs
COX inhibitionAspirin
ADP (P2Y12) receptor inhibitionClopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor
GP IIb/IIIa inhibitionAbciximab, tirofiban, eptifibatide

  • Doctor: physiology table – not asked, just know the names

qs.q: Define ITP and explain its pathogenesis.
qs.a:
• Immune (idiopathic) thrombocytopenic purpura – primary isolated thrombocytopenia
  • Mediated by autoantibodies, most often against platelet GP IIb/IIIa
  • Antibody-coated platelets are removed prematurely by the RE system (spleen)
  • Often follows a viral infection; children and young females (20s)
  • Most cases are discovered accidentally on routine CBC

qs.q: Mention the causes of secondary ITP.
qs.a:
• Connective tissue diseases
  • HIV infection
  • B-cell malignancies
  • H. pylori (every ITP patient → H. pylori stool test)
  • Pregnancy
  • Certain drugs
  • ITP + autoimmune haemolytic anaemia = Evans syndrome

qs.q: Correlate the platelet count with symptoms.
qs.a:
Platelet countSymptoms
50–100 × 10³/µLProlonged bleeding after trauma
< 50 × 10³/µLEasy bruising; purpura after minor trauma
< 20 × 10³/µLSpontaneous bleeding, petechiae; spontaneous internal and intracranial bleeding

qs.q: Mention the clinical features of ITP.
qs.a:
• Adults: females more, insidious onset; preceding viral infection more in children
  • Mild: counts > 50 × 10⁹/L – discovered by chance
  • Moderate: easy bruising, epistaxis or menorrhagia
  • Severe: spontaneous bleeding when platelets < 20 × 10⁹/L
  • Connective tissue disease features may appear at presentation or years later
  • Splenomegaly in 7% only

qs.q: Mention the investigations of ITP.
qs.a:
• CBC: low platelet count; film normal apart from few platelets (RBCs, WBCs normal)
  • Bleeding time prolonged
  • Anti-platelet antibodies
  • Bone marrow: hyperplasia of megakaryocytes (production fine, destruction in spleen)
  • Marrow in patients > 60 years to look for an accompanying B-cell malignancy
  • HIV and viral hepatitis testing; autoantibodies if CTD likely
  • Pancytopenia instead → aplastic anaemia (empty marrow, low retics) or hypersplenism

qs.q: Mention the management of ITP.
qs.a:
• Platelets > 30 × 10⁹/L and stable: conservative – follow-up CBC only (not steroids, not platelets), except before surgery or biopsy
  • 30 leaves a safety margin of 10 above the spontaneous-bleeding level of 20
  • First line for spontaneous bleeding: prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day (suppresses antibody and phagocytosis)
  • IVIg blocks RE antibody receptors; can be combined with steroids (expensive)
  • Platelet transfusion only for persistent or life-threatening bleeding
  • Relapses: re-introduce steroids; two relapses or refractory → splenectomy
  • About one third remit spontaneously

qs.q: Describe the management of refractory ITP.
qs.a:
• Splenectomy: complete remission ~70%, improvement ~20% → only 10% need further therapy
  • Before splenectomy: vaccinate against encapsulated organisms (H. influenzae, pneumococci, meningococci)
  • Persistent after splenectomy: romiplostim (TPO analogue) or eltrombopag (TPO receptor agonist) – raise production; expensive
  • Others: low-dose steroids, rituximab, cyclosporin, tacrolimus – strong immunosuppression → strict infection precautions

qs.q: Mention the causes of thrombocytopenia.
qs.a:
• Decreased production: marrow hypoplasia (aplastic, Fanconi), infiltration (leukaemia, lymphoma)
  • Familial: Bernard–Soulier and other inherited forms
  • Increased consumption: ITP, hypersplenism (the two commonest)
  • Thrombotic microangiopathies: HUS, TTP

qs.a:

qs.q: Classify coagulation disorders.
qs.a:
• Inherited (↓ synthesis of a factor): von Willebrand disease, haemophilia A and B
  • Acquired:
  • Under-production: liver failure
  • Increased consumption: DIC
  • Inhibition of function: heparin, warfarin, immune inhibitors (acquired haemophilia A – antibody against F8)

qs.q: Mention the characteristics and genetics of haemophilia A.
qs.a:
• Factor VIII deficiency – most common congenital coagulation factor deficiency
  • F8 made mainly by the liver (80%) and endothelium (20%) (basis of DDAVP)
  • Half-life ~12 hours (repeat dose every 12 h if bleeding continues)
  • Protected from proteolysis by binding vWF
  • Gene on the X chromosome → X-linked recessive: males affected, females carriers
  • All daughters of a haemophiliac male are obligate carriers; each of their pregnancies has a 1 in 4 chance of an affected male

qs.q: Mention the clinical manifestations of haemophilia A.
qs.a:
• Bleeding after circumcision in a male child (only PTT prolonged)
  • Child falls in the garden → knee haematoma = haemophilia (classic exam case)
  • Massive bruising, muscle haematoma, retroperitoneal haemorrhage
  • Haemophilic arthropathy
  • Internal bleeding is difficult – surgical exploration increases bleeding

qs.q: Describe the severity grades of haemophilia A.
qs.a:
• Pattern of bleeding relates to the residual factor VIII level
  • Severe: < 1% (< 0.01 U/mL) → spontaneous bleeding into skin, muscles, joints; retroperitoneal and intracranial (can be fatal)
  • Moderate: 1–5% (0.01–0.05 U/mL) → bleeding after mild trauma or surgery
  • Mild: > 5–40% (> 0.05–0.4 U/mL) → excess bleeding after major injury or surgery
  • Summary: severe < 1%; mild–moderate 1–40%

qs.q: Describe the musculoskeletal complications of haemophilia.
qs.a:
• Bleeding into large joints: knees, elbows, ankles, hips
  • Untreated → hot, swollen, very painful joint
  • Recurrent haemarthrosis → synovial hypertrophy, cartilage destruction, secondary osteoarthrosis (target joints)
  • Muscle haematomas: calf and psoas
  • Psoas bleed → compresses the femoral nerve
  • Calf haematoma → compartment syndrome → ischaemia, necrosis, fibrosis, shortened Achilles tendon

qs.q: Mention the laboratory findings of haemophilia A.
qs.a:
• Prolonged PTT with normal PT
  • Normal platelet count and normal bleeding time (normal platelet function)
  • Low factor VIII level (check F8 first – commonest; if normal → F9 for haemophilia B)
  • Exam case: PTT prolonged + normal platelet count and function = haemophilia

qs.q: Mention the treatment of severe haemophilia A.
qs.a:
• IV factor VIII concentrate (or cryoprecipitate if unavailable) to raise F8 level
  • Plasma-derived concentrate is screened for HBV, HCV, HIV and virus-inactivated twice
  • Recombinant F8 is safer but more expensive
  • On demand for bleeds; prophylaxis 2–3 times/week in children (limited by cost)
  • Supportive: rest the bleeding site (bed rest / splint), then mobilise with physiotherapy
  • Hepatitis B vaccination for all non-vaccinated recipients of blood products

qs.q: What is the role of DDAVP (desmopressin) in haemophilia A? Mention its contraindication.
qs.a:
• Vasopressin receptor agonist → releases stored vWF and F8 from endothelium, raising them 3–4-fold
  • Used in mild or moderate haemophilia A (and vWD)
  • Dose higher than in DI: 0.3 µg/kg IV or SC, or 300 µg intranasal (dose not required)
  • Contraindicated in severe arterial disease (e.g. coronary disease) – may provoke thrombosis / MI

qs.q: Mention the complications of coagulation factor therapy and the treatment of inhibitors.
qs.a:
• Before 1986: transmission of HIV, HBV, HCV and vCJD (now solved by recombinant factor)
  • Anti-factor VIII antibodies (inhibitors) in ~20% of severe haemophiliacs → neutralise infusions
  • Treatment of inhibitors: activated factor VIIa (NovoSeven) or FEIBA (factor eight inhibitor bypassing activity) – activate the common pathway bypassing F8

qs.q: Describe haemophilia B (Christmas disease).
qs.a:
• Factor IX gene aberration, also on the X chromosome (X-linked)
  • Clinically indistinguishable from haemophilia A but less common
  • Diagnosis by factor IX assay
  • Bleeding frequency relates to F9 level
  • Treatment: factor IX concentrate
  • Inhibitors uncommon (< 1%), but may come with severe allergic reaction

qs.q: Define von Willebrand disease and explain the functions of vWF.
qs.a:
• Common, usually mild bleeding disorder (haemophilia is worse)
  • Quantitative (types 1, 3: low vWF) or qualitative (type 2: abnormal vWF, normal level)
  • vWF made by endothelial cells and megakaryocytes
  • Carrier protein for factor VIII – deficiency lowers F8 (mild haemophilia)
  • Platelet adhesion: binds GP Ib, bridges platelets to subendothelial collagen
  • So bleeding is both platelet-type and coagulation-type (purpura + ecchymosis)

qs.q: Mention the genetics and classification of von Willebrand disease.
qs.a:
• Gene on chromosome 12
  • Usually AD; type 2N and type 3 are AR
  • Type 1: most common, partial deficiency, AD
  • Type 2: abnormal form of vWF, AD
  • Type 3: most severe, severe deficiency, AR
  • Doctor: classification for reading only

qs.q: Mention the investigations of von Willebrand disease. How do you differentiate it from haemophilia A?
qs.a:
• Platelet count: normal
  • Platelet function: adhesion defect; bleeding time prolonged
  • PT normal, PTT prolonged (low F8 – intrinsic)
  • vWF assay reduced; low factor VIII
  • Differentiating point: platelet function (adhesion) / bleeding time abnormal in vWD but normal in haemophilia

qs.q: Mention the treatment of von Willebrand disease.
qs.a:
• Mild haemorrhage: local measures or DDAVP (↑ vWF → secondary ↑ F8)
  • Tranexamic acid for mucosal bleeding
  • Serious or persistent bleeds: selected factor VIII concentrates rich in vWF
  • Type 3: factor VIII concentrate ONLY

qs.q: Enumerate the causes of congenital coagulopathy.
qs.a:
• Any four:
  • Haemophilia A (F8)
  • Haemophilia B (F9)
  • von Willebrand disease
  • Parahaemophilia (factor V deficiency)
  • Factor XIII deficiency
  • Others: severe F7 or F10 deficiency (AR), factor XI deficiency (bleeding unpredictable; severe if < 15%)

qs.q: Enumerate the causes of acquired coagulopathy.
qs.a:
• Liver failure
  • Renal failure
  • Cholestasis (vitamin K malabsorption)
  • Splenomegaly (hypersplenism)
  • Acquired haemophilia (antibody against F8)
  • Also DIC (consumption) and drugs (heparins, warfarin, DOACs)
  • ITP is NOT a coagulopathy – it is a platelet disorder

qs.q: Classify the causes of coagulopathy (Davidson).
qs.a:
• Congenital – X-linked: haemophilia A and B
  • Congenital – autosomal: vWD; factor II, V, VII, X, XI, XIII deficiencies; combined; hypo/dysfibrinogenaemia
  • Acquired – under-production: liver failure
  • Acquired – consumption: DIC
  • Acquired – immune: acquired haemophilia, acquired vWD
  • Acquired – drugs: heparins, fondaparinux, argatroban, rivaroxaban, apixaban, dabigatran, warfarin

qs.q: Explain the mechanisms of bleeding in liver failure and its treatment.
qs.a:
• Bleeding sources more likely: oesophageal varices, peptic ulcer
  • ↓ Hepatic synthesis of factors V, VII, VIII, IX, X, XI, prothrombin and fibrinogen
  • ↑ Plasminogen activator (reduced clearance) → fibrinolysis
  • Thrombocytopenia from hypersplenism (portal hypertension)
  • Cholestatic jaundice (chronic, e.g. PBC) → ↓ vitamin K absorption → ↓ factors II, VII, IX, X
  • Treatment: plasma or platelets only for acute bleeds or procedures (e.g. liver biopsy); parenteral vitamin K for deficiency

qs.q: Explain the bleeding tendency in renal failure and its treatment.
qs.a:
• Severity proportional to plasma urea
  • Platelet dysfunction (uraemic toxins → thrombasthenia); GI haemorrhage common
  • Multifactorial: anaemia, mild thrombocytopenia, retained low-molecular-weight waste inhibiting platelets
  • Treatment: dialysis to lower urea
  • Rarely, severe bleeding → platelet concentrates and red cell transfusion
