qs.q: Describe the initial assessment of a bleeding patient.
qs.a:
• Assess severity: active bleeding or not; site and amount of blood loss
  • Assess haemodynamic stability: BP, pulse (tachycardia is the first sign), level of consciousness
  • Falling BP means the patient is deteriorating
  • Immediate resuscitation if unstable: IV access (cannula), fluids, blood products
  • Keep packed RBCs ready – a patient with Hb 10 gets fluids, but transfuse if Hb drops suddenly

qs.q: How does the type of bleeding help in diagnosis?
qs.a:
• Mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia, petechiae) → platelet or vascular disorder
  • Deep bleeding (haemarthrosis, muscle haematoma, intracranial bleeding) → coagulation factor deficiency

qs.q: What is the significance of age at onset and family history in bleeding disorders?
qs.a:
• Since childhood → inherited; recent onset → acquired
  • A child with excessive bleeding at circumcision → inherited, usually haemophilia
  • Positive family history → inherited (haemophilia, vWD)
  • Haemophilia is X-linked → more in males

qs.q: Mention the drugs to ask about in a bleeding patient and how they are monitored.
qs.a:
• Warfarin → follow up by INR
  • Unfractionated heparin → follow up by PTT
  • DOACs and LMWH → no routine monitoring needed (no specific antidote for DOACs)
  • Antiplatelets: aspirin, clopidogrel; NSAIDs
  • Recent antibiotics → vitamin K deficiency
  • UFH acts on antithrombin (factors 2, 9, 10); LMWH mainly on factor 10

qs.q: Mention the associated medical conditions that cause bleeding.
qs.a:
• Liver disease
  • Renal failure (uraemic toxins affect platelet function and coagulation factors)
  • Malignancy
  • Autoimmune disease
  • Recent infection or sepsis

qs.q: Mention the physical signs to look for in a bleeding patient.
qs.a:
• Petechiae, purpura, ecchymosis
  • Joint swelling (haemarthrosis) – haemophilia
  • Hepatosplenomegaly
  • Signs of chronic liver disease
  • Telangiectasia or palpable purpura (telangiectasia usually hereditary)

qs.q: Mention the initial laboratory investigations of a bleeding patient.
qs.a:
• CBC and platelet count
  • PT / INR
  • aPTT
  • Bleeding time (if available)
  • Peripheral blood film – schistocytes: prosthetic valve, malignancy, MAHA

qs.q: Mention the causes of a low platelet count in a bleeding patient.
qs.a:
• ITP (IgG antibody → splenic destruction)
  • DIC
  • TTP / HUS
  • Hypersplenism
  • Bone marrow failure

qs.q: Mention the causes of normal platelet count with prolonged bleeding time.
qs.a:
• = platelet function defect
  • Aspirin effect
  • Uraemia
  • Toxins
  • von Willebrand disease (adhesive protein)

qs.q: Mention the causes of isolated prolonged PT, isolated prolonged aPTT, and prolonged both.
qs.a:
ResultPathwayCauses
PT only ↑ExtrinsicVitamin K deficiency, warfarin, early liver disease
aPTT only ↑IntrinsicHaemophilia A or B, heparin, lupus anticoagulant
PT + aPTT ↑Combined / commonAdvanced liver disease, DIC, massive transfusion

qs.q: Why does lupus anticoagulant prolong the aPTT, and why does massive transfusion prolong PT and aPTT?
qs.a:
• Antiphospholipid syndrome: antibodies against phospholipid interfere with the coagulation cascade in the test → prolonged PTT
  • Massive transfusion: packed RBCs carry few clotting factors → dilution of coagulation factors → PT and PTT prolonged

qs.q: What is the mixing study and how is it interpreted?
qs.a:
• Done if PT or aPTT is prolonged: patient plasma mixed 50:50 with normal plasma
  • Correction after mixing → factor deficiency
  • No correction → inhibitor present (e.g. lupus anticoagulant, factor VIII inhibitor)

qs.q: Mention the special investigations for bleeding disorders.
qs.a:
• Factor assays (VIII, IX, XI)
  • vWF antigen and activity
  • Fibrinogen level
  • D-dimer (DIC)
  • Liver and renal function tests

qs.q: Mention the general principles of management of bleeding disorders.
qs.a:
• Treat the underlying cause and stop offending drugs
  • Platelet transfusion if indicated (e.g. ITP < 20,000 with bleeding; steroids, IVIG, splenectomy as later steps)
  • FFP for factor deficiency (e.g. liver disease)
  • Specific factor replacement (e.g. haemophilia)
  • Vitamin K (liver disease / deficiency)
  • Antifibrinolytics (tranexamic acid)

qs.q: Case: A 28-year-old woman has easy bruising, epistaxis and menorrhagia 3 weeks after a viral URTI. Petechiae, no splenomegaly. Platelets 18 × 10⁹/L; PT and aPTT normal. Give the diagnosis, pathophysiology, why PT/aPTT are normal, and treatment.
qs.a:
• Diagnosis: immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP)
  • Pathophysiology: IgG autoantibodies against platelet GP IIb/IIIa → premature splenic destruction
  • PT/aPTT normal: coagulation factors are normal; the defect is in primary haemostasis (platelets)
  • Spontaneous bleeding usually when platelets < 20 × 10⁹/L
  • Treatment: prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day; IVIG if severe bleeding; platelet transfusion only for life-threatening bleeding

qs.q: Case: A 7-year-old boy has a painful swollen knee after minor trauma, bled excessively after circumcision; maternal uncles affected. Platelets and PT normal, aPTT prolonged, factor VIII < 1%. Give the diagnosis, inheritance, lab explanation, common bleeding site and treatment.
qs.a:
• Diagnosis: haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) – severe (< 1%)
  • Inheritance: X-linked recessive
  • PT normal, aPTT prolonged: factor VIII is in the intrinsic pathway
  • Commonest site in severe disease: large joints (haemarthrosis) – knees, elbows, ankles
  • Acute bleed treatment: factor VIII concentrate; cryoprecipitate if unavailable
  • Severity: mild > 50%, moderate 1–50%, severe < 1% (per this lecture)

qs.q: Case: A 22-year-old woman has lifelong easy bruising, nosebleeds and bleeding after dental extraction; her mother is similar. Platelets and PT normal, bleeding time prolonged, aPTT mildly prolonged, low vWF and F8. Give the diagnosis, vWF roles, why aPTT is prolonged, inheritance and treatment.
qs.a:
• Diagnosis: von Willebrand disease (type 1 most likely)
  • vWF roles: mediates platelet adhesion to subendothelium; carrier protein for factor VIII
  • aPTT prolonged: low vWF → low factor VIII
  • Inheritance (commonest type): autosomal dominant
  • Mild bleeding: desmopressin (DDAVP) ± tranexamic acid (releases vWF from cells)

qs.q: Case: A 55-year-old cirrhotic man has haematemesis, melena, jaundice, ascites and splenomegaly; platelets 70 × 10⁹/L, PT/INR and aPTT prolonged, low fibrinogen. Explain the bleeding mechanisms and the role of plasma transfusion.
qs.a:
• Mechanisms: ↓ synthesis of clotting factors + thrombocytopenia + hyperfibrinolysis
  • Low platelets: hypersplenism from portal hypertension
  • Reduced factors: II, V, VII, IX, X, XI and fibrinogen
  • Avoid prophylactic plasma: does not correct bleeding risk and may cause volume overload (may worsen variceal bleeding)
  • Plasma indicated: active bleeding or before invasive procedures
  • Severity graded by Child classification

qs.q: Case: A 40-year-old man has recurrent epistaxis, fatigue, small red lesions on lips and tongue; father similar. Hb 9, platelets, PT and aPTT normal. Give the diagnosis, pathology, why tests are normal, complication to screen for and management.
qs.a:
• Diagnosis: hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler–Weber–Rendu)
  • Pathology: abnormal blood vessel formation (endothelial defect)
  • Normal coagulation tests: bleeding is from vascular fragility, not platelets or factors
  • Screen for: pulmonary arteriovenous malformations (PAVMs)
  • Management: iron therapy, local cautery, laser therapy

qs.q: Mention the physiological balance between procoagulant and anticoagulant factors.
qs.a:
• Procoagulant factors: coagulation factors, platelets (main), leucocytes, erythrocytes & vessel-wall components (helpers)
    • Increased → thrombosis (e.g. polycythaemia rubra vera, essential thrombocythaemia, leukaemia)
    • Decreased → bleeding (thrombocytopenia, liver failure)
  • Natural anticoagulant system: protein C, protein S, antithrombin III
    • Decreased → thrombosis (inherited thrombophilias)
  • Thrombosis occurs when the balance is disturbed: ↑ procoagulants or ↓ anticoagulants

qs.q: Mention the components of Virchow's triad with examples.
qs.a:
• Stasis of blood: immobility (bedridden), varicose veins, venous obstruction by tumour / pregnancy, long travel, AF (left atrium)
  • Hypercoagulability (thrombophilia): inherited or acquired
  • Vascular wall abnormalities: vasculitis, trauma, surgery, repeated venipuncture, atherosclerosis
  • Thrombosis usually occurs in veins (slow flow) – the lower limb is the commonest site

qs.q: Mention the medical conditions predisposing to venous thrombosis.
qs.a:
• Inflammatory bowel disease
  • Malignancy
  • Nephrotic syndrome (loss of antithrombin & protein S in urine)
  • Stroke (immobility)
  • Myeloproliferative: polycythaemia rubra vera, essential thrombocythaemia, myelofibrosis
  • PNH
  • Inherited thrombophilia: protein C & S deficiency, antithrombin III deficiency, factor V Leiden
  • Age, obesity, family history
  • Pregnancy / puerperium, contraceptive pills (especially estrogen-containing)
  • Immobility (long travel, hemiplegia, paraplegia, bedridden)
  • IV drug users (especially femoral vein), venipunctures

qs.q: Mention the surgical conditions predisposing to venous thrombosis.
qs.a:
• Major surgery (release of tissue factor)
  • Abdominal & pelvic surgery (especially for cancer)
  • Major lower-limb orthopaedic surgery
  • Trauma / fractures
  • Varicose veins
  • Previous DVT (highest risk of recurrence)
  • Every surgical patient gets a VTE risk score → prophylactic LMWH if high

qs.q: Why does inherited thrombophilia rarely cause arterial thrombosis?
qs.a:
• Blood flow in arteries is fast (heart rate ~ 60 and high pressure) → little stasis
  • Inherited thrombophilias predispose mainly to venous thrombosis
  • Arterial thrombosis needs an inherited factor + a provoking factor (or atherosclerosis risk factors, APS)

qs.q: Define provoked thrombosis and mention the transient provoking factors.
qs.a:
• Provoked thrombosis: occurs in the setting of a clear, identifiable risk factor
  • Transient factors (clear start and end):
    • Recent surgery (orthopaedic, abdominal), trauma or fractures
    • Immobilization (bed rest, casts, long flights > 8–12 h), hospitalization
    • Pregnancy & postpartum (up to 6 weeks)
    • Estrogen: oral contraceptives, hormone replacement therapy
    • Acute medical illness (sepsis, severe infection)
  • Lower recurrence risk once the factor is gone → anticoagulation 3 months

qs.q: Mention the persistent provoking factors of thrombosis.
qs.a:
• Active cancer (e.g. HCC → portal vein thrombosis)
  • Chronic inflammatory diseases: IBD, SLE
  • Nephrotic syndrome
  • Chronic paralysis
  • Behave closer to unprovoked in recurrence risk → extended treatment

qs.q: Define unprovoked thrombosis and mention its consequences.
qs.a:
• Thrombosis without any identifiable provoking factor: no recent surgery / trauma, no immobilization, no estrogen, no active cancer or major illness
  • Example: first DVT in a healthy ambulatory patient
  • Consequences:
    • Higher risk of recurrence
    • Extended or lifelong anticoagulation (≥ 6 months)
    • Needs thrombophilia screening and cancer screening (hidden malignancy)

qs.q: Compare provoked and unprovoked venous thrombosis.
qs.a:
ProvokedUnprovoked
CauseClear, transientNone / persistent
Anticoagulation3 months≥ 6 months, maybe life
RecurrenceLowerHigher
ScreeningNot neededThrombophilia + cancer

qs.q: Mention the indications of thrombophilia testing.
qs.a:
• Unprovoked venous thrombosis
  • Young patients (venous thrombosis < 45 years)
  • Recurrent VTE
  • Strong family history
  • Thrombosis in an unusual site (cerebral sinus, mesenteric, hepatic veins)
  • (Recurrent pregnancy loss)
  • Not needed when there is a clear provoking factor, e.g. 70-year-old with DVT after hip replacement

qs.q: Mention the investigations of unprovoked thrombosis (thrombophilia screen).
qs.a:
• Antithrombin, protein C, protein S levels
  • Antiphospholipid antibodies: lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2GPI
  • Genetic: factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, JAK2 (myeloproliferative)
  • Flow cytometry for PNH (CD55 / CD59)
  • Cancer screening
  • DVT & PE are manifestations, not causes, of thrombophilia

qs.q: Mention the clinical presentations of venous thromboembolic disease.
qs.a:
• Most common: deep venous thrombosis of the leg and pulmonary embolism
  • Rarer: jugular vein thrombosis (central lines), upper-limb DVT (breast cancer), cerebral sinus thrombosis, intra-abdominal venous thrombosis e.g. Budd–Chiari syndrome (hepatic veins → ascites)
  • Case mortality ~ 2%

qs.q: Describe the clinical picture of lower-limb deep venous thrombosis.
qs.a:
• Starts in the distal (calf) veins and may extend proximally into the IVC
  • Pain, tender calf muscles, hotness, swelling, pitting oedema
  • Dilated superficial veins (collaterals)
  • Usually unilateral; bilateral suggests malignancy or IVC anomaly
  • Look for risk factors, examine for malignancy, and seek symptoms & signs of PE
  • Clinical probability scores (e.g. Wells score) rank the likelihood
  • Do not squeeze the calf – may dislodge the thrombus (PE)

qs.q: Mention the differential diagnosis of unilateral leg swelling.
qs.a:
• Calf muscle tear (spontaneous or traumatic) – sudden onset, localized tenderness
  • Ruptured Baker's cyst – sudden onset, localized tenderness
  • Infective cellulitis – marked erythema & heat in a well-demarcated area ± source of entry (leg ulcer)

qs.q: Mention the investigations of deep venous thrombosis.
qs.a:
• D-dimer: degradation product of cross-linked fibrin (endogenous fibrinolysis); negative + low probability excludes DVT
  • Compression (Doppler) ultrasound: imaging of choice; sensitivity 99.5% for proximal DVT (popliteal or above)
  • Contrast venography: rarely used (obsolete)
  • In proven DVT, imaging for PE is not required unless massive PE is suspected
  • Unprovoked → thrombophilia & cancer screening

qs.q: Mention the management of deep venous thrombosis.
qs.a:
• General: leg elevation and analgesia (rest, avoid massage)
  • Anticoagulation = mainstay:
    • LMWH (enoxaparin) + warfarin started together
    • LMWH continued at least 5 days until INR is in the target range (2–3)
    • Or rivaroxaban (oral Xa inhibitor) – rapid onset, used from diagnosis without LMWH
  • IVC filter if anticoagulation contraindicated or new PE despite anticoagulation
  • Thrombolysis for limb-threatening DVT

qs.q: Mention the duration of anticoagulation in venous thromboembolism.
qs.a:
• Provoked (temporary, removed risk factor): 3 months
  • Unprovoked or permanent risk factor: ≥ 6 months or for life
  • Active cancer: LMWH for at least 6 months before switching to an oral anticoagulant
  • Previous emboli / persistent prothrombotic state → long-term

qs.q: Mention the indications of inferior vena cava filter and thrombolysis in DVT.
qs.a:
• IVC filter:
    • Strong contraindication to anticoagulation (e.g. high bleeding risk)
    • New PE despite therapeutic anticoagulation
  • Thrombolysis: limb-threatening DVT

qs.q: Mention the sources of pulmonary embolism.
qs.a:
• 80% arise from propagation of lower-limb DVT (calf → popliteal → IVC → right heart → pulmonary artery)
  • Rare: septic emboli (tricuspid / pulmonary valve endocarditis), tumour (choriocarcinoma), fat, air, amniotic fluid, placenta
  • Paradoxical embolism through ASD
  • VTE accounts for ~ 5% of in-hospital deaths

qs.q: Compare acute massive and acute small/medium pulmonary embolism.
qs.a:
Acute massive PEAcute small / medium PE
Pathophysiology↓ cardiac output, acute right heart failure, hypoxiaOcclusion of segmental branch → infarction ± effusion
SymptomsFaintness / collapse, crushing central chest pain, severe dyspnoeaPleuritic chest pain, restricted breathing, haemoptysis
SignsTachycardia, hypotension, ↑ JVP, RV gallop, loud P2, cyanosisPleural rub, effusion, raised hemidiaphragm, sinus tachycardia
  • Chronic PE: exertional dyspnoea, late RV failure, minimal signs
  • DD of massive PE: MI, pericardial tamponade, aortic dissection

qs.q: Mention the investigations of pulmonary embolism.
qs.a:
• Chest X-ray: often normal; wedge-shaped opacity (Hampton hump), effusion, raised hemidiaphragm, oligaemia
  • ABG: hypoxaemia (± hypocapnia)
  • ECG: sinus tachycardia, RV strain; excludes MI
  • D-dimer: high negative predictive value
  • CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) – first-line diagnostic test
  • Echocardiography: RV dilatation, pulmonary hypertension, thrombus
  • Colour Doppler of the leg veins
  • Ventilation/perfusion scintigraphy – if renal impairment or contrast allergy

qs.q: Mention the chest X-ray findings in pulmonary embolism.
qs.a:
• May be normal
  • Wedge-shaped, subpleural opacity (Hampton hump) – pulmonary infarction
  • Pleural effusion
  • Raised hemidiaphragm
  • Enlarged pulmonary artery
  • Oligaemia of the affected zone

qs.q: Mention the advantages and precautions of CT pulmonary angiography in PE.
qs.a:
• First-line diagnostic test
  • Advantages: shows the distribution and extent of emboli (e.g. saddle embolus) and highlights an alternative diagnosis (consolidation, pneumothorax, aortic dissection)
  • Precautions: contrast may be nephrotoxic → care in renal impairment; avoid with iodinated contrast allergy → use V/Q scan instead

qs.q: Discuss the value of D-dimer in venous thromboembolism.
qs.a:
• Specific degradation product of cross-linked fibrin during endogenous fibrinolysis
  • Raised D-dimer has limited value – also raised in MI, pneumonia, sepsis, surgery, malignancy
  • Low level (< 500 ng/mL by ELISA) with low clinical risk → high negative predictive value → no further tests
  • In high-risk patients, ignore a normal D-dimer – further imaging is mandatory

qs.q: Mention the general measures in the management of pulmonary embolism.
qs.a:
• Early recognition and treatment are lifesaving
  • Oxygen to keep SaO2 > 90%
  • Circulatory shock: IV fluids or plasma expander
    • Inotropes of limited value (RV already maximally stimulated)
  • Avoid diuretics and vasodilators (↓ cardiac output)
  • Opiates for pain & distress – cautiously if hypotensive

qs.q: Mention the anticoagulant therapy of pulmonary embolism.
qs.a:
• Start immediately if high / intermediate probability (may withhold in low probability pending tests)
  • Heparin reduces clot propagation and further emboli and lowers mortality – most easily as SC LMWH
  • LMWH for at least 5 days while warfarin is started (loading dose then maintenance by INR)
  • Continue LMWH until INR ≥ 2 for at least 24 h
  • Warfarin has a narrow therapeutic index and interacts with food & drugs → regular INR monitoring
  • Fondaparinux – alternative to LMWH
  • New oral thrombin / Xa inhibitors – predictable dosing, no monitoring

qs.q: Mention the indications of extended (lifelong) anticoagulation after unprovoked VTE.
qs.a:
• Duration at least 6 months, and may be for life especially if:
    • Males
    • D-dimer remains elevated 1 month after stopping anticoagulation
    • Post-thrombotic syndrome (chronic venous insufficiency)
    • Those in whom recurrent PE may be fatal
  • Disadvantage: INR monitoring and major haemorrhage ~ 3% per year

qs.q: Mention the indications of thrombolysis, embolectomy and caval filters in pulmonary embolism.
qs.a:
• Thrombolysis: acute massive PE with cardiogenic shock
    • Without shock: consider if RV dilatation & hypokinesis or severe hypoxaemia
    • Screen carefully for bleeding risk (intracranial haemorrhage)
  • Surgical embolectomy: selected patients – high mortality
  • Caval (IVC) filter: anticoagulation contraindicated, or massive / recurrent PE despite anticoagulation (retrievable filters useful)

qs.q: Enumerate the causes of inherited thrombophilia.
qs.a:
• Antithrombin III deficiency
  • Protein C deficiency
  • Protein S deficiency
  • Factor V Leiden (activated protein C resistance)
  • Prothrombin G20210A mutation

qs.q: Mention the general features of inherited thrombophilia.
qs.a:
• Predispose to venous thrombosis, not arterial
  • Slightly ↑ adverse pregnancy outcome (recurrent early fetal loss)
  • Most carriers get VTE only with an additional temporary risk factor – except antithrombin III deficiency and homozygous factor V Leiden (thrombosis without additional risk)
  • None per se requires anticoagulation; high-risk periods (e.g. AT III deficiency in pregnancy) → heparin prophylaxis for the period of risk

qs.q: Describe antithrombin III deficiency.
qs.a:
• AT III is a natural anticoagulant that inactivates activated factors IIa, IXa, Xa, XIa
  • Heparins, fondaparinux, idraparinux act by potentiating AT
  • Autosomal dominant; homozygosity is incompatible with life
  • ~ 70% have VTE before age 60
  • Pregnancy: high risk → LMWH doses higher than prophylactic (≥ 100 U/kg/day)

qs.q: Describe protein C and protein S deficiency.
qs.a:
• Vitamin K-dependent natural anticoagulants
  • Inactivate factors Va & VIIIa and limit thrombin generation
  • Inherited deficiency → prothrombotic state with ~ 5-fold risk of VTE
  • Protein C deficiency often appears only with other risk factors (doctor's case: obese, smoker, sedentary → PE)

qs.q: Describe factor V Leiden (activated protein C resistance).
qs.a:
• Normally protein C inactivates factor V → ↓ activation of prothrombin
  • Factor V mutation → factor V resistant to inactivation by protein C
  • Factor V stays active → prothrombin → thrombin → thrombotic state
  • Autosomal dominant
  • Risk of venous thrombosis × 5 in heterozygotes and × 50 in homozygotes

qs.q: Describe the prothrombin G20210A mutation.
qs.a:
• Gain-of-function mutation in the non-coding 3′ end of the prothrombin gene
  • → ↑ plasma prothrombin level
  • Heterozygotes: 2–3-fold ↑ risk of VTE

qs.q: Mention the clinical features of antiphospholipid syndrome.
qs.a:
• Recurrent venous thrombosis
  • Arterial thromboembolism (typically stroke)
  • Recurrent abortion & fetal death (recurrent first-trimester loss)
  • Livedo reticularis, transverse myelitis, thrombocytopenia
  • Primary (isolated) or secondary (most typically SLE)
  • Now most frequently diagnosed in women with adverse pregnancy outcome

qs.q: Enumerate the antibodies of antiphospholipid syndrome. Which is most strongly associated with thrombosis?
qs.a:
• Lupus anticoagulant – more strongly associated with thrombosis than anticardiolipin
  • Anticardiolipin antibody
  • Anti-β2 glycoprotein I antibody
  • Directed against proteins that bind phospholipids; lupus anticoagulant prolongs aPTT in vitro but causes thrombosis in vivo

qs.q: Mention the management of antiphospholipid syndrome.
qs.a:
• VTE: high recurrence → long-term anticoagulation after a first event (warfarin)
  • Arterial thrombosis (stroke): warfarin + aspirin
  • Pregnancy: LMWH ± low-dose aspirin → ↑ successful pregnancy outcome

qs.q: Define disseminated intravascular coagulation and mention its causes.
qs.a:
• Systemic activation of coagulation → intravascular fibrin clots → multi-organ failure + simultaneous consumption of factors & platelets → bleeding
  • Induced by cytokines (systemic inflammation) or release of tissue factor
  • Causes:
    • Severe sepsis / infection
    • Severe trauma, burns, severe pancreatitis (tissue destruction)
    • Obstetric: amniotic fluid embolism, placental abruption, pre-eclampsia
    • Severe liver failure
    • Malignancy (chronic DIC)
    • Toxic / immunological: incompatible blood transfusion, snake bites
  • Acute DIC → bleeding predominates; chronic DIC → thrombosis predominates

qs.q: Mention the laboratory findings of DIC.
qs.a:
• Platelets: decreased
  • PT and aPTT: prolonged
  • Fibrinogen: decreased
  • FDPs and D-dimer: increased
  • Blood film: microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia – ↓ Hb, schistocytes

qs.q: Mention the management of DIC.
qs.a:
• Treat the underlying cause
  • ICU – correct acidosis, dehydration, renal failure, hypoxia
  • Blood components (FFP, cryoprecipitate, platelets) only if bleeding or before high-risk interventions – not based on lab tests alone
  • Prophylactic heparin unless contraindicated; established thrombosis → cautious therapeutic UFH

qs.q: Mention the pentad of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.
qs.a:
• Thrombocytopenia
  • Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (schistocytes)
  • Neurological sequelae
  • Fever
  • Renal impairment

qs.q: Describe the pathogenesis, causes and treatment of TTP.
qs.a:
• Acute autoimmune disorder with antibodies against ADAMTS-13
  • ADAMTS-13 normally cleaves vWF multimers → deficiency leaves large vWF multimers → cross-link platelets → thrombocytopenic thrombosis in brain & kidneys
  • Rare (1 in 750 000); normal PT / aPTT
  • Causes: alone, or with drugs (ticlopidine, ciclosporin), HIV, shiga toxins, malignancy
  • Treatment: emergency plasma exchange + corticosteroids, aspirin, immunosuppression (rituximab)
  • Mortality 20–30% at 6 months even with therapy

qs.q: Describe the pathogenesis of paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.
qs.a:
• Rare acquired stem-cell disorder with deficiency of the GPI anchor (glycosyl phosphatidyl inositol)
  • Lack of GPI → absence of CD55 and CD59 on cell membranes
  • → ↑ sensitivity to complement attack → intravascular haemolysis (worse in mild acidosis at night)

qs.q: Mention the clinical picture of PNH.
qs.a:
• Intravascular haemolytic anaemia → haemoglobinuria: dark red-brown urine in the early morning
  • Haemolytic jaundice (indirect hyperbilirubinaemia)
  • Venous thrombosis in unusual sites (hepatic – Budd–Chiari, abdominal) due to lack of CD59 on platelets
  • Bone marrow failure: hypoplastic marrow, aplastic anaemia, myelodysplastic syndrome

qs.q: Mention the diagnosis and management of PNH.
qs.a:
• Diagnosis: flow cytometry – absence of CD55 & CD59 on RBC surface
  • Management:
    • Supportive: blood transfusion
    • Anticoagulants
    • Eculizumab (anti-complement C5 monoclonal antibody) – ↓ haemolysis
    • Stem cell transplantation

qs.q: Mention the causes of thrombosis with paradoxical thrombocytopenia.
qs.a:
• TTP
  • DIC
  • HIT (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia)
  • APS
  • ± PNH
  • (ITP causes thrombocytopenia without thrombosis – the EXCEPT answer)

qs.a:

qs.q: Mention the causes of acquired thrombophilia.
qs.a:
• Antiphospholipid syndrome
  • DIC
  • TTP
  • PNH
  • HIT
  • Others: myeloproliferative disorders, malignancy, nephrotic syndrome, pregnancy / estrogen

qs.q: Compare antiplatelets and anticoagulants in the prevention of thrombosis.
qs.a:
• Antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel): less value in VTE but better in arterial thrombosis → drugs of choice in ACS and ischaemic stroke
  • Anticoagulants (warfarin, heparin, DOACs): favoured in VTE

qs.q: Mention the mechanism of action of heparin and warfarin.
qs.a:
• Heparin (UFH / LMWH): binds antithrombin via a pentasaccharide → potentiates it → ↑ inactivation of factor Xa and thrombin (IIa)
  • Warfarin: vitamin K antagonist (inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase) → blocks carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, X in the liver
    • Monitored by INR (target 2–3); takes 3–5 days to act → overlap with LMWH
  • DOACs: dabigatran (direct thrombin inhibitor); rivaroxaban, apixaban (direct Xa inhibitors)

qs.q: What is the antidote of heparin? Why is UFH preferred in some situations?
qs.a:
• Protamine sulphate
  • UFH is more completely reversed by protamine than LMWH → drug of choice when rapid reversal is needed (e.g. end of cardiopulmonary bypass)

qs.q: Describe heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT).
qs.a:
• Pathogenesis: anti-heparin/PF4 antibodies bind and activate platelets via Fc receptors → prothrombotic state with paradoxical thrombocytopenia
  • Clinical: typically 5–14 days after heparin, platelet fall > 30% from baseline; venous or arterial thrombosis, skin necrosis
    • Re-exposure within 100 days → abrupt fall in first 24 h
  • More common: surgical (cardiac, orthopaedic), UFH > LMWH, high doses
  • Investigations: 4Ts score (Thrombocytopenia, Timing, Thrombosis, oTher cause) + anti-PF4 ELISA
  • Management: stop heparin and substitute argatroban (direct thrombin inhibitor) or danaparoid
  • Established HIT has a poor prognosis

qs.q: Mention the side effects and drawbacks of warfarin.
qs.a:
• Narrow therapeutic window
  • Metabolism affected by many foods (vitamin K)
  • Drug interactions through cytochrome P450
  • Inter-individual variation in dose needed
  • Major bleeding – most common serious side effect
  • Fatal haemorrhage, most commonly intracranial
  • (Teratogenic; needs INR monitoring)

qs.q: Mention the management of warfarin over-anticoagulation.
qs.a:
• INR above target, no bleeding: withhold or reduce the dose; small dose vitamin K 1–2.5 mg orally or IV
  • INR above target with bleeding: withhold warfarin
    • Minor bleeding: vitamin K 1–2.5 mg IV
    • Major bleeding: vitamin K 5–10 mg slowly IV + prothrombin complex concentrate (30–50 U/kg) (factors II, VII, IX, X)
    • FFP 15–30 mL/kg if PCC unavailable

qs.q: Mention the new oral anticoagulants, their advantages and indications.
qs.a:
• Examples: dabigatran (direct thrombin inhibitor), rivaroxaban, apixaban (direct Xa inhibitors)
  • Advantages: fixed doses, predictable effect, no monitoring, fewer interactions
  • Indications:
    • Prevention of perioperative VTE
    • Treatment of established VTE
    • Prevention of cardioembolic stroke in atrial fibrillation

qs.q: Mention the coagulation pathways measured by PT and aPTT.
qs.a:
• Extrinsic (PT / INR): tissue factor (III) + VII → X
  • Intrinsic (aPTT): XII → XI → IX → VIII → X
  • Common: X → V → II (thrombin) → I (fibrin)
  • Warfarin is monitored by INR; UFH by aPTT

qs.q: Define diabetes mellitus.
qs.a:
• Syndrome of disordered metabolism + inappropriate hyperglycaemia due to:
  • Deficiency of insulin secretion (absolute – type 1), or
  • Insulin resistance + inadequate compensatory secretion (relative – type 2)

qs.q: Mention the islet cells and their hormones.
qs.a:
• β cells: insulin (+ C-peptide, amylin)
  • α cells (≈ 20%): glucagon
  • δ cells: somatostatin
  • F (PP) cells: pancreatic polypeptide

qs.q: Mention the steps of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.
qs.a:
• (1) Glucose enters via GLUT1 / GLUT2
  • (2) Glucokinase → G-6-P → glycolysis → ↑ ATP (glucokinase = glucose sensor)
  • (3) ATP closes KATP channel (4 KIR6.2 + 4 SUR1) → depolarisation
  • (4) Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open → Ca²⁺ influx
  • (5) Vesicles fuse → insulin secretion; GLP-1/GIP amplify via cAMP

qs.q: Define the incretin effect.
qs.a:
• More insulin secreted after oral glucose than IV glucose for the same glucose level
  • Due to GLP-1 (L cells) and GIP (K cells) from duodenum / upper jejunum
  • Glucose-dependent → no hypoglycaemia; diminished in type 2 DM

qs.q: Mention the two phases of insulin secretion.
qs.a:
• 1st (rapid): release of pre-formed granules, within 15 min
  • 2nd (prolonged): de novo synthesis over 2–3 h

qs.q: Mention the metabolic actions of insulin.
qs.a:
Metabolism Increases ↑ Decreases ↓
Carbohydrate Glucose uptake (GLUT4), glycogen synthesis, glycolysis Gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis
Lipid TG & FA synthesis, adipose LPL Lipolysis, ketogenesis, FA oxidation
Protein AA transport, protein synthesis Protein degradation

qs.q: Mention the actions and inhibitors of glucagon.
qs.a:
• Actions: ↑ hepatic glucose output (glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis), lipolysis, ketogenesis; key defence against hypoglycaemia
  • Inhibitors: insulin (paracrine), somatostatin, amylin

qs.q: Mention the ketone bodies and their importance.
qs.a:
• Acetoacetate, 3-hydroxybutyrate, acetone
  • Alternative brain fuel in fasting / illness (cross BBB, unlike FFAs)
  • Production > removal → ketoacidosis

qs.q: Mention the value of C-peptide.
qs.a:
• Secreted 1 : 1 with insulin, absent in synthetic insulin → marker of endogenous secretion
  • Undetectable → type 1; high → type 2
  • High insulin + low C-peptide = exogenous (factitious) insulin
  • Not measured right after DKA (glucotoxicity)

qs.q: Mention the classification of diabetes mellitus.
qs.a:
• Type 1: 1A autoimmune (> 95%), 1B idiopathic (< 5%)
  • Type 2
  • Other specific types: MODY, mitochondrial DNA, Wolfram, secondary DM
  • Gestational DM

qs.q: Mention the features of type 1 DM.
qs.a:
• β-cell destruction, autoimmune (T-cell) in > 95%
  • Children & young adults (peaks before school & at puberty)
  • Catabolic: insulin absent, glucagon ↑, ketosis
  • HLA-DR3/DR4 in 95%; HLA ≈ 40% of genetic risk
  • ⅓ present first with DKA
  • Requires exogenous insulin

qs.q: Mention the islet autoantibodies of type 1 DM.
qs.a:
• Anti-GAD (glutamic acid decarboxylase)
  • ICA (islet cell) · IAA (insulin) · IA-2 (tyrosine phosphatase)

qs.q: Mention autoimmune diseases screened for in type 1 DM.
qs.a:
• Thyroid disease (Graves / Hashimoto → TSH) – most important
  • Coeliac disease · Addison's disease
  • Pernicious anaemia · myasthenia gravis (rare)

qs.q: Mention the features of LADA and how it differs from MODY.
qs.a:
• LADA: adult > 30, non-obese, no family history, single high-titre anti-GAD, oral drugs fail after months → insulin
  • MODY: < 25–30, strong AD family history, antibodies negative, non-obese

qs.q: Mention the features of type 2 DM.
qs.a:
• ≈ 90% of DM; insulin resistance + β-cell dysfunction
  • Obesity (visceral) = most important environmental factor
  • Strong family history; now seen in children
  • Insulin enough to prevent ketoacidosis but not hyperglycaemia
  • Acanthosis nigricans = clinical sign of resistance

qs.q: Mention the natural history of type 2 DM.
qs.a:
• Insulin resistance → compensatory hyperinsulinaemia (euglycaemic) → prediabetes (IGT/IFG) → overt type 2 → β-cell exhaustion → insulin
  • Compliant ≈ 10–12 y; non-compliant ≈ 4–5 y to insulin

qs.q: Mention the NCEP-ATP III criteria of the metabolic syndrome.
qs.a:
• ≥ 3 of:
  • Waist > 102 cm (M), > 88 cm (F)
  • TG ≥ 150 mg/dl
  • HDL < 40 (M), < 50 (F)
  • BP ≥ 130/85
  • FPG ≥ 100 mg/dl
  • Old Q: criteria given → "criteria of what?" = metabolic syndrome

qs.q: Mention the features of MODY.
qs.a:
• Monogenic, autosomal dominant, onset ≤ 25 y, non-obese, non-insulin-requiring
  • Impaired glucose-induced insulin secretion; 6 types
  • MODY 2: glucokinase defect · MODY 3: HNF-1α – most common (⅔), responds to SU
  • Genetic screening: age < 30 + endogenous insulin + negative antibodies

qs.q: Mention the components of Wolfram syndrome.
qs.a:
• DIDMOAD: Diabetes Insipidus, Diabetes Mellitus, Optic Atrophy, Deafness
  • Autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder of childhood

qs.q: Mention causes of secondary diabetes mellitus.
qs.a:
• Drugs (resistance): corticosteroids, sympathomimetics, niacin
  • Drugs (↓ secretion): thiazides, β-blockers, phenytoin, calcineurin inhibitors, atypical antipsychotics
  • Hormonal tumours: acromegaly, Cushing, glucagonoma, phaeochromocytoma, somatostatinoma
  • Liver: cirrhosis, haemochromatosis
  • Pancreas: pancreatitis, haemosiderosis, haemochromatosis
  • Muscle / fat: myotonic dystrophy, lipodystrophy, truncal obesity

qs.q: Define gestational DM.
qs.a:
• Diabetes diagnosed in the 2nd or 3rd trimester not clearly overt before pregnancy
  • DM in 1st trimester = type 2
  • HbA1c is NOT diagnostic for GDM

qs.q: Mention the clinical presentation of type 1 and type 2 DM.
qs.a:
• Type 1: polyuria, polydipsia, enuresis, weight loss / failure to gain weight → severe DKA
  • Type 2: asymptomatic, 3 P's, nocturia, blurred vision, skin infections, vaginitis/pruritus vulvae, obesity, acanthosis; may present with a complication (MI, stroke, neuropathy)

qs.q: Mention the diagnostic criteria of diabetes mellitus.
qs.a:
• Classic symptoms + random plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dl
  • FPG ≥ 126 mg/dl (fasting ≥ 8 h)
  • 2-h glucose ≥ 200 mg/dl during 75 g OGTT
  • HbA1c ≥ 6.5%

qs.q: Mention the criteria defining prediabetes.
qs.a:
• IFG: FPG 100–125 mg/dl
  • IGT: 2-h OGTT 140–199 mg/dl
  • HbA1c 5.7–6.4%
  • 5–10%/year progress to DM; ↑ macrovascular risk

qs.q: Mention the causes of falsely low and falsely high HbA1c.
qs.a:
• Falsely low (short RBC life): chronic blood loss, sickle cell, thalassaemia, pregnancy, IV iron & EPO in CKD, after transfusion
  • Falsely high (long RBC life): iron / B12 / folate deficiency anaemia, splenectomy
  • Alternative: fructosamine (control over 1–2 weeks)

qs.q: Mention the features of diabetic dyslipidaemia.
qs.a:
• High TG (300–400 mg/dl)
  • Low HDL (< 30 mg/dl)
  • Small dense LDL (more atherogenic)

qs.q: Mention ADA diet and exercise recommendations in DM.
qs.a:
• Lifestyle = the most important point in treating DM
  • Diet: 45% CHO, 25–35% fat, 10–35% protein; Mediterranean pattern
  • Exercise: 150 min/week moderate or 75 min vigorous; resistance ≥ 2 days/week; avoid sitting > 90 min
  • Insulin users: carbohydrate counting; reduce bolus before exercise

qs.q: Mention the ominous octet of type 2 DM with the drugs for each defect.
qs.a:
Defect Drugs
↓ Insulin secretion (β cell) SU, meglitinide, GLP-1 RA, DPP-4i
↑ Glucagon (α cell) GLP-1 RA, DPP-4i, amylin
↑ Hepatic glucose output Metformin, insulin, TZD
Neurotransmitter dysfunction GLP-1 RA, amylin, bromocriptine
↑ Lipolysis (adipose) TZD
↑ Glucose reabsorption (kidney) SGLT2 inhibitors
↓ Glucose uptake (muscle) Metformin, insulin, TZD
↓ Incretin effect (gut) Metformin, α-glucosidase inhibitors

qs.q: Mention the stepwise treatment of type 2 DM.
qs.a:
• 1st: lifestyle (diet + exercise)
  • Step 1: add metformin
  • Step 2: add a 2nd drug by clinical characteristics
  • Step 3: add a 3rd drug
  • Step 4: intensive insulin + metformin

qs.q: Mention the indications of insulin therapy.
qs.a:
• Type 1 DM · gestational DM
  • Type 2: severe or symptomatic hyperglycaemia, metabolic decompensation (DKA, HHS), failure of diet + oral drugs

qs.q: Mention the classes of oral anti-diabetic drugs with examples.
qs.a:
• Secretagogues: sulfonylureas (glibenclamide, glimepiride, gliclazide); glinides (repaglinide, nateglinide)
  • Biguanide: metformin
  • TZDs: pioglitazone, rosiglitazone
  • α-glucosidase inhibitors: acarbose
  • DPP-4 inhibitors: sitagliptin, vildagliptin, saxagliptin, linagliptin
  • SGLT2 inhibitors: canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin
  • Injectable: GLP-1 RA (liraglutide, semaglutide), pramlintide

qs.q: Mention the mechanism and side effects of sulfonylureas.
qs.a:
• Close β-cell KATP channel → insulin secretion (glucose-independent)
  • Side effects: hypoglycaemia + weight gain (old Q: drug causing weight gain = SU)

qs.q: Mention the mechanism, side effects and renal precautions of metformin.
qs.a:
• MOA: ↓ hepatic glucose production (AMPK activator), ↑ peripheral uptake → insulin sensitiser; no hypoglycaemia
  • SE: GI upset (20%), B12 malabsorption, lactic acidosis (rare, most serious)
  • Renal: halve dose if eGFR < 45; stop if eGFR < 30; stop in acute illness

qs.q: Mention the mechanism and side effects of thiazolidinediones.
qs.a:
• PPAR-γ agonists → insulin sensitisation, ↓ FFAs; pioglitazone ↓ NASH
  • SE: weight gain, fluid retention → heart failure, fractures / osteoporosis, ± bladder cancer

qs.q: Mention the actions and side effects of GLP-1 receptor agonists.
qs.a:
• Actions: glucose-dependent insulin release, ↓ glucagon, delay gastric emptying, ↓ appetite → weight loss; ↓ CV events
  • SE: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea; ↑ pancreatitis
  • Contraindicated: medullary thyroid carcinoma / MEN 2, pancreatitis
  • Main line in obese diabetics

qs.q: Mention the benefits and side effects of SGLT2 inhibitors.
qs.a:
• Benefits: glycosuria → ↓ glucose, weight loss, ↓ BP; ↓ CV events (esp. HF) + renoprotection (down to GFR 20)
  • SE: genital fungal infections, UTI, Fournier's gangrene (rare)
  • Euglycaemic DKA – off-label in type 1, or type 2 during acute illness / dehydration

qs.q: Compare GLP-1 receptor agonists and DPP-4 inhibitors.
qs.a:
Feature GLP-1 RA DPP-4 inhibitors
Examples Liraglutide, semaglutide Sitagliptin, vildagliptin
Route Injection Oral
Weight Loss Neutral
CV effect ↓ MACE Neutral
SE GI upset, pancreatitis Hypersensitivity, pancreatitis

qs.q: Mention the long-acting insulins with their duration.
qs.a:
• NPH: onset 2–4 h, peak 6–7 h, 10–20 h
  • Glargine (Lantus): ≈ 24 h, peakless
  • Detemir (Levemir): ≈ 17 h (approved in pregnancy)
  • Degludec (Tresiba): > 42 h

qs.q: Mention the methods of insulin administration.
qs.a: • Syringes & needles · pen injectors · insulin pumps · inhaled insulin

qs.q: Mention the complications of insulin therapy.
qs.a:
• Hypoglycaemia (most common)
  • Hypoglycaemic unawareness
  • Insulin allergy
  • Lipodystrophy (atrophy)
  • Lipohypertrophy → prevent by rotating sites

qs.q: Mention the chronic complications of diabetes.
qs.a:
• Microvascular: retinopathy (+ cataract, glaucoma), neuropathy, nephropathy
  • Macrovascular: coronary heart disease, PVD, cerebrovascular disease
  • Others: skin, bone & joint complications

qs.q: Mention the mechanisms of chronic complications.
qs.a:
• Non-enzymatic glycosylation → AGEs
  • Polyol pathway: aldose reductase → sorbitol accumulation
  • Haemodynamic changes: abnormal microvascular flow, endothelins
  • Others: reactive oxygen species; growth factors (TGF-β, VEGF)

qs.q: Mention the stages and features of diabetic retinopathy.
qs.a:
• Non-proliferative: microaneurysms, haemorrhages, exudates, cotton-wool spots
  • Proliferative: new vessels → vitreous haemorrhage → fibrosis → tractional detachment
  • Macular oedema: most common cause of vision loss
  • Rubeosis: new vessels in angle → glaucoma

qs.q: Mention the management of diabetic retinopathy.
qs.a:
• Glycaemic control · aggressive BP control
  • Laser photocoagulation if vision threatened
  • Vitrectomy for vitreous haemorrhage / fibrous bands
  • Screening: type 2 at diagnosis, type 1 after 5 y → annually

qs.q: Mention the pathology sequence and screening of diabetic nephropathy.
qs.a:
• Hyperfiltration → GBM thickening (microalbuminuria) → overt proteinuria → nodular glomerulosclerosis → ↓ GFR
  • Screen: ACR in early-morning urine; 30–300 = microalbuminuria; ≥ 2 positive samples over 3–6 months
  • Microalbuminuria = nephropathy risk in type 1, CV risk in type 2

qs.q: Mention the management of diabetic nephropathy.
qs.a:
• BP control · ↓ CV risk factors · glycaemic control
  • ACEi / ARB (relax efferent arteriole)
  • SGLT2 inhibitor (proteinuria > 300 mg/day, eGFR ≥ 20)

qs.q: Mention the types of diabetic neuropathy.
qs.a:
• Somatic: symmetrical sensory polyneuropathy (most common); asymmetrical motor (amyotrophy); mononeuropathy
  • Autonomic (visceral): CVS, GIT, GU, sudomotor, vasomotor, pupillary

qs.q: Mention the features of diabetic foot.
qs.a:
• Stocking-glove loss of vibration (first), pain, temperature
  • Loss of small foot muscles → clawing, exposed metatarsal heads → callus → ulcer
  • Charcot arthropathy (rocker-bottom foot)
  • Loss of 10 g monofilament = high risk
  • Gangrene 30× (PVD + neuropathy + infection)

qs.q: Mention the features of autonomic neuropathy.
qs.a:
• CVS: postural hypotension, resting tachycardia, fixed heart rate
  • GIT: gastroparesis, nocturnal diarrhoea, constipation, dysphagia
  • GU: atonic bladder, erectile dysfunction, retrograde ejaculation
  • Sudomotor: gustatory / nocturnal sweating, anhidrosis
  • Vasomotor: cold feet, oedema · pupillary: small pupils, ↓ light reflex

qs.q: Mention the treatment of painful diabetic neuropathy.
qs.a:
• Glycaemic control
  • Anticonvulsants: gabapentin, pregabalin
  • TCAs: amitriptyline · duloxetine
  • Capsaicin (topical) · opiates: tramadol
  • α-lipoic acid (numbness)

qs.q: Mention the management of cardiovascular risk in DM.
qs.a:
• Control glycaemia & HTN (< 140/90; ACEi/ARB)
  • Statins: LDL < 100 (< 70 with CVD) – DM = coronary risk equivalent
  • Aspirin: secondary prevention; primary only if high risk + low bleeding risk
  • MI = leading cause of death in type 2

qs.q: Mention the skin complications of diabetes.
qs.a:
• Pyogenic & candidal infections
  • Eruptive xanthomas (↑ TG)
  • Necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum
  • Shin spots (diabetic dermopathy)

qs.q: Mention the bone and joint complications of diabetes.
qs.a:
• Cheiroarthropathy (prayer sign) · frozen shoulder
  • Carpal tunnel · Dupuytren's contracture
  • DISH

qs.q: Mention the precipitating factors and clinical features of DKA.
qs.a:
• Precipitants: insufficient / interrupted insulin, infection, emotional stress, alcohol (type 2: sepsis, MI, stroke)
  • Features: anorexia, vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul breathing, fruity acetone breath, dehydration, altered consciousness

qs.q: List lines of treatment of a patient presenting with DKA.
qs.a:
• High-volume normal saline (most important)
  • IV regular insulin
  • Electrolytes: K⁺ depleted despite initial hyperkalaemia → give K⁺ once ≤ 5 mEq/L
  • Switch to SC insulin when AG & HCO₃⁻ normalise
  • Treat the precipitating cause

qs.q: Compare DKA, HHS and lactic acidosis.
qs.a:
Feature DKA HHS Lactic acidosis
Glucose > 250 > 600 —
pH < 7.3 > 7.3 < 7.3
HCO₃⁻ < 15 > 15 < 15
Ketones Positive — Absent
Other ↑ AG Osm > 310, normal AG AG > 15, lactate > 5

qs.q: Mention the precipitating factors, diagnosis and treatment of HHS.
qs.a:
• Type 2, elderly; severe hyperglycaemia without ketosis, profound dehydration
  • Precipitants: non-compliance, inability to drink, infection, stroke, steroids, diuretics
  • Diagnosis: glucose ≥ 600–700, osmolality > 310 (2Na + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8), no acidosis
  • Treatment: high-volume fluids, electrolytes, insulin

qs.q: Mention the causes of lactic acidosis.
qs.a:
• Tissue hypoxia: cardiogenic / haemorrhagic shock
  • Metformin where contraindicated (renal failure)
  • Main feature: marked hyperventilation

qs.q: Mention the ADA levels of hypoglycaemia.
qs.a:
• Level 1: < 70 but ≥ 54 mg/dl (alert)
  • Level 2: < 54 mg/dl (clinically significant)
  • Level 3: severe – cognitive impairment needing external help

qs.q: Mention Whipple's triad.
qs.a: • (1) Symptoms of hypoglycaemia (2) low plasma glucose (3) relief after fast-acting carbohydrate

qs.q: Mention the symptoms of hypoglycaemia.
qs.a:
• Autonomic: sweating, trembling, palpitations, hunger, anxiety
  • Neuroglycopenic: confusion, drowsiness, speech difficulty, poor concentration, incoordination, irritability
  • Non-specific: nausea, tiredness, headache

qs.q: Mention the emergency treatment of hypoglycaemia.
qs.a:
• Conscious (level 1–2): oral fast-acting CHO 10–15 g → recheck after 10–15 min, repeat up to 3 cycles → then long-acting CHO
  • Unconscious (level 3): IV 75 ml 20% or 150 ml 10% dextrose over 15 min, or IM glucagon 1 mg
  • Confused but swallowing: 40% glucose gel between teeth and gums
  • Do not omit insulin; review regimen; SU-induced → admit (may last 48 h)

qs.q: Mention the causes / risk factors of hypoglycaemia in diabetic patients.
qs.a:
• Excess insulin: wrong dose / type, overdose, lipohypertrophy
  • ↑ Insulin sensitivity: exercise, weight loss, ↓ steroids, Addison's
  • ↓ CHO intake: missed meal, gastroparesis, malabsorption, early pregnancy, breast feeding
  • ↓ Gluconeogenesis: alcohol, CKD, liver disease
  • ↓ Awareness: impaired awareness, strict control, old age, sleep

qs.q: Differentiate the Somogyi effect from the dawn phenomenon.
qs.a:
Feature Somogyi effect Dawn phenomenon
Mechanism Rebound hyperglycaemia after nocturnal hypo ↑ Cortisol, GH, epinephrine early morning
2 AM glucose Low High
Management ↓ Evening insulin ↑ Insulin

qs.q: Mention the causes of fasting hypoglycaemia in adults (without diabetes).
qs.a:
• Insulinoma (pancreatic β-cell tumour)
  • Surreptitious insulin / sulfonylureas (most common)
  • Extrapancreatic tumours (IGF-2)

qs.q: Mention the investigations of insulinoma.
qs.a:
• 72-hour fast
  • ↑ Insulin, proinsulin & C-peptide with glucose < 45 mg/dl
  • Exclude factitious: low C-peptide (insulin), SU drug level
  • Localisation: CT, MRI, endoscopic US
  • Treatment: surgical resection; meanwhile diazoxide / somatostatin analogues

qs.q: Mention the differential diagnosis of spontaneous hypoglycaemia by insulin & C-peptide.
qs.a:
Insulin / C-peptide Cause
↓ insulin, ↓ C-peptide Alcohol, drugs, critical illness, Addison's, non-islet tumour
↑ insulin, ↓ C-peptide Exogenous insulin
↑ insulin, ↑ C-peptide Insulinoma, sulfonylureas

qs.q: Mention the causes of reactive (post-prandial) hypoglycaemia.
qs.a:
• After gastric surgery (late dumping, 1–3 h)
  • Occult diabetes (functional, 4–5 h after glucose)
  • Alimentary, non-insulinoma pancreatogenous

qs.q: Mention drugs causing hypoglycaemia in non-diabetics.
qs.a:
• Fluoroquinolones, pentamidine, quinine
  • ACE inhibitors, salicylates, β-blockers, tramadol
  • Alcohol (blocks gluconeogenesis)

qs.q: Mention the normal serum calcium and how to correct it for albumin.
qs.a:
• Normal serum calcium = 9.0–10.5 mg/dL
  • Calcium is carried on albumin, so low albumin lowers total calcium without true hypocalcaemia
  • If albumin < 4.0 g/dL use corrected calcium
  • Corrected Ca = serum Ca + 0.8 × (4 − serum albumin)

qs.q: Mention the primary mediators and organs of calcium regulation.
qs.a:
• Mediators: parathyroid hormone (PTH) and calcitonin (plus active vitamin D)
  • Organs: parathyroids, bone, kidney, and the small bowel (passive role)
  • Calcium stabilises neuronal membranes → significant disturbances always give neurological symptoms
  • Most mild disturbances are asymptomatic (symptoms usually when Ca changes > 2 mg above/below normal)

qs.q: Describe the actions of PTH on calcium and phosphate.
qs.a:
• Bone: stimulates osteoclasts → bone resorption → ↑ serum Ca
  • Kidney: ↑ calcium reabsorption, ↑ phosphate excretion
  • Kidney: activates 1α-hydroxylase → calcidiol (25-OH D) to calcitriol (1,25-(OH)₂D)
  • Gut (via calcitriol): ↑ absorption of Ca and PO₄
  • Net: ↑ calcium, ↓ phosphate

qs.q: Describe the actions of calcitonin.
qs.a:
• Released when Ca > 10.5
  • Bone: inhibits osteoclasts, increases osteoblast activity
  • Kidney: increases excretion of Ca and PO₄
  • Gut: decreases Ca and PO₄ absorption

qs.q: Enumerate the causes of hypercalcaemia.
qs.a:
• Hypercalcaemia = serum Ca > 10.5 mg/dL
  • #1 cause: primary hyperparathyroidism (adenoma, MEN 1 and 2A)
  • Malignancy: PTHrP (e.g. small-cell / squamous lung cancer) or bone demineralisation (metastases, multiple myeloma)
  • Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia
  • Thiazide diuretics
  • Vitamin D toxicity or ↑ 1,25-(OH)₂D from sarcoidosis / granulomatous disease
  • Others: hyperthyroidism, adrenal tumour, acromegaly, vitamin A toxicity, immobilisation

qs.q: How do thiazides and granulomatous diseases cause hypercalcaemia?
qs.a:
• Thiazides: act on the early distal convoluted tubule (NaCl channels) → ↑ calcium reabsorption into the interstitium
  • Effect persists for about 2–3 months after stopping → follow up the patient
  • Granulomas (sarcoidosis): non-ceasing granulomas secrete active vitamin D (calcitriol)

qs.q: Enumerate the causes of hypocalcaemia.
qs.a:
• Hypocalcaemia = serum Ca < 9.0 mg/dL
  • #1 cause: hypoparathyroidism
  • Hypovitaminosis D (malnutrition)
  • Malabsorption (coeliac disease, Crohn's, intestinal failure)
  • Drugs: loop diuretics (↑ Ca and Mg excretion at thick ascending limb), bisphosphonates (inhibit osteoclasts), phenytoin, phenobarbital (cytochrome P450 → ↓ vitamin D)
  • Also: renal failure, hypomagnesaemia, hungry bone syndrome

qs.q: Mention the clinical picture of hypercalcaemia ("stones, bones, groans, psychic moans").
qs.a:
• Stones (kidney): nephrolithiasis, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (polyuria), nephrocalcinosis
  • Bones: osteoporosis, bone pain, osteitis fibrosa cystica – subperiosteal resorption of distal phalanges, brown tumours, "pepper-pot" skull
  • Groans (abdominal): abdominal pain, pancreatitis, constipation, peptic ulcer (↑ HCl)
  • Psychic moans: neuronal hypoactivity – lethargy, malaise, fatigue, depression, confusion, coma
  • Heart: hypertension, short QT, prolonged PR, heart block (first degree)

qs.q: Mention the clinical picture of hypocalcaemia.
qs.a:
• Neuronal hyperactivity: paraesthesias, hyperactive reflexes, muscle spasms, spasticity, tetany, seizures
  • Chvostek's sign: spasm of facial muscles on tapping the facial nerve
  • Trousseau's sign: carpal spasm with BP cuff inflation
  • ECG: QT prolongation

qs.q: Why does alkalosis (e.g. hyperventilation) cause tetany?
qs.a:
• In alkalosis H⁺ is low, so albumin releases H⁺ and binds more calcium
  • → ↓ ionised calcium with normal total calcium
  • → tetany, carpopedal spasm, paraesthesias

qs.q: Describe the approach to an adult with hypercalcaemia.
qs.a:
• Confirm: corrected calcium (albumin) and repeat testing; ionised Ca in some cases
  • Drug history: thiazides (also vitamins)
  • Measure PTH
  • High-normal / high PTH (PTH-dependent) → measure urinary calcium:
  • > 250 mg/24 h or Ca/Cr clearance > 0.02 → primary (or tertiary) hyperparathyroidism
  • < 100 mg/24 h or Ca/Cr < 0.01 → familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (CaSR mutation)
  • Suppressed PTH (< 20 pg/mL, PTH-independent) → measure PTHrP, 25(OH)D, 1,25(OH)₂D:
  • ↑ PTHrP → solid tumour malignancy; ↑ 1,25(OH)₂D → chest X-ray (lymphoma, sarcoid, thymoma); ↑ 25(OH)D → vitamin D toxicity
  • Normal → hyperthyroidism, multiple myeloma, adrenal tumour, acromegaly, vitamin A toxicity, immobilisation (ALP and X-ray for metastases/MM; Bence Jones protein for MM)

qs.q: How do you manage an emergency patient with severe hypercalcaemia (prolonged PR, bradycardia, hypotension)?
qs.a:
• Life-threatening hypercalcaemia with ECG changes, prolonged PR, bradycardia, hypotension
  • Isotonic saline hydration first
  • Calcitonin or steroids are life-saving (calcitonin acts in 4–6 h)
  • Then bisphosphonates for sustained effect; dialysis if refractory or renal failure

qs.q: Case: A 65-year-old woman has raised calcium and PTH, low phosphate, mildly raised ALP, nephrolithiasis, osteopenia, fatigue and depression. What is the diagnosis? Mention its features.
qs.a:
• Diagnosis: primary hyperparathyroidism
  • Excess PTH from the parathyroids → hypercalcaemia with loss of negative feedback
  • Usually an adenoma (cause unknown); genetic factors may be involved (MEN)
  • Incidence rises after age 50; 2–4 times more in women
  • Carcinoma is rare

qs.q: Define secondary hyperparathyroidism and mention its causes.
qs.a:
• ↑ PTH unrelated to intrinsic parathyroid disease – response to chronic low ionised calcium
  • Tissue resistance to vitamin D
  • Hypovitaminosis D, malabsorption or drugs
  • Excessive inorganic phosphate intake (binds Ca → ↓ Ca → ↑ PTH)
  • Pseudohypoparathyroidism (receptor problem)
  • Severe hypomagnesaemia
  • Chronic renal failure (↓ vitamin D activation)

qs.q: Explain the dual effect of magnesium deficiency on PTH.
qs.a:
• Mild / chronic hypomagnesaemia: Mg is needed for PTH synthesis/secretion → ↓ PTH and ↓ Ca (functional hypoparathyroidism)
  • Severe hypomagnesaemia: kidney and bone become resistant to PTH → ↓ Ca → PTH rises (secondary hyperparathyroidism)
  • Mg also acts on the calcium-sensing receptor and ↓ 1α-hydroxylase (less calcitriol)
  • Treatment: replace magnesium (PO and IV) and recheck

qs.q: Define tertiary hyperparathyroidism with an example.
qs.a:
• Excessive autonomous PTH after long-standing secondary hyperparathyroidism, causing hypercalcaemia
  • Some reserve the term for secondary HPT that persists after successful renal transplant
  • Example: CKD → low Ca, low vitamin D → 2ry HPT; after transplant the cause is corrected but PTH stays high

qs.q: Describe familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (FHH).
qs.a:
• Autosomal dominant
  • Reduced function of the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) in parathyroid and kidney
  • Neonates: may show severe hyperparathyroidism
  • Adults: asymptomatic or chronic fatigue, weakness, recurrent pancreatitis
  • Mild Ca rise (< 11), low urine calcium (< 50 mg/24 h)
  • PTH normal or slightly raised; phosphate normal
  • 4% of PHPT have urine Ca < 100 → FHH gene testing is the gold standard

qs.q: What is the difference in vitamin D replacement between a patient with liver disease and one after total parathyroidectomy?
qs.a:
• Liver disease: give the inactive form of vitamin D (kidney can still activate it)
  • Parathyroids totally removed: give the active form (calcitriol) – no PTH to stimulate 1α-hydroxylase

qs.q: Describe the approach to an adult with hypocalcaemia.
qs.a:
• Drug history: loop diuretics, EDTA, calcitonin, chemotherapy
  • Measure PTH
  • Low PTH: likely post-thyroidectomy hypoparathyroidism → also check magnesium (replace PO/IV and recheck)
  • Post-thyroidectomy: treat with calcium and calcitriol + aluminium hydroxide gel to lower phosphate
  • Normal or high PTH: check renal function → high BUN/creatinine = renal failure
  • Normal renal function → vitamin D level: low = vitamin D deficiency (ergocalciferol, cholecalciferol); normal = malabsorption (e.g. coeliac – anti-gliadin, anti-tTG; Ca + gluten-free diet)

qs.q: Why is aluminium hydroxide given with calcitriol after thyroidectomy-induced hypocalcaemia?
qs.a:
• Active vitamin D increases intestinal absorption of both Ca and PO₄
  • Without PTH, phosphate is not excreted → phosphate rises markedly
  • Aluminium hydroxide binds phosphate in the gut to lower it

qs.q: Enumerate the causes of hypoparathyroidism.
qs.a:
• Surgical (thyroidectomy / parathyroidectomy)
  • Idiopathic
  • Genetic and autoantibodies against the parathyroids
  • Functional: chronic hypomagnesaemia
  • Hungry bone syndrome – after treating long starvation, bone takes up calcium; treat with parenteral calcium infusion

qs.q: Describe pseudohypoparathyroidism and pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism.
qs.a:
• Pseudohypoparathyroidism: target tissue resistance to PTH (receptor defect)
  • Biochemistry: hypocalcaemia, hyperphosphataemia, ↑ PTH
  • Phenotype = Albright hereditary osteodystrophy: short stature, short metacarpals and metatarsals, obesity, mild mental retardation
  • Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism: same AHO phenotype but normal biochemistry (normal Ca, PTH) and no PTH resistance

qs.q: Case: A 60-year-old heavy smoker has confusion, polyuria, constipation; Ca 13.4, low phosphate, normal ALP; chest X-ray shows a lung mass. What is the cause of hypercalcaemia?
qs.a:
• Parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP) – humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy
  • Squamous lung cancer secretes PTHrP → PTH-like action: ↑ Ca, ↓ phosphate
  • Intact PTH is suppressed

qs.q: Case: A 46-year-old woman with breast cancer has back pain, vomiting, lytic thoracic spine lesions; Ca 13.1, albumin 3.4, PTH 10 pg/mL. What is the mechanism of her hypercalcaemia?
qs.a:
• Key answer: production of PTHrP by tumour cells
  • Suppressed PTH → PTH-independent; breast cancer commonly secretes PTHrP
  • Lytic metastases also release calcium by direct bone resorption
  • Corrected Ca = 13.1 + 0.8 × (4 − 3.4) ≈ 13.6 mg/dL

qs.q: Case: A man ascends rapidly to 10,000 feet and develops dyspnoea, tachypnoea, paraesthesias and carpopedal spasm. What happens to his calcium?
qs.a:
• Hyperventilation → respiratory alkalosis
  • Increased calcium bound to albumin → ↓ ionised calcium (total Ca unchanged)
  • Low ionised Ca → tetany / carpopedal spasm

qs.q: Case: A 56-year-old smoker has calcium 11.2 (10.9 a year ago), albumin 4.0, normal creatinine. What is the best next step?
qs.a:
• Measure serum PTH – the first step after confirming true hypercalcaemia
  • High/normal PTH → PTH-dependent (primary HPT, FHH); suppressed PTH → look for PTHrP, vitamin D, malignancy

qs.q: Case: A healthy 39-year-old woman has perioral tingling and cramps; Ca 6.5, phosphate 5.8, albumin 3.8, normal renal function. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a:
• Primary hypoparathyroidism
  • Low calcium + high phosphate with normal renal function → lack of PTH (PTH would excrete phosphate)
  • Renal failure excluded by normal creatinine; vitamin D deficiency would give low phosphate

qs.q: Case: A 60-year-old man with stage 3 CKD (thyroidectomy 5 years ago) has low calcium, high phosphate and high PTH. What is the cause?
qs.a:
• Renal failure → secondary hyperparathyroidism
  • CKD: ↓ phosphate excretion and ↓ calcitriol → ↓ Ca → ↑ PTH
  • Post-thyroidectomy hypoparathyroidism would give low PTH

qs.q: Case: A 56-year-old woman with CKD has Ca 10.8, PTH 100 pg/mL, phosphate 3.0, kidney stones and osteoporosis. What is the cause of hypercalcaemia?
qs.a:
• Primary hyperparathyroidism
  • High calcium with high PTH and normal phosphate; CKD alone would give low/normal calcium and high phosphate
  • Stones and osteoporosis support PHPT
